veracity.statement: If the dire current state of the New Zealand economy is all someone else’s fault, why is it that the New Zealand economy shrunk by almost 1 percent at a time when other economies around the world that have been hit harder by Donald Trump’s tariffs—many of whom had a higher rate of inflation at the peak of the global pandemic—have been growing faster than New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Asserts NZ GDP shrank by almost 1% while other, harder-hit economies grew faster — a contested, load-bearing comparative claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP for the quarter referenced (true if the economy contracted by ~1%, false if materially different), plus OECD/comparable-economy GDP over the same period for the claim that harder-tariff-hit economies grew faster than NZ.

veracity.statement: In quarter 4 last year, this economy was growing. In quarter 1 this year economic growth was increasing. In quarter 2, our economy—as a small economy, a trading economy—got smashed around by uncertainty associated with tariffs. It’s now growing again in quarter 3; the growth in quarter 4 will step up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts positive growth in the two named past quarters — the crux of the disputed recovery narrative.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP for Q4 of last year and Q1 of this year: true if both quarters recorded positive growth as stated, false if either was flat or negative. (The Q3/Q4 claims are predictions and are excluded.)

veracity.statement: You cannot increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation, drive up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and raise unemployment.
veracity.explanation: The '84 percent' spending-increase figure is specific, contested and load-bearing to the causal argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Budget core Crown expenditure figures for the previous government's term: true if total government spending rose by ~84% over that period, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: You put the country into the biggest recession in 35 years, you created the longest COVID hangover of any in the Western world, you actually made sure that you tripled the debt, for goodness’ sake, and we now have a $10 billion interest bill.
veracity.explanation: Bundles several checkable claims; 'longest COVID hangover of any in the Western world' is the most likely to be hyperbolic, while the debt figures are closer to accurate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ recession depth vs prior recessions (true if the recent contraction is the deepest in ~35 years), OECD recovery timing for the 'longest COVID hangover in the Western world' claim, and Treasury figures on net core Crown debt roughly tripling and annual finance costs reaching ~$10 billion.

veracity.statement: Why are there 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs in this country since he took office, if not because of his Government’s billions of dollars of cuts to investment?
veracity.explanation: Two specific, contested labour-market figures that carry the argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey: change in youth unemployment and total employment since the current PM took office (late 2023); true if youth unemployment rose ~10,000 and jobs fell ~36,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the last administration, with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment, the Labour-Greens Government drove a 50 percent increase and put 60,000 more people on jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: Specific, contested figures on jobseeker numbers and the unemployment rate under the previous government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD jobseeker-support recipient numbers over the previous government's term: true if the count rose ~50% (about 60,000 more) while the unemployment rate sat at 3.2–3.5%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that is—I’ll tell you what the landlord cut did create: rents have gone down $5 a week, instead of up $180 a week.
veracity.explanation: Claims rents fell $5/week rather than rising $180/week — a specific, contested figure at odds with general rent trends.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MBIE rental price data since the policy: true if average rents fell about $5 a week (versus a counterfactual rise of ~$180), false if rents rose. The $180 counterfactual is a modelled comparison and the harder part to verify.

veracity.statement: Growing and strengthening the education workforce is exactly what this Government is doing, and, as I’ve already told the member on numerous occasions, the schooling teacher workforce grew by 2.5 percent in 2024, delivering 864 new teachers—the largest year-on-year increase since records began in 2009.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific, checkable facts: 2.5% workforce growth in 2024, 864 new teachers, and that this is the largest annual increase since 2009. Contested (the education workforce is a live political dispute) and load-bearing to her claim the Government is strengthening the workforce.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education teacher workforce / staffing data for the 2024 school year and the year-on-year series back to 2009; true if the 2024 increase is ~2.5% / ~864 FTE and is the largest since 2009, false if materially different or not the record.

veracity.statement: On provisional figures for 2025, there’s been a 30 percent increase in domestic students enrolling in initial teacher education for the first time.
veracity.explanation: A specific figure — a 30% rise in first-time domestic enrolments into initial teacher education on provisional 2025 data. Non-obvious, contested, and central to the 'more people than ever' claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Provisional 2025 initial teacher education enrolment figures for first-time domestic students versus the prior year (Ministry of Education / TEC data); true if ~30% increase, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Our Government has turned around the delivery of school property, we’ve halved the cost of building new classrooms, and children deserve to live in safe, warm, dry classrooms and we’re delivering just that.
veracity.explanation: The load-bearing claim is that the cost of building new classrooms has been halved — a specific, contested quantitative comparison the opposition would dispute.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education figures on average cost per new classroom before and after the policy change; true if the average build cost roughly halved, false if the reduction is materially smaller or absent.

veracity.statement: This survey follows an identical survey in 2022, and most critically, it shows that in nearly every single measure for nearly every type of person, attitudes to attendance are improving.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific finding of the ERO 'Back to class' report — that attitudes to attendance improved across nearly every measure versus the 2022 survey. 'Nearly every single measure for nearly every type of person' is a strong, checkable characterisation of the report.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ERO report 'Back to class: How are attitudes to attendance changing?' compared with its 2022 predecessor; true if attitudes improved across nearly all measured dimensions, false if improvement is mixed or absent on many measures.

focus.statement: How can she claim that this change will incentivise young people when her Government has increased university fees, increased youth unemployment, cut the Apprenticeship Boost, and made life even harder for working Kiwi families struggling with the cost of living crisis?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny naming specific policies and outcomes — university fees, youth unemployment, the Apprenticeship Boost — rather than content-free party-bashing. On-policy accountability, which scores high even though it targets the government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because what we don’t want to see is the welfare dependency that we saw blow out in the six years of the previous Government; as I said, a 47 percent increase in the length of time a young person under 25 would go on to spend on welfare.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point (welfare dependency, a named figure) carried substantially on party framing ('the six years of the previous Government'). A real policy claim wrapped in tribal attribution.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m advised that around 4,300 fewer 18- and 19-year-olds will be eligible for the jobseeker support as a result of the parental assistance test, which has two parts: the parental income test and the parental support gap test.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure directly — the estimated number affected and the mechanism (the two parts of the parental assistance test). Squarely on the policy at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I believe the most important number in New Zealand today is the number of children who go to school, because the amount of education that we pass from one generation to another more powerfully defines our future than anything else we can do on this day.
focus.explanation: Addresses the policy topic before the House — school attendance and its importance — rather than the opposing party. On-policy, no tribal content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Critically, 82 percent of students from poorer families said that going to school is important for their future.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the education/attendance policy, citing a survey finding rather than attacking the other party. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the farrowing-crate policy — the evidence base and the mechanism (piglet mortality) — directly on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How does he justify extending the use of cruel farrowing crates indefinitely when every animal welfare organisation in New Zealand, including the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee [NAWAC], and 73 percent of New Zealanders oppose the use of farrowing crates because of worse welfare outcomes for mother pigs and piglets?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy (extending farrowing crates), naming specific opponents and a figure. This is the job of an opposition MP — high focus.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is he aware that it is a profound behavioural need of mother pigs to build a nest 24 hours before giving birth, and if they are caged it is deeply distressing for them, they will literally paw the ground, often bloodying their snouts, trying to build a nest?
focus.explanation: Directly engages the animal-welfare substance of the policy — the nesting-behaviour harm — rather than attacking a person or party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
focus.explanation: Engages the infrastructure-investment substance with named figures and timeframes — on-policy, defending the Government's programme.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We built more social housing in our last 23 months than that Government did in its last three years.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy output (social housing built) and a comparison — accountability for a commitment, on-policy rather than tribal.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Isn’t the point that the damage is done, with 20,000 jobs gone after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy decision (pausing infrastructure builds) tied to a specific outcome (job losses). On-policy accountability.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny of the infrastructure pipeline, naming specific outcome figures for the construction sector.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If the economy is recovering, then why are 200 New Zealanders leaving every day, including thousands of builders, heading to Australia instead of staying here to build in New Zealand?
focus.explanation: Names a specific outcome (net departures to Australia) linked to the economic/infrastructure policy argument — on-policy, though wrapped in some framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Critically, 82 percent of students from poorer families said that going to school is important for their future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — 82% of students from poorer families rated school as important to their future — attributable to the ERO attendance survey being discussed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education Review Office 2025 attendance/engagement survey figure for the share of students from lower-income families who said going to school is important for their future; true if ~82%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a review of 22 relevant scientific articles shows a 14% higher piglet mortality risk without post-farrowing confinement. A specific, contested, load-bearing quantitative claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The review/meta-analysis of 22 studies the Minister relied on; true if it reports ~14% higher piglet mortality without sow confinement, false if it reports no such difference or a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: With the other changes I’m proposing, an independent economic analysis estimated the cost of transition at more than $675,000 for the average indoor pig farm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an independent economic analysis put the transition cost above $675,000 for the average indoor pig farm — a specific, checkable figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The independent economic/regulatory impact analysis of the farrowing-crate transition; true if it estimates >$675,000 for the average indoor pig farm, false if materially lower or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: How does he justify extending the use of cruel farrowing crates indefinitely when every animal welfare organisation in New Zealand, including the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee [NAWAC], and 73 percent of New Zealanders oppose the use of farrowing crates because of worse welfare outcomes for mother pigs and piglets?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every NZ animal welfare organisation including NAWAC, and 73% of New Zealanders, oppose farrowing crates. Two checkable factual claims — the organisational positions and the polling figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public NAWAC/SPCA positions on farrowing crates and any published poll on public opposition; true if a poll shows ~73% opposition and the named bodies oppose, false if the poll figure or organisational positions differ materially.

veracity.statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a record $61.8bn budgeted over four years and a comparison with $50.6bn invested by the previous Government 2019–2023. Specific, contested, load-bearing figures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget/Crown infrastructure investment figures for the current four-year plan and the 2019–2023 period; true if ~$61.8bn budgeted and ~$50.6bn prior, false if materially different or not like-for-like.

veracity.statement: We built more social housing in our last 23 months than that Government did in its last three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current Government built more social housing in 23 months than the previous Government in its last three years — a contested comparative claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD/Kāinga Ora social-housing completion figures for the current Government's first 23 months versus the previous Government's final three years; true if the current figure exceeds the prior, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Isn’t the point that the damage is done, with 20,000 jobs gone after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds?
veracity.explanation: Asserts 20,000 jobs were lost following the Government's decision to pause infrastructure builds — a specific, contested figure with an attributed cause.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Construction-sector employment change data (Stats NZ/MBIE) over the relevant period; true if ~20,000 jobs lost coinciding with the paused builds, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
veracity.explanation: Asserts 761 construction employers closed in the last year and two construction firms are liquidated every day. Specific, checkable figures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company liquidation/insolvency records for the construction sector over the last year; true if ~761 employers closed and ~2 liquidations per day, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: If the economy is recovering, then why are 200 New Zealanders leaving every day, including thousands of builders, heading to Australia instead of staying here to build in New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Asserts about 200 New Zealanders leave for Australia every day, including thousands of builders. A specific migration figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ net migration data on NZ citizen departures to Australia for the period; true if the net outflow is ~200/day, false if materially different.

focus.statement: There are not enough jobs in this country for the beneficiaries that this Government is intent on punching down upon.
focus.explanation: Strip the rhetoric ("punching down upon") and a genuine policy point remains: the labour market cannot absorb beneficiaries pushed off support. Squarely engages the jobs-versus-sanctions substance of the measure at issue, so high Focus even though it is not precise.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, again, some of those basic facts: there are 36,000 fewer jobs and there are 10,000 more unemployed young people in the two years since this Government came to office and implemented their economic policies of firing up the shredder and cutting billions of dollars of investment in our economy and in our people.
focus.explanation: Names specific outcomes (job losses, youth unemployment) and holds the Government to account for the effect of its economic policy. This is legitimate scrutiny of a named record, not content-free party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have scaled back infrastructure in hospitals, resulting in 15,000 fewer construction sector jobs.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (scaled-back hospital infrastructure) and a specific outcome (15,000 fewer construction jobs). Accountability for a named commitment and its result — the job of an opposition MP.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Greens have spent the last 18 months outlining our solutions and our clear policies, which would see free early childhood education, free dentistry, and free GPs.
focus.explanation: Engages policy substance directly, naming specific measures (free ECE, dentistry, GPs) offered as an alternative. Squarely about the policy rather than about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The jeering from the other side of the House during the last speaker’s speech is exactly why that side of the House and the Government is so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders, because you can jeer and laugh at the teenagers who need jobs, you can jeer and laugh at the fact that we are doing nothing for climate change in this House because of that Government, and you can jeer and laugh at the fact that this economy is tanking because of their inaction, but they won’t think that’s funny, because they are so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: Touches on policy areas (jobs, climate, the economy) but the weight is party framing — the repeated charge that the other side is "disconnected from everyday New Zealanders." A real policy point wrapped heavily in tribal framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government isn’t on the side of ordinary New Zealanders; they’re on the side of tobacco companies, of property speculators, of the oil and gas industry.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the party's alleged allegiances (tobacco, property speculators, oil and gas) with no specific policy, measure or figure named. Content-free characterisation of the other side — the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But, again, some of those basic facts: there are 36,000 fewer jobs and there are 10,000 more unemployed young people in the two years since this Government came to office and implemented their economic policies of firing up the shredder and cutting billions of dollars of investment in our economy and in our people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific figures: 36,000 fewer jobs and 10,000 more unemployed young people over the two years since late 2023. Contested and load-bearing to the whole argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / employment counts for the quarter around October 2025 against two years earlier (late 2023): true if total employment fell by roughly 36,000 and the number of unemployed 15–24-year-olds rose by roughly 10,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: They have scaled back infrastructure in hospitals, resulting in 15,000 fewer construction sector jobs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a figure (15,000 fewer construction-sector jobs) and attributes it causally to reduced hospital infrastructure spending. A specific, contested quantity.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction-sector employment (HLFS industry breakdown / filled jobs) comparing the recent quarter to the prior peak: true if construction employment fell by roughly 15,000, false if materially different; the causal link to hospital-infrastructure cuts is a separate, weaker claim.

veracity.statement: In his own words, he is “wealthy and sorted”.
veracity.explanation: Relays a direct quote attributed to the Prime Minister, that he described himself as "wealthy and sorted." A checkable attribution the other side would dispute.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record (interviews, media reports) of Christopher Luxon's own statements: true if he used the words "wealthy and sorted" or self-described in those terms, false if no such statement exists.

veracity.statement: It’s quite interesting to see, today, the Minister of Finance saying, “I didn’t take any credit for it”, despite, in the first question before that, saying the Government takes credit for it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Minister of Finance contradicted herself in the same question time — declining credit for falling interest rates after earlier claiming the Government takes credit. A specific, checkable claim about today's proceedings.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of question time on 2025-10-08: true if the Minister of Finance both said she took no credit for falling interest rates and, in an earlier question, said the Government takes credit; false if the record does not show that contrast.

focus.statement: It’s the Greens—it’s the sanctimonious “tofu wouldn’t melt in your mouth” Greens—who are the ones who are driving the division and acrimony within our body politic, aided and abetted by Labour.
focus.explanation: Content-free party tribalism: it names no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome, only characterises the Greens and Labour as the source of aggression. No individual is insulted, so it is the classic policy-versus-party case Focus exists to catch. There is a bill on intimidation before the House, so a policy question is genuinely available to engage — this statement does not engage it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My encouragement to all parties across the House is to just think twice about the approach that is taken around intimidation and, frankly, to support this legislation that we have before the House to ensure that no New Zealander has to suffer people intimidating them in their private home—in their castle—and to do the right thing by that.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual measure before the House — the intimidation legislation — and its stated purpose (protecting people from being intimidated in their homes), directing the argument at the policy rather than at the other parties.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s interesting that we’ve seen Duncan Webb saying, “Well, no, actually, we’re going to stick to our guns. We think people should protest outside MPs’ houses.” and Mr Hipkins has said that they shouldn’t, but they both voted against the bill that we’ve got in the House that deals with it.
veracity.explanation: The load-bearing checkable assertion is that Duncan Webb and Chris Hipkins both voted against the government bill dealing with protest/intimidation outside MPs' homes. Contested and central to Goldsmith's hypocrisy charge against Labour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record in Hansard for the relevant reading of the bill dealing with protests/intimidation outside MPs' homes; true if both Webb and Hipkins (or Labour on their behalf) are recorded voting against it, false if they voted for it or the vote does not exist.

veracity.statement: There have been 14 inquiries in the last 18 months into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori, and not a single allegation was upheld.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count (14 inquiries in 18 months) into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori, and that none upheld any allegation. This is the thesis of the speech and squarely contested.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A tally of formal inquiries/investigations into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori between ~April 2024 and October 2025 and their published findings; true if the count is about 14 and none upheld an allegation, false if the count is materially different or any inquiry upheld an allegation.

veracity.statement: Stats NZ: claims of misuse of census data—claims proven to be false, and the CEO of Stats NZ resigned over this manner.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that claims of census-data misuse were proven false, and that the Stats NZ chief executive resigned over the matter. Both are checkable against the record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public findings on the Stats NZ census/data-misuse allegations and the resignation announcement of the Government Statistician/Stats NZ CEO; true if an inquiry cleared the misuse claims and the CEO resigned in connection with it, false if the claims were substantiated or no such resignation occurred.

veracity.statement: The latest Electoral Commission figures show that, since April 2023, almost 31,000 voters have switched to the Māori roll, and more than 25,000 first-time voters have gone for the Māori electoral option.
veracity.explanation: A sourced quantitative claim (Electoral Commission figures) with two specific numbers: ~31,000 roll switches since April 2023 and >25,000 first-time voters choosing the Māori roll.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission published statistics on Māori roll changes since April 2023; true if switches to the Māori roll are about 31,000 and first-time Māori-roll enrolments exceed 25,000, false if the figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: When faced with the Treaty principles bill, over 100,000 people hikoi-ed and over 300,000 submissions were made—over 90 percent in opposition.
veracity.explanation: Three quantitative claims about the response to the Treaty Principles Bill: over 100,000 people on the hīkoi, over 300,000 submissions, and over 90 percent of them opposed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reported hīkoi participation figures, and the select committee's tally of submissions and their stance on the Treaty Principles Bill; true if submissions exceeded 300,000 with ~90%+ opposed and hīkoi participation exceeded 100,000, false if any of these figures is materially lower.

veracity.statement: For years, I sat on the board of New Zealand Apples and Pears, and under the Labour Government the apple industry could never meet the $1 billion export mark.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand apple (apples and pears) export earnings never reached $1 billion during the Labour government's term (2017-2023). A contested, load-bearing comparison she builds her growth argument on.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Apples and Pears / Stats NZ / MPI export figures for the apple and pear industry across 2017-2023; true if annual apple/pear export value stayed below $1 billion in every Labour-government year, false if it reached or exceeded $1 billion in any of those years.

veracity.statement: In fact, our horticulture exports have hit record highs: $8.5 billion this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure ($8.5 billion) for New Zealand horticulture exports for the current year, described as a record high. Specific, non-obvious, and load-bearing to the growth claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries / Stats NZ horticulture export value for the year referenced; true if horticulture exports are ~$8.5 billion and a record, false if materially different or not a record.

veracity.statement: Around 360,000 Kiwis are employed in our food and fibre sector, about 15 percent of the total workforce.
veracity.explanation: Two specific quantitative claims: about 360,000 people employed in the food and fibre sector, and that this is about 15 percent of the total workforce.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI food and fibre sector employment figures and Stats NZ total employed workforce; true if food and fibre employment is ~360,000 and that share is ~15% of the workforce, false if either figure is materially off (e.g. 360,000 is closer to 12-13% of a ~2.9m workforce).

veracity.statement: That COVID hangover was caused by the previous Labour Government spending $66 billion of taxpayer money and raking up debt, over twice, to 44 percent of gross domestic product.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the previous Labour Government spent $66 billion of taxpayer money in its COVID response and roughly doubled debt to 44 percent of GDP. A contested, load-bearing figure claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / Budget records on the COVID Response and Recovery Fund and net core Crown debt as a share of GDP under the 2017-2023 Labour government; true if COVID spending was ~$66bn and debt rose to ~44% of GDP, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: That was the largest debt-fuelled spending binge in the developed world, according to the IMF.
veracity.explanation: Relays an IMF assessment that New Zealand's pandemic fiscal stimulus was the largest in the developed world. The claim is attributed to the IMF, so the check is on whether the IMF actually ranks NZ's stimulus highest.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: IMF Fiscal Monitor tables ranking discretionary fiscal response to COVID as a share of GDP across developed economies; true if NZ is the largest, false if other developed countries exceeded it.

veracity.statement: Light rail to nowhere; the Skypath, $50 million of money spent and nothing delivered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $50 million was spent on the Skypath project with nothing delivered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public records of expenditure on the Auckland Harbour Bridge SkyPath / cycling-crossing project and its delivery status; true if ~$50m was spent and the project was cancelled with nothing built, false if materially less spent or something delivered.

veracity.statement: Not only has the party dipped into the 20s but Christopher Luxon is not the preferred Prime Minister in this country.
veracity.explanation: Relays results attributed to the pollster Curia: that National's party vote is in the 20s and that Luxon is not the preferred Prime Minister. The check is on those poll figures.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The latest Curia poll (early October 2025) party vote for National and preferred-Prime-Minister ranking; true if National polls in the 20s and Luxon is not top of the preferred-PM question, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: The gentailer's share prices soared.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that gentailer share prices rose sharply on the day the government announced its energy reforms, used to argue the reforms favoured incumbents rather than households.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Share price movements of NZX-listed gentailers (e.g. Meridian, Contact, Mercury, Genesis) on the trading day of the energy reform announcement in early October 2025; true if prices rose notably, false if flat or fell.

focus.statement: Light rail to nowhere; the Skypath, $50 million of money spent and nothing delivered.
focus.explanation: Names specific infrastructure policies (light rail, the Skypath) and a specific outcome ($50m spent, nothing delivered). This is scrutiny of named commitments, which is on-policy accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Under the fast-track regime, we have just consented a new project at the Port of Auckland to improve the extension of the Fergusson north berth.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific policy (the fast-track consenting regime) and a specific named project. Squarely on-policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The National Party has dipped into the 20s, that psychological number that has every backbencher shaking in their boots, watching their majority disappear.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's polling and political standing, with no policy content at all. This is the content-free party-versus-party case Focus exists to catch; nobody is personally insulted, so it stays eligible and scores 0.0.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There was an opportunity to do something to relieve New Zealand businesses and households of the burden of a broken energy system, and they fumbled it.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about the government's energy reforms and the state of the energy market, but carried substantially by party framing ('they fumbled it').
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In a few months, this Government—and it's set out in the Government's quarter four plan—will introduce a new resource management system with two focused laws: a natural environment Act which sets clear environmental rules suited to each region, so we stop arguing over trivia and focus on the real environmental risks that we need to manage.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance of the resource management reform, naming the planned legislation and the mechanism it uses. Wholly on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the last quarter alone, GDP fell 0.9 percent, and whilst Christopher Luxon, like that member, likes to talk about rights and responsibilities, you’ll never hear him—or her—take responsibility for the damage they are doing to our economy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantitative fact: that New Zealand GDP fell 0.9 percent in the most recent quarter. Contested and load-bearing to the whole speech; the surrounding material is rhetoric that is not a checkable fact.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP percentage change for the quarter referenced (mid-2025); true if GDP fell approximately 0.9% that quarter, false if it rose or fell by a materially different amount.

veracity.statement: Australia is up 0.6 percent, the United Kingdom is up 0.3 percent, the United States is up 0.8 percent, Japan is up 0.5 percent, and China is up 1.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: A set of specific comparative growth figures attributed to five named economies for the comparable period. Non-obvious figures a reader could not confirm from memory, used to support the claim that comparator economies are outperforming New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official quarterly real GDP growth for Australia, the UK, the US, Japan and China for the quarter matching the New Zealand figure cited; true if each matches within rounding, false if any is materially different.

veracity.statement: Our first Māori MP was elected in 1867—James Carroll.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that James Carroll was New Zealand's first Māori MP and that he was elected in 1867. A specific, non-obvious historical date-and-attribution claim (the Māori Representation Act was 1867 and the first Māori MPs were elected in 1868, and Carroll was not among the first four).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical parliamentary record of New Zealand's first Māori MPs and their election dates; true if James Carroll was the first Māori MP and was elected in 1867, false if the first Māori MPs were others elected in 1868 or if Carroll entered later.

veracity.statement: There was also Peter Buck; Āpirana Ngata; Māui Pōmare; Iriaka Matiu Rātana, the first female Māori MP who served for 20 years; and Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan, the first female Minister, who, at the time she left Parliament, was the longest-serving female MP.
veracity.explanation: Contains specific first/longest attributions, chiefly that Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan was 'the first female Minister'. This appears to conflate her (first Māori woman Cabinet minister) with New Zealand's first woman Cabinet minister, Mabel Howard. Also asserts Iriaka Rātana as first female Māori MP serving 20 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical record of New Zealand's first woman Cabinet minister and first Māori woman MP; the 'first female Minister' claim is true if Tirikatene-Sullivan was NZ's first woman minister, false if that was Mabel Howard (1947) and Tirikatene-Sullivan was instead first Māori woman minister.

veracity.statement: Then, over the last days, the party that Benjamin Doyle represented has been associated with an attack on a Minister of the Crown’s home.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a recent factual event — an attack on a Minister of the Crown's home — and links it to the party the departing member represented. Contested (she herself notes the connection is disputed) and load-bearing to her argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: News and police reports from late September / early October 2025 on whether a Minister of the Crown's home was attacked, and on any established link between that attack and the named party; true if such an attack occurred and was connected to the party, false if no such attack occurred or no connection is established.

focus.statement: He promised that he would actually bring prices down, and that’s what New Zealanders are not seeing right now in this cost of living crisis.
focus.explanation: Holds the government to a named commitment (bringing prices/cost of living down) against the current outcome. Legitimate policy scrutiny, which scores high on Focus even when aimed at the PM's record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, there are 20,000 fewer construction jobs in New Zealander under his watch.
focus.explanation: Names a specific sector and a specific figure for job losses — accountability for an economic outcome, squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are 36,000 fewer people employed in New Zealand right now, over the past two years, under the watch of Christopher Luxon.
focus.explanation: A specific figure for total employment change under the government — economic accountability, on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Every single day, 200 New Zealanders leave our country.
focus.explanation: Cites an emigration figure as an outcome under the government — on the record of population/economic policy, not party abuse.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Smithfield meat works in Timaru shut its doors after 138 years of operating in New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Names a specific plant closure and job loss as evidence in the jobs debate — concrete, on-policy scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Believe it or not, Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering has been removed at a time when talking about infrastructure, when those people opposite are talking about wanting to drive growth, they have cut the Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific policy decision (removing Apprenticeship Boost eligibility for civil engineering) against the government's stated infrastructure/growth aims — on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government has no vision.
focus.explanation: A content-free judgement of the other side with no policy, mechanism, figure or outcome named — tribalism Civility passes because no individual is insulted. This is the gap Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A 2016 report confirmed the scheme contributes more than $100 million annually to the regional GDP and supports over 1,300 full-time job equivalents.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the water-storage policy with a mechanism, a source and quantified economic effects — squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I say to 18- and 19-year-olds in Northland that there are opportunities out there, opportunities that are better than being on welfare.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy question at issue (regional jobs vs welfare for young people) with a substantive claim about opportunities from the reservoir projects, rather than attacking the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our economy hasn’t grown; it’s gone backwards.
focus.explanation: A claim about the economic outcome under the government — on the policy record, not a personal jibe.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: She even promised before the election that National will take action to get food prices under control once more.
focus.explanation: Holds a named minister to a named pre-election commitment on food prices — specific policy accountability, on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, there are 20,000 fewer construction jobs in New Zealander under his watch.
veracity.explanation: Asserts construction employment fell by 20,000 over two years; a specific, contested, load-bearing figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction-sector employment level ~Oct 2023 vs ~Oct 2025; true if the net fall is ~20,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: There are 36,000 fewer people employed in New Zealand right now, over the past two years, under the watch of Christopher Luxon.
veracity.explanation: Asserts total employment is 36,000 lower over two years; a specific contested figure sensitive to series and dates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey total employment ~Oct 2023 vs ~Oct 2025; true if a net fall of ~36,000, false if materially different (including if employment rose).

veracity.statement: Every single day, 200 New Zealanders leave our country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 200 New Zealanders leave the country daily; checkable but sensitive to gross departures vs net loss.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration data on NZ-citizen departures and/or net loss; true if ~200/day (~73,000/year) on the relevant measure, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Smithfield meat works in Timaru shut its doors after 138 years of operating in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Smithfield Timaru works closed after 138 years; a specific factual and date claim checkable against records.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company/news records for the Smithfield (Alliance Group) Timaru plant closure and founding date; true if it closed after ~138 years, false if the duration is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: Believe it or not, Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering has been removed at a time when talking about infrastructure, when those people opposite are talking about wanting to drive growth, they have cut the Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering.
veracity.explanation: Asserts civil engineering was cut from Apprenticeship Boost; a specific, checkable, contested policy claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC/government announcements on Apprenticeship Boost eligibility; true if civil engineering apprenticeships were removed from the scheme, false if they remain eligible.

veracity.statement: A 2016 report confirmed the scheme contributes more than $100 million annually to the regional GDP and supports over 1,300 full-time job equivalents.
veracity.explanation: Attributes specific GDP and jobs figures to a specific 2016 report; a checkable, non-obvious quantitative claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The named 2016 report on the Kerikeri irrigation scheme; true if it states a regional GDP contribution above $100m/year and over 1,300 FTE, false if the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Our economy hasn’t grown; it’s gone backwards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the economy shrank rather than grew; contested and load-bearing, sensitive to aggregate vs per-capita GDP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ GDP and GDP-per-capita growth over the relevant period; true if the economy contracted (or per-capita GDP fell), false if it grew on the stated measure.

veracity.statement: She even promised before the election that National will take action to get food prices under control once more.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Nicola Willis promised pre-election to act on food prices; a checkable attribution of a specific commitment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Pre-2023-election National/Willis statements on grocery/food prices; true if Willis committed to bringing food prices under control, false if no such promise is on record.

focus.statement: This bill establishes the Auckland Future Fund, a mechanism to secure growth and protect long-term capital that can be used to support Auckland’s most important needs.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance of the measure before the House — what the fund is and what it does. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Labour supports this bill and its provision of statutory protection for the Auckland Future Fund.
focus.explanation: States a position on the measure before the House and names its key provision. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The thing is, the promises that this Government made to Aucklanders haven’t been achieved.
focus.explanation: A general charge that the Government's promises are unmet, with no specific policy, measure or outcome named. Legitimate scrutiny in kind, but the weight is party framing rather than a named commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In December 2024, the board sold Auckland Council’s shares in Auckland International Airport Limited at $8.08 per share.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific sale price and date for the council's disposal of its Auckland Airport shareholding — a specific, non-obvious, load-bearing figure underpinning his case that the fund performs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Future Fund records or NZX disclosure of the December 2024 sale of the council's Auckland International Airport Limited shareholding; true if sold at ~$8.08/share, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Also, between December 2024 and June 2025, the fund delivered a return of 4.06 percent, a strong result in a volatile global market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific fund return figure over a stated period. Contested and load-bearing to the claim the fund is delivering.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Future Fund reported return for December 2024–June 2025; true if ~4.06%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the 2024-25 financial year, the fund generated $38.4 million in distribution income compared to just $10.2 million in dividends that would have come from retaining the airport shares.
veracity.explanation: A specific comparison of distribution income against a counterfactual dividend stream — the load-bearing figure for the argument that the fund outperforms holding the shares.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Future Fund 2024-25 financial statements for distribution income, and the dividends the retained Auckland Airport shares would have paid over the year; true if ~$38.4m vs ~$10.2m, false if materially different.

focus.statement: Your investment in transport has taken us backwards.
focus.explanation: Engages a named policy area (the Government's transport investment) and asserts an outcome. This is legitimate scrutiny of a government record, which the Focus rubric scores high; the absence of a figure is Specificity's concern, not Focus's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It's time for them to step up and answer the call of our city, of business leaders, of community leaders, and this is a great example of something that can be achieved.
focus.explanation: A real point about the bill (it holds it up as 'a great example of something that can be achieved') wrapped in party-directed exhortation to 'step up'. The policy reference is present but the weight is on framing the other side's inaction.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It requires the council to ensure that the fund is governed and managed with the intent of maintaining or increasing its value, and it mandates that investment decisions are made by suitably qualified and formally appointed managers.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill directly — the governance mechanism, the value-maintenance duty, and who is empowered to make investment decisions. Entirely about the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We often see central government imposing rules and unfunded mandates on local authorities, and this bill takes a very different approach.
focus.explanation: Addresses the substantive question of central-versus-local government mandates and situates the bill against it. Some party framing ('this Government' elsewhere) but the content is a policy contrast, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There have been far too many bills going through a curtailed process and it will not only have bad effects in the community but it will waste time in the next Parliament when we could be working constructively.
focus.explanation: Engages the legislative-process question (curtailed select committee scrutiny) and its consequences. On-policy critique of how legislation is handled rather than party-directed abuse.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: People are paying more for public transport in our city than they ever have in the last two decades.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland public transport fares are at a 20-year high — a contested, specific comparison that the argument leans on, not scene-setting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / Auckland Regional Transport published fare schedules over the past twenty years, compared on a like-for-like basis (nominal and inflation-adjusted); true if current fares exceed all prior points in that window, false if fares were higher earlier (e.g. before the 2022-23 half-price fare scheme).

focus.statement: The whole idea of wrapping that fund around with this legislation which we’re talking about at the moment is to say to councils that there is a discipline on you that you cannot simply go and raid the piggy bank; you have to do that in a careful and measured way.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the mechanism of the bill before the House — the spending discipline the legislation imposes on councils. No party framing; it is about what the measure does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It aims to protect intergenerational wealth and secure Auckland's economic future.
focus.explanation: Engages the purpose of the bill before the House — its intent to protect intergenerational wealth and secure Auckland's finances. On-policy, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I would note that of all the big metropolitan councils in the country, their rates increase over the last two years is the smallest.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland Council's rates increase over the last two years is the smallest of any big metropolitan council — a specific, contested comparative claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published average residential/general rates increases for the last two years for the major metropolitan councils (Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, Hamilton, Tauranga, Dunedin), from each council's long-term/annual plans; true if Auckland's is the lowest of that set, false if another big metro council was lower.

veracity.statement: They declared not only their normal dividend but also special dividend of $45 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ports of Auckland declared a special dividend of $45 million (over and above its normal dividend), which went into the Auckland Future Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ports of Auckland / Auckland Council financial disclosures on dividends declared; true if a special dividend of ~$45 million was declared as stated, false if no such special dividend or a materially different figure.

focus.statement: Auckland Council has seen sense that recycling assets and transferring the capital into an arrangement that can earn a better rate of return and, potentially, if they make more courageous decisions, lead to the deployment of that capital into new infrastructure that produces economic growth and makes Auckland a better place to live.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the mechanism of the bill before the House — asset recycling, rate of return, redeployment of capital into infrastructure. On-policy substance, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It's projects like that that have cost half a billion dollars or more, wasting Auckland ratepayers’ money and that have led to the situation where Auckland’s run out of money for infrastructure.
focus.explanation: Engages council financial management — a named waste (the food-scraps collection scheme) and its consequence for infrastructure funding. On-policy scrutiny, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That must sound like Armageddon to the Green Party.
focus.explanation: Content-free party framing about how the Greens would react. No individual is insulted, so Civility passes it cleanly; no policy, figure or outcome is named. This is the tribalism gap Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: None of those homes can be delivered without the enabling infrastructure, such as a four-lane bypass around the little town of Kumeū, which, if that bypass goes in, will be able to grow and flourish just like other towns are when bypasses go in.
focus.explanation: Names a specific infrastructure measure (a four-lane Kumeū bypass) and ties it to a policy outcome (housing delivery, growth). Fully on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It's projects like that that have cost half a billion dollars or more, wasting Auckland ratepayers’ money and that have led to the situation where Auckland’s run out of money for infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the food-scraps collection programme has cost half a billion dollars or more. A specific, load-bearing figure that reads as likely overstated for a kerbside-collection scheme.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Transport budget and reporting on the kerbside food-scraps collection programme (fleet purchase + operating cost); true if total cost is ~$500m or more, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: That is why, in addition to all the other things that Auckland Council already has on its list—there’s a $4 billion shortfall between the infrastructure it knows it needs to fund and the amount of money it can get from ratepayers—it also is going to have to turn its mind to another million people coming, according to the Auckland plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific $4 billion gap between Auckland Council's identified infrastructure need and ratepayer funding. Contested figure, load-bearing to the case for the fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council long-term plan / infrastructure funding documents on the gap between identified infrastructure need and available rates revenue; true if a shortfall of ~$4 billion is documented, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, this Government has committed to the City Rail Link projects and put down around $200 million for the first stage of grade separation in some of those really important parts of the network out in South Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific government funding commitment (~$200m for a first stage of grade separation). Checkable figure, non-obvious to a general reader.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government / Budget announcements and NZTA-KiwiRail funding records for rail grade-separation in South Auckland; true if ~$200m was committed for a first stage, false if materially different or not committed.

veracity.statement: Well, that was never planned or funded by the previous Labour Government or the previous ex-Labour mayor, Phil Goff.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that grade separation was never planned or funded by the previous Labour government or mayor Phil Goff — a contested claim about their record, load-bearing to the poor-planning argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / KiwiRail / prior government funding records on whether grade separation of the Auckland rail network was planned or funded before the current term; false if such planning or funding existed under the previous Labour government or Goff's mayoralty, true if it did not.

veracity.statement: Every day, 15,000 vehicles—including heavy trucks and freight and stock trucks—trundle down the main street of Kumeū and the neighbouring town of Huapai on their way to and from Auckland City.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific daily traffic volume of 15,000 vehicles through Kumeū and Huapai. A specific, non-obvious figure a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA / Auckland Transport traffic-count data for the state highway through Kumeū/Huapai; true if daily volume is ~15,000 vehicles, false if materially different.

focus.statement: No, this has to be in the long-term plan; it’s been publicly consulted on; it’s going to be publicly notified in accordance with the documents as set out in the Local Government Act; and then get the 75 percent majority.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill directly — the procedural safeguards (long-term plan inclusion, public consultation, notification under the Local Government Act, a 75% supermajority). Squarely on the measure before the House, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are great things happening for Auckland aside from the investment, like the new City Rail Link, and, of course, the great news that members seem so disappointed about today, with those lowering interest rates saving them $400 a fortnight—great news.
focus.explanation: Contains real policy content (City Rail Link, interest rate movements) but the weight of the sentence is party framing — characterising the other side as 'so disappointed' by good news — rather than engaging the bill under debate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It's a pleasure to rise in support of this bill, but how revealing that we had a National Party MP just stand up and tell us that he was half-hearted about Auckland—a third of New Zealand's population.
focus.explanation: Spends the opening on the opposing party's stance ('how revealing that we had a National Party MP...') rather than the bill's substance. The residual factual point about Auckland's population does not engage the measure; the primary content is party framing of the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The previous system would have, if it had been continued, cost an additional $1 million to administer that fund, so it is useful to have that system.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance directly — an administrative cost comparison between the previous fund system and the new one, tied to the merits of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There were delays in terms of the appointment of the global investment manager, and while the distribution to the council measure was achieved, the gross return and net return for that third quarter weren't, so no doubt there will be things that we will need to continue to watch, but certainly this fund is placing Auckland in the right direction.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the fund — reports specifics from the third-quarter report, including where performance targets were and were not met. On-policy scrutiny of the measure itself, even acknowledging shortcomings.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are great things happening for Auckland aside from the investment, like the new City Rail Link, and, of course, the great news that members seem so disappointed about today, with those lowering interest rates saving them $400 a fortnight—great news.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that lowering interest rates are saving 'them' $400 a fortnight — a specific quantitative claim about the mortgage-repayment effect of falling interest rates over the period. Contested political figure that depends on assumed mortgage size.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare fortnightly mortgage repayment savings from OCR/retail interest rate cuts over the referenced period against a representative mortgage; true if a typical affected borrower saves on the order of $400 a fortnight, false if the figure requires an atypical loan size or is materially lower.

veracity.statement: The previous system would have, if it had been continued, cost an additional $1 million to administer that fund, so it is useful to have that system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure: continuing the previous system would have cost an additional $1 million to administer the fund. A load-bearing quantitative claim supporting her argument for the new system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official cost estimates or council/fund administration documents comparing the annual administration cost of the previous system with the new one; true if the differential is around $1 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: There were delays in terms of the appointment of the global investment manager, and while the distribution to the council measure was achieved, the gross return and net return for that third quarter weren't, so no doubt there will be things that we will need to continue to watch, but certainly this fund is placing Auckland in the right direction.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific, checkable facts from the fund's third-quarter report: the distribution-to-council measure was achieved, but the gross and net return targets for that quarter were not. Specific and non-obvious performance claims.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The named fund's published third-quarter report; true if the distribution-to-council measure was met while gross and net return measures were missed, false if the report shows otherwise.

focus.statement: The current mechanisms, including letters of expectation, statements of intent, and council policies, are weak tools for protecting Māori interests.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanisms in the bill (letters of expectation, statements of intent, council policies) and argues they are inadequate protections. Squarely on the policy substance, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If this fund is to protect intergenerational wealth, then Māori must have a say in what gets sold, how funds are invested, and who benefits from the returns.
focus.explanation: Addresses the governance substance of the fund — asset disposal, investment, distribution of returns — a specific policy point about how the fund should operate.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, make no mistake, there's more work that needs to be done to ensure that councils across the country—and certainly in our largest city—have the resources that they need to do well and to provide the basic essentials that people deserve, whether it's picking up the rubbish, whether it's clean drinking water, whether it's adequate public transport, and a thriving natural environment to protect us against extreme weather events.
focus.explanation: Directed at the policy question of council funding and service delivery, naming concrete services. Policy-focused though fairly general; no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: To answer the question from that member, the official cash rate (OCR) has dropped from 5.5 percent to less than half of that, to 2.5 percent.
focus.explanation: Contains real economic figures and outcomes, but is a digression from the fund into defending the government's record in response to the other side; a genuine policy point wrapped in that framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As Dr Cheung correctly gave us a nice synopsis in his contribution before, the reason—and perhaps one of the only reasons—that it needs to come to this mechanism is because of the supermajority clause: clause 11 in the bill.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the substance of the bill — why it requires the local-bill mechanism — pointing to clause 11's supermajority requirement. Fully on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How can we talk about securing the future for generations to come when Māori, the fastest-growing population in Tāmaki Makaurau, over 250,000 strong, are not explicitly included in the governance of this fund?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Māori are the fastest-growing population in Auckland and number over 250,000 there. A specific demographic claim, not the argument's main opinion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census figures for the Māori population of the Auckland region and population growth rates by ethnicity there; true if Māori exceed 250,000 in Auckland and are the fastest-growing ethnic group, false if the count is materially lower or another group (e.g. Asian) is growing faster.

veracity.statement: To answer the question from that member, the official cash rate (OCR) has dropped from 5.5 percent to less than half of that, to 2.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific movement in the official cash rate from 5.5% down to 2.5%.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reserve Bank of New Zealand OCR decision record up to the debate date; true if the OCR peaked at 5.5% and stood at 2.5% at the time, false if either figure is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: What that means is, when you refix the average mortgage, anywhere in New Zealand, you are saving $400 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: Quantified claim that refixing the average NZ mortgage now saves $400 a fortnight relative to the higher-rate period; load-bearing to his argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Calculation of fortnightly repayment change on the average NZ mortgage size given a fall in mortgage rates tracking the OCR from 5.5% to 2.5% (per RBNZ average residential mortgage data); true if the saving is approximately $400/fortnight, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It is growing at a rate of about 50,000 people per year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Auckland's annual population growth is about 50,000 people. A specific, checkable figure that carries the speaker's case about infrastructure need.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates / growth for the Auckland region; true if annual growth is ~50,000 ± rounding, false if materially lower or higher.
