focus.explanation: Accountability against a named outcome (a record 73,900 citizens departing) tied to the government's economic plan. On-policy scrutiny with a specific figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Are a record number of New Zealanders leaving because the cost of utilities are up 19.3 percent from a year earlier, including rates, water charges, and energy bills?
focus.explanation: Engages cost-of-living policy with a specific figure and named components (rates, water, energy). Directly on the substance of household costs.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Was the Prime Minister or Cabinet Office made aware of any potential conflict of interest with the Minister for the Environment attempting to influence a consent process from which a National MP’s company could benefit, and does he consider this an appropriate action for his Minister to take?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Minister attempted to influence a consent process benefiting a National MP's company — a contested, load-bearing allegation. I have no independent knowledge of the underlying facts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Records/reporting on the Minister for the Environment's communications with the relevant council regarding consents, and whether a National MP's company stood to benefit; true if she pressed the consent process to that company's advantage, false if no such intervention occurred.

veracity.statement: Well, because we had a very poor inheritance from the previous Government, which was Government spending that went up 84 percent, a lot of it very wasteful.
veracity.explanation: Claims government spending rose 84% under the previous government — a specific, contested figure central to the argument. Nominal spending did rise steeply over that period, so roughly plausible, but the exact 84% and baseline are uncertain.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Core Crown expenses (or total Crown expenditure) at the start versus end of the 2017–2023 Labour-led government, from Treasury financial statements; true if the rise is approximately 84%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I’m actually very proud that we’ve accelerated $7 billion worth of infrastructure investment that’s actually starting before Christmas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific accelerated infrastructure figure and timeline. Plausible as a government claim but the $7bn and 'starting before Christmas' framing are the sort of number that needs checking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/Treasury announcements on accelerated infrastructure spending and its start dates; true if approximately $7 billion of investment was brought forward to commence before Christmas 2025, false if materially less or not starting on that timeline.

veracity.statement: Interest rates are down eight times under this Government; they were up 12 times under his.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable comparison of OCR movements. The 12 rises over 2021–2023 is roughly right; the eight cuts by October 2025 is plausible but needs confirmation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision history; true if there were about 8 cuts since the change of government and about 12 rises under the previous government, false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “Economic growth is going to influence every decision I take this year.”; if so, why did he shrink the economy by almost 1 percent in the last quarter?
veracity.explanation: Claims the economy contracted by almost 1% in the last quarter — contested and load-bearing. A contraction of that order is plausible for a recent NZ quarter but the exact figure needs the GDP release.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP for the most recent quarter referenced; true if real GDP fell by approximately 1%, false if it grew or fell materially less.

veracity.statement: On the topic of construction, does he agree with Christopher Luxon, “At the most basic level, the problem is not enough money being spent on new and existing infrastructure.”; if so, why did he slash nearly $3 billion in infrastructure investment in his first year as Prime Minister?
veracity.explanation: Claims a nearly $3 billion cut to infrastructure investment in the first year — directly contested by Luxon's counter-claim of accelerated spending, so it turns on definition and baseline. Genuinely uncertain.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget/Treasury figures on infrastructure investment in the government's first year versus the prior baseline; true if net infrastructure investment fell by approximately $3 billion, false if it rose or the cut was materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “We’re determined to get the building and construction sector firing on all cylinders.”; if so, is 20,000 job losses in the construction sector the type of firing he was referring to?
veracity.explanation: Claims 20,000 construction-sector job losses. Plausible given the 2024–25 construction downturn, but the exact figure and period need the employment data.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction-sector employment (filled jobs) change over the relevant period; true if losses are approximately 20,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: As a share of GDP, core Crown expenses fell from 33.1 percent in 2023-24 to 32.5 in 2024-25.
veracity.explanation: A specific pair of figures attributed to Treasury's year-end statements. Likely accurate as a direct reading of the published accounts, but the precise numbers are worth confirming.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Government financial statements for 2024-25 on core Crown expenses as a share of GDP; true if the figures are 33.1% and 32.5% (± rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Is the record 73,900 New Zealand citizens leaving the country a sign that her economic plan is a success; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: A specific migration figure asserted as a record. Citizen departures near or above 70,000 have been reported; the exact 73,900 and 'record' status need the migration release.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for citizen departures over the annual period referenced; true if approximately 73,900 New Zealand citizens departed and this is a record, false if the figure or the 'record' claim is wrong.

veracity.statement: Are a record number of New Zealanders leaving because the cost of utilities are up 19.3 percent from a year earlier, including rates, water charges, and energy bills?
veracity.explanation: A specific 19.3% rise in utility costs. Utility and rates costs did rise sharply, but the exact composite figure needs the CPI/household-costs data to confirm.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI/household living-costs data for the utilities grouping (rates, water charges, energy) over the year referenced; true if the rise is approximately 19.3%, false if materially different.

focus.statement: The Government’s intention is to put downward pressure on energy prices, which will come from a combination of Resource Management Act (RMA) reform, planning reform, sorting out the dysfunctionality of the energy market through the Electricity Authority, and the hard work being led by the Minister of Energy, and it will come from long-term stability when it comes to gas supply, which is why I repeat, again, that the Opposition should get on board with rational economic policy and realise that New Zealand’s energy security is underpinned by thermal electricity powered by gas.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the energy policy: names concrete mechanisms (RMA reform, the Electricity Authority, gas supply). Docked slightly for the 'Opposition should get on board with rational economic policy' party framing, but the weight is on substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of course we do, but the facts are this: under that last Government’s epic mismanagement of the economy, people fled New Zealand.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (net migration / economic outcomes) but delivered mostly as a characterisation of the previous government ('epic mismanagement'). A policy claim wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our students’ reading ability has declined over many decades, but with a focus on teaching the basics brilliantly, an hour a day of reading, and implementing an evidence-based structured literacy approach, we are building the strong foundations required to turn that around.
focus.explanation: Entirely engaged with the education policy — the intervention (structured literacy, daily reading) and the outcome it targets. No party content; a minister staying wholly on substance where she could have pivoted to attack.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I tell you, this Government is not going to shut down Kiwi farms and send that production to less carbon-efficient places, less productive places, and make global greenhouse gas emissions worse.
focus.explanation: Engages the methane/emissions policy on the merits — the emissions-leakage argument (production shifting to less efficient countries). On-policy, though framed against an implied opposition position.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I reject the characterisation of that question, but I just say to the member, as part of a Labour-Greens Government who wanted to shut down New Zealand farms and send production overseas, why don’t you come on board and actually support that policy too?
focus.explanation: Mostly about the other side — characterising the 'Labour-Greens Government' and inviting them aboard. A thin policy referent (farm production), but the weight is party framing rather than substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look, I think we’ve traversed this many times before. The Court of Appeal lowered the threshold. We had a high threshold under the legislation. We’re just returning it to what Parliament intended.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the takutai moana / Marine and Coastal Area Act change on the merits — the customary-title threshold and its legislative history. On-policy, no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, I think farmers should be deeply valued and not treated like villains as they were under a Labour-Greens Government.
focus.explanation: Largely about the other side's alleged treatment of farmers rather than any measure. A gesture at farm policy, but the content is a characterisation of the previous government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Did the Prime Minister give agricultural polluters a free ride instead of requiring them to do their fair share of emissions reductions, given that this means that households and businesses will have to shoulder more of the emissions reduction, increasing the cost of living for everyday New Zealanders?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny naming a specific policy (agricultural emissions reductions) and a specific consequence (the burden shifting to households/businesses). On-policy accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand that weakening methane targets actually harms farmers’ livelihoods and increases their long-term cost of living as farmers are at the front line of climate-driven extreme weather events that threaten global food production and raise insurance premiums?
focus.explanation: Engages the methane-target policy on substance — the mechanism by which weakening targets is argued to harm farmers (extreme weather, food production, insurance). Fully on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he claim that his targets are based on anything other than corporate interests when world-leading climate scientists have described his weakening of methane targets as “a great way of shooting yourself in the foot” and “New Zealand is setting a dangerous precedent that other governments must not follow”?
focus.explanation: Engages the methane target and cites external expert assessment of it, which is policy substance; docked for the 'corporate interests' motive-framing that carries part of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Are a record number of New Zealanders leaving because the service sector has been contracting for every month since she took office?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny that names specific outcomes — net departures and service-sector contraction — and ties them to the government's tenure. On-policy economic accountability.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The latest report shows an incredible improvement in the number of students who are reaching 20 weeks at school at expected levels of phonics, up from 36 percent in term 1 to 58 percent in term 3.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific figures (36% → 58%) from a named report on 20-week phonics attainment. Load-bearing to the achievement claim and specific/non-obvious, so checkable and worth checking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Education phonics-check report referenced (2025, 20-week check): true if it records students at expected phonics levels rising from 36% in term 1 to 58% in term 3, false if the figures materially differ.

veracity.statement: Our farmers are the world’s most productive, best, and most carbon-efficient farmers in the world.
veracity.explanation: A contested superlative. NZ pastoral dairy is often cited as low emissions-intensity, but 'most carbon-efficient in the world' across all farming is a strong, disputable claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative agricultural emissions-intensity data (e.g. per-kg-of-product emissions for NZ dairy/meat vs other producing nations): true if NZ ranks as the most carbon-efficient across major products, false if other producers match or beat it.

veracity.statement: The Court of Appeal lowered the threshold.
veracity.explanation: Load-bearing to the government's whole justification for amending the Act. Contested — the government asserts the court lowered the bar; critics dispute that framing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal's decision on the s58 customary marine title test under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act (the Edwards/Whakatōhea line): true if it interpreted the test so as to lower the bar relative to the earlier reading, false if it did not change or raised the threshold.

veracity.statement: Are a record number of New Zealanders leaving because the service sector has been contracting for every month since she took office?
veracity.explanation: The load-bearing, specific claim is that the service sector has contracted 'every month' since the Minister took office — an absolute claim checkable against the monthly PSI. 'Every month' is strong enough that a single expansionary reading falsifies it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The BusinessNZ–BNZ Performance of Services Index by month since the relevant Minister took office (late 2023): true if every month has been below 50 (contraction), false if any month recorded 50 or above.

focus.statement: It’s important that we provide certainty to our farmers, processors, and exporters that is fair, pragmatic, and backed by science. This is why the Government has set the methane target at a range of 14 to 24 percent below 2017 levels by 2050.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the policy at issue — the methane target — naming a specific figure (14 to 24 percent below 2017 by 2050) and the rationale. On-substance, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government has been backing teachers since the day we took office: backing them with a knowledge-rich curriculum, professional learning and development, and resources so that more Kiwi kids succeed at school.
focus.explanation: Engages the education policy substance (curriculum, PLD, resourcing) rather than attacking the opposition. On-policy; that the claim is self-promotional is Specificity/Veracity's concern, not Focus's.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In 2023, there was a terrible strike action—tens of thousands of primary and area school and secondary principals and teachers participated in the historic walkout, followed by a further three days after that, and then rolling strikes for a whole term.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about the current dispute by pointing to strikes under the previous government. It names a specific event (2023 strikes) but the weight is deflection to the other side's record rather than engaging the present policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We continue to hold the position that recognition of a Palestinian State is a matter of when, not if. We will recognise a Palestinian State when the conditions are right.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the policy question asked — New Zealand's position on recognition of a Palestinian State — setting out the government's stance and conditions. On-substance, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, the silence over the past week from some of the so-called pro-Palestinian protesters around this country has been absolutely deafening.
focus.explanation: Content-free attack on the perceived hypocrisy/silence of political opponents, with no policy named. This is the off-policy tribalism case Focus exists to catch; the target is a movement, not a person, so it stays eligible.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To back the new target, the Government is already investing more than $400 million with industry to speed up the development and roll-out of methane-cutting tools.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific dollar figure for government investment in methane-cutting tools — specific, non-obvious and the sort of figure the opposition would dispute. Not a verdict.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/MPI funding announcements on agricultural methane-reduction R&D and tool development; true if committed co-investment with industry is at least ~$400 million, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Our primary sector earns nearly $60 billion in export revenue each year for New Zealand. It provides more than one in 10 Kiwi jobs.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable quantitative claims: primary-sector export revenue and its share of employment. Non-obvious figures a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries export revenue figure and primary-sector employment share; true if primary export revenue is near $60 billion/year and employment share exceeds 10%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The evidence shows this is working, with the phonics data announced yesterday.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a specific, recently-announced phonics dataset demonstrates the policy is working — contested and load-bearing to her defence. Not a verdict on whether it does.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The phonics/structured-literacy check results referenced (announced the prior day); true if the data show improvement attributable to the programme, false if flat or declining.

veracity.statement: In 2023, there was a terrible strike action—tens of thousands of primary and area school and secondary principals and teachers participated in the historic walkout, followed by a further three days after that, and then rolling strikes for a whole term.
veracity.explanation: Quantified claim about the scale and duration of 2023 strikes; 'rolling strikes for a whole term' is the checkable, potentially overstated part.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZEI/PPTA and news records of the 2023 teacher strike action; true if tens of thousands participated with a further three-day and term-long rolling action, false if the scale or duration is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: We note that while Hamas has released 20 hostages, Israel has released around 2,000 Palestinian prisoners.
veracity.explanation: Two specific reported figures on the hostage/prisoner exchange — checkable and quantified, though widely reported.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: News and official records of the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire exchange; true if ~20 living hostages were released by Hamas and ~2,000 Palestinian prisoners by Israel, false if the figures are materially different.

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand that Māori exercise kaitiakitanga and protection for the benefit of all of us here in Aotearoa—for example, when they veto applications for private companies to mine in our precious moana, and that by removing recognition of customary rights in the takutai moana, his Government has taken this away?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named policy — the removal of recognition of customary rights in the takutai moana and its effect on mining vetoes. Engages a substantive measure, not the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As a Government, we’re just returning what was a lowered threshold under the courts—we’re returning it back to what Parliament intended.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy substance — the legal threshold, court decisions, and legislative intent behind the takutai moana regime. On-topic, if vague.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Today, 90 percent of adults without a community services card pay $70 or less to see their general practitioner.
focus.explanation: On-policy defence of affordability with a specific figure and cohort named. Precisely the accountability case that scores high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What good is capping fees when under-funded practices start charging for double consultations, leading to the pensioner who wrote to me saying, “I pay $91 for a 15-minute visit, and you’re only allowed to talk about one thing. If you want to talk about two things, you need to pay for another $91. I cannot afford to pay this.”?
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the policy — that a fee cap can be undercut by charging for double consultations. On-policy scrutiny of the affordability claim.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As I say, you can’t trust Labour when it comes to GP fees.
focus.explanation: Content-free party framing — a general 'can't trust Labour' verdict with no policy, figure or mechanism attached. No person is insulted, so this is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he stand by his decision to exclude Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the Regulatory Standards Bill, given that this bill defines the constitutional test for every future law?
focus.explanation: Engages a named measure (the Regulatory Standards Bill) and a specific design choice within it. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is he proceeding with the Regulatory Standards Bill without a public mandate, when 99 percent of the 159,000 submitters opposed it?
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny of the named bill, citing a specific submission figure. Accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, not every bill needs a reference to the Treaty in it.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the policy question about whether Treaty references belong in the bill. On-topic.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, again, I’d just say to the member, it’s interesting that I’ve never had a question from that member about what we are doing to improve literacy with young Māori students.
focus.explanation: Deflects from the measure at issue to the member's own questioning record. Once that is removed nothing about the bill remains; the weight is on what the other side does, not the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that the success of policies such as structured literacy and charter schools make the case that it is possible to uplift young Māori educational outcomes without making any reference to the Treaty whatsoever?
focus.explanation: Engages named policies (structured literacy, charter schools) and an educational-outcomes question. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m advised that the Ministry of Housing and Urban Development does not record the pregnancy status of applicants for emergency housing.
focus.explanation: Directly answers the substantive question about emergency-housing data collection. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We, on this side of the House, are genuinely concerned by those who may be rough sleeping, and that’s why Minister Bishop and myself have taken direct action over the last six weeks to announce an additional 300 funded places for Housing First and additional support for transitional housing, and have also given some direction around both redirections and also the exercise of discretion by Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora—the Ministry of Social Development (MSD).
focus.explanation: Engages the housing policy with concrete measures — funded Housing First places, transitional housing, MSD discretion. On-policy, specific actions named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he continue to deny the link between his tightening of the emergency housing entry criteria and the unprecedented increase in homelessness, when even pregnant women are now being denied access?
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny — links a named policy change (tightened emergency-housing entry criteria) to a claimed outcome. Accountability, not tribalism; 'unprecedented' carries no stated figure, so it is not a resolvable veracity claim.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it the case, like when MSD issued grants for homeless people to buy tents, or when women and children fleeing domestic violence were denied emergency housing, that the Minister knew there was an issue, but only acted when this was made public?
focus.explanation: Engages the policy pattern — prior MSD/emergency-housing failures cited to scrutinise the Minister's responsiveness. On-policy accountability.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As the member will be aware, this follows a 30 percent increase in GP fees between 2017 and 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts GP fees rose 30 percent over 2017–2023. A specific figure, contested by the opposition, and load-bearing to his defence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Data on average GP fee increases between 2017 and 2023 (e.g. Health NZ / prior Ministry of Health fee monitoring, or patient-fee surveys); true if the average rise is ~30% over that window, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Today, 90 percent of adults without a community services card pay $70 or less to see their general practitioner.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 90 percent of non-CSC adults pay $70 or less for a GP visit. Specific figure, contested, and repeatedly relied on.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ / Ministry of Health data on standard adult GP consultation fees for non-community-services-card holders; true if ~90% are at $70 or below, false if the share is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Why is he proceeding with the Regulatory Standards Bill without a public mandate, when 99 percent of the 159,000 submitters opposed it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts 99% of 159,000 submitters on the Regulatory Standards Bill opposed it. Two specific figures, contested, and load-bearing to the 'no mandate' argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee's official summary of submissions on the Regulatory Standards Bill; true if total submissions ≈159,000 and ~99% opposed, false if the counts or opposition share differ materially.

veracity.statement: We, on this side of the House, are genuinely concerned by those who may be rough sleeping, and that’s why Minister Bishop and myself have taken direct action over the last six weeks to announce an additional 300 funded places for Housing First and additional support for transitional housing, and have also given some direction around both redirections and also the exercise of discretion by Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora—the Ministry of Social Development (MSD).
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific action: 300 additional funded Housing First places announced in the last six weeks. A concrete, checkable figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/HUD announcements over the six weeks before 2025-10-14 on Housing First funding; true if an additional ~300 funded places were announced, false if no such announcement or a materially different number.

veracity.statement: Is it the case, like when MSD issued grants for homeless people to buy tents, or when women and children fleeing domestic violence were denied emergency housing, that the Minister knew there was an issue, but only acted when this was made public?
veracity.explanation: Asserts MSD issued grants that homeless people used to buy tents. A specific, checkable past event, cited as precedent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reporting and MSD records on hardship/special-needs grants used for tents or camping gear; true if such grants were issued, false if no record exists.

focus.statement: Those are my two questions: firstly, why do we have a preamble in this bill, because it’s not a Treaty settlement bill; and, secondly, why does the preamble not accurately reflect the decision of the Supreme Court?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House — names the bill, its preamble, and the Supreme Court decision, and puts a specific accountability question to the Minister. Legitimate scrutiny of the bill, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In doing so, it recognised that customary rights of Māori are rights in respect of coastal and marine areas that have existed since at least 1840; that is to say that they are property rights.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of what the legislation does — the nature of the customary rights it deals with. Entirely policy-directed, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s easy to say that it wasn’t the intention, but words matter in this, and the preamble is the start of what we would consider, in the Māori world, the wairua to the rest of the bill.
focus.explanation: About the preamble and how it frames the bill — on-policy engagement with the text before the House. Slightly less concrete than a named figure or clause, but plainly directed at the measure, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Then the next one is whether he can give an example of where, in previous cases, a marine and coastal area, or a customary title, has been recognised, and what makes this particular one different to others that have been recognised in the past.
focus.explanation: Asks for a specific precedent and a comparison against past customary-title recognitions — substantive scrutiny of how this bill operates. Fully policy-directed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, obviously enabling one group of New Zealanders who had received customary marine title to grant resource consents is a very significant deviation from normal expectations of New Zealanders living in this country in a democratic, modern democracy to have an equal say in decisions affecting their lives and their environment and what goes on around them.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy mechanism — the resource-consent rights conferred by customary marine title — and the rationale for the bill. On-policy argument, whatever one makes of its merits.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Supreme Court agreed with the Government that the Court of Appeal had got that wrong, and indicated their own expression of what section 58 meant.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Supreme Court sided with the Government against the Court of Appeal on the meaning of section 58 and substituted its own test. Contested — Webb characterises the Supreme Court as having instead resolved the concerns — and load-bearing for the case for the bill. Checkable against the judgment itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court's judgment in the customary marine title appeal (the Edwards / Whakātōhea line of litigation, 2024) on section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011; true if the Court held the Court of Appeal had erred in its interpretation of section 58 and set out its own interpretation, false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's interpretation.

veracity.statement: It is still the view of the Government that it still deviates from Parliament’s intention, because we’ve seen a couple of decisions that have been made since the Supreme Court decision and the Supreme Court test which have seen very large proportions of coastlines in the Wairarapa and Kāpiti that have been given customary marine title.
veracity.explanation: The checkable claim is that post-Supreme-Court decisions have awarded customary marine title over very large proportions of the Wairarapa and Kāpiti coastlines. Specific, contested, and load-bearing for the Government's justification of the bill. (The leading 'view of the Government' clause is opinion; the resolvable content is the factual claim about the decisions.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Court decisions on customary marine title issued after the Supreme Court's section 58 ruling covering the Wairarapa and Kāpiti coasts; true if such decisions granted customary marine title over very large proportions of those coastlines, false if they granted it over only small portions or not at all.

focus.statement: I explained, and it has been very well traversed in this House, that the bill was seeking to balance two things: on the one hand, the ability to assert customary marine rights and for those to be acknowledged through the legislation, with the accompanying abilities to, effectively, grant or not grant resource consents in that particular area; and to balance that with the natural expectations of all New Zealanders living in a modern democracy to have an equal say in what goes on in their community.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance of the bill — the two interests it seeks to balance (customary marine rights and resource-consent powers versus public say). No party framing; addresses the measure's mechanism directly.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, to the question of what Parliament intended in the original legislation, in 2011, what is the actual basis of independent analysis, which shows that Parliament’s intent in 2011 is not fulfilled by the determinations of the Supreme Court, in its 2 December 2024 finding, and its more recent finding, this year?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny that names the specific legislation, the premise of the bill, and the dated court findings, pressing the Minister for the evidential basis of his claim. On-policy accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I think it is for the Minister to establish clearly his case about why, in 2011, what was passed was his version of how this law should be interpreted, and not in fact what the Minister at the time, or the official documentation of the day, said it was.
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny placing the burden on the Minister to justify his reading of the 2011 legislation against the record of the day. Engages the interpretive substance of the bill, not the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: On page 15 of that analysis, point 44: “If the Supreme Court ruled in favour of the Crown, it could mean the additional time and resource on progressing amendments would not be required”, and the Supreme Court did rule in favour of the Crown.
