focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, by far the most important reports I have seen are the weekly auction results, which are giving renewed hope to our long-suffering wool growers. Great news: there has been a resurgence in wool prices. Over the last 12 months, the strong wool indicator is up 32 percent, mid micron up 41 percent, and fine wool up 35 percent. These are levels not seen in nine years, and much of this increase has occurred in the last few weeks.
focus.explanation: Answers squarely on the wool topic with specific market figures and detail. Fully on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he accept the report’s finding that climate change is driving significant changes in our oceans, and, if so, does he believe that the attempts to drill for more fossil fuels will help or harm our moana?
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the oceans report and the drilling policy directly. On-policy scrutiny, no personal or tribal content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On the question of fisheries, the proposed mining, God willing, to proceed off the coast of Taranaki will have minimal impact on the strength or the vitality of fisheries. Sadly, fish do move around. Consequently, it behoves the Government to change, from time to time, its regulatory approach so that the harvesters, the guardians, and the regulators of our fisheries resource have multiple options in front of them to deal with the changing fortunes of the oceanic environment. But to suggest that a single Minister or a Government or 5.2 million people at the distant end of the South Pacific can effect change when larger climate change emitters are doing zero is fanciful.
focus.explanation: Engages the fisheries/mining policy and the regulatory approach substantively. On-topic, addressed to the measure rather than to any person.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I thank the member for that question. Obviously, setting total allowable commercial catch limits for any fish species is a balance, as reflected in the purpose of the Fisheries Act. Not only do we have to be mindful of the scientific evidence and the pressure on stocks, we also have to take account of the statutory status of utilisation. I’m confident that the information fed into that decision will stand the test in good time.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the catch-limit-setting question, the Fisheries Act purpose, and the balance of considerations. Squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Why did he say to New Zealanders that there will be more people wearing hi-vis and hard hats when there has been, under his watch, $2.9 billion less spent on infrastructure and when his Government has cut Apprenticeship Boost for civil engineering, there are 20,000 fewer construction jobs in New Zealand, and 760 construction firms have gone under, under his watch?
veracity.explanation: Asserts several specific quantitative claims about infrastructure spend, construction jobs and firm failures under the current government. Contested and load-bearing; exact figures unverified from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Check each figure against source data: MBIE/Treasury infrastructure spend to test the $2.9 billion reduction; Stats NZ construction employment for the 20,000 fewer jobs; and company-liquidation records for 760 construction firm failures over the stated period. True if the figures match the record, false if materially off.

veracity.statement: Obviously, our contribution to global emissions is 0.17 percent—less than 1 percent! It is the height of conceit to imagine that somehow by closing down New Zealand industry we’re going to save the planet. The planet is more than capable of saving itself and we will adapt in good time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts NZ contributes 0.17 percent of global emissions. Specific figure, load-bearing to the argument; roughly the commonly cited share.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's share of global greenhouse gas emissions per an authoritative dataset (e.g. Our World in Data / Global Carbon Project). True if approximately 0.17%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: With respect to mining fossils, which is what four countries are doing—namely, China, USA, India, and Russia—and contributing to 60 percent of the emissions, what hope have we got to change that?
veracity.explanation: Asserts those four countries account for 60 percent of emissions. Specific and load-bearing; the combined share is plausibly in that range.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Combined share of global greenhouse gas emissions attributable to China, the USA, India and Russia per an authoritative emissions dataset. True if approximately 60%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, by far the most important reports I have seen are the weekly auction results, which are giving renewed hope to our long-suffering wool growers. Great news: there has been a resurgence in wool prices. Over the last 12 months, the strong wool indicator is up 32 percent, mid micron up 41 percent, and fine wool up 35 percent. These are levels not seen in nine years, and much of this increase has occurred in the last few weeks.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific year-on-year percentage rises across three wool categories and a nine-year high. Specific and checkable; a minister's own good-news claim, unverified from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wool price indicator movements over the prior 12 months (strong wool, mid micron, fine wool) per auction / NZ wool market indices. True if approximately +32%/+41%/+35% and at a nine-year high, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve got spending under control, inflation down to 2.7 percent, and mortgage rates cut eight times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two concrete figures about the government's economic record: that annual inflation is at 2.7 percent, and that mortgage/interest rates have been cut eight times over the relevant period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation rate for the quarter referenced (true if 2.7% ± rounding), and the RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision record for the number of cuts (true if eight reductions occurred over the stated period).

veracity.statement: We’ve delivered tax relief for the first time in 14 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the government delivered personal tax relief and that this was the first such tax relief in 14 years — i.e. no comparable income-tax cut occurred in the preceding 14-year window.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Record of NZ personal income-tax threshold/rate changes; true if the most recent prior tax relief was ~14 years earlier (e.g. 2010) and none intervened, false if any income-tax relief was delivered in that window.

veracity.statement: Ram raids are down 85 percent; gang patches banned—I’m not sure what their position is on gang patches.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ram-raid offences have fallen by 85 percent (baseline and endpoint implied to be recent), and that gang patches have been banned.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded ram-raid offence statistics comparing the periods implied; true if a fall of ~85% is supported on a defensible baseline, false if the reduction is materially smaller or depends on an unrepresentative comparison window.

veracity.statement: We’re reducing wait-lists for hips, knees and cataracts, all of which went up under Chris Hipkins when he was Minister of Health.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that elective surgery wait-lists for hip, knee and cataract procedures rose during Chris Hipkins' tenure as Minister of Health, and are now being reduced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Ministry of Health elective surgery wait-list data for hip, knee and cataract procedures across Hipkins' period as Health Minister; true if all three increased over that period, false if any did not.

veracity.statement: We’ve delivered 33 new cancer medicines, delivered the biggest funding boost for general practitioners, and just today announced an extension to breast screening, which, by the way, Labour promised in 2017 with their coalition agreement with New Zealand First but failed to deliver.
veracity.explanation: Contains a specific historical accountability claim: that an extension to breast screening was a commitment in the 2017 Labour–New Zealand First coalition agreement and was not delivered by that government. (Also asserts 33 new cancer medicines funded.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the 2017 Labour–NZ First coalition agreement and subsequent BreastScreen Aotearoa policy record; true if a breast-screening extension was committed in that agreement and not implemented, false if no such commitment appears or it was delivered.

veracity.statement: Now, David Seymour was the only guy in this entire precinct that voted against the zero carbon Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that David Seymour was the sole member of Parliament to vote against the Zero Carbon Act (Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division/vote record for the third reading of the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Bill; true if Seymour was the only MP recorded voting against, false if others also voted against or it passed on voices.

veracity.statement: Farmers in rural New Zealand are worth almost $60 billion—60 billion—and Chris Hipkins knows this, as the leader of that party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the rural farming sector's economic value is almost $60 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI/Stats NZ figures for the food-and-fibre or agricultural sector's export revenue or GDP contribution; true if a defensible measure is close to $60 billion, false if the sector's value on the intended measure is materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s a damnable shame that here we are and we are talking about a gas that decays back to carbon dioxide, and it is, factually, two parts per million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two factual claims about methane: that it decays back to carbon dioxide, and that its concentration is 'two parts per million'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Atmospheric chemistry sources on methane oxidation to CO2, and measured atmospheric methane concentration; true if methane oxidises to CO2 and its atmospheric concentration is ~2 ppm, false if the concentration figure is materially off (global CH4 is ~1.9 ppm).

focus.statement: Two years ago today, Christopher Luxon stood in front of New Zealanders and he made a promise: his promise was that he was going to lower the cost of living and fix the economy. Two years on, it is abundantly clear he has failed to do both of those things.
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment (lower the cost of living, fix the economy) and holds the Government to account for it. This is scrutiny of a named promise and outcome, not content-free tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Increasing unemployment; an economy that’s shrinking; more kids living in poverty; more people homeless and living on the streets; the construction sector—remember, they were going to get things done and get things building again—is at its lowest point in seven years, two years into this Government’s leadership; $3 billion less spending on building stuff in the last year compared to when they became the Government.
focus.explanation: Engages a string of named policy outcomes — unemployment, GDP, poverty, homelessness, construction activity, building spend. On-policy accountability.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It shows that they have no plan. They know they can’t defend their own record; they know they don’t know how to fix the mess that they have been creating; all they can do is scaremonger and attack, because they don’t know how to turn things around.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side — no plan, can't defend their record, all they do is scaremonger and attack. No policy, figure or outcome named; content-free party characterisation. Nobody is personally insulted, so it is the tribalism case Focus exists for.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Their answer is pretty simple: more cuts, more asset sales, less hope for everyday New Zealanders, who are flogging their guts out trying to get ahead with a Government that’s working against them.
focus.explanation: Names policy directions (cuts, asset sales) but the weight is party framing about a Government 'working against' people rather than engagement with a specific measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need a Labour Government that will get New Zealand back to work, because, under National, New Zealand does not work.
focus.explanation: 'Under National, New Zealand does not work' is a slogan about the party rather than about any policy; almost no substantive content to engage.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There is one thing the Government has broken records on, and that is the number of New Zealanders giving up and leaving.
focus.explanation: Points to a specific outcome — record emigration — rather than pure party abuse, though it is wrapped in attack framing ('giving up').
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Instead you left us with an utter mess and you left house owners in a terrible situation, paying interest rates they shouldn’t have been paying, because of your behaviour as the Government that then sat around spending New Zealanders’ money, borrowing money for New Zealanders to pay so that New Zealand is now paying interest every single year that is more than Corrections, Police, and Defence, and our fire service all together because of him and his former Government.
focus.explanation: Engages the fiscal record with a concrete comparison (debt-servicing cost against named budgets), though heavily wrapped in 'utter mess' party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The economy is turning. It’s turning the right way. We see interest rates dropping. We see New Zealand businesses getting a bit more confidence, and that will help them to employ more people.
focus.explanation: Engages the economy directly — interest rates, business confidence, employment — rather than attacking the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s why they’re going because New Zealand, in the last six years of the Labour Government, decided to cut the mines. It took years and years to get any consents, and they ended our ability to be able to have those high-paying jobs and to build our economy.
focus.explanation: Engages a real policy area — mining, consenting, jobs — attributing emigration to Labour's consenting regime, though framed as 'why they're going'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: At the same time, war has broken out in Te Pāti Māori.
focus.explanation: Entirely about another party's internal state; no policy content. This is about the party's cohesion rather than a personal insult, so it stays eligible and scores 0.0 — the tribalism case Focus exists for.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Despite what the left say, we have the fourth largest search and rescue area in the world.
focus.explanation: Engages defence/search-and-rescue capability as justification for the defence build-up — a substantive point, though prefaced with 'despite what the left say'.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Increasing unemployment; an economy that’s shrinking; more kids living in poverty; more people homeless and living on the streets; the construction sector—remember, they were going to get things done and get things building again—is at its lowest point in seven years, two years into this Government’s leadership; $3 billion less spending on building stuff in the last year compared to when they became the Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the construction sector is at its lowest point in seven years and that building/infrastructure spend fell by about $3 billion in the last year compared with when the Government took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Two load-bearing figures. Construction: Stats NZ construction activity / building-consents series — true if activity is at a seven-year low, false otherwise. Building spend: Treasury/Budget capital-spend figures — true if Crown building spend is ~$3bn lower year-on-year versus late 2023, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: There is one thing the Government has broken records on, and that is the number of New Zealanders giving up and leaving.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that emigration of New Zealanders has reached record levels under this Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration data on departures / net outflow of NZ citizens; true if NZ-citizen departures or net outflow reached a record level during this Government's term, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Instead you left us with an utter mess and you left house owners in a terrible situation, paying interest rates they shouldn’t have been paying, because of your behaviour as the Government that then sat around spending New Zealanders’ money, borrowing money for New Zealanders to pay so that New Zealand is now paying interest every single year that is more than Corrections, Police, and Defence, and our fire service all together because of him and his former Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts NZ's annual debt-servicing (interest) cost now exceeds the combined annual spend on Corrections, Police, Defence and the fire service.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare annual Crown finance costs (debt-servicing) against the combined annual appropriations for Vote Corrections, Vote Police, Vote Defence and Fire and Emergency NZ; true if finance costs exceed that sum, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Despite what the left say, we have the fourth largest search and rescue area in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand has the fourth-largest search and rescue area (region) in the world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ's designated maritime search and rescue region (SRR) area versus other nations' SRRs; true if NZ's SRR ranks fourth-largest in the world, false otherwise.

focus.statement: It is Luxon’s fault that a visit in New Zealand now to the GP, a standard adult visit to the GP, can cost nearly $100.
focus.explanation: Names a specific outcome (a standard adult GP visit costing nearly $100) and ties it to healthcare funding — legitimate scrutiny of a named policy area. Some party framing ('Luxon's fault') pulls it slightly below the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They repealed free prescriptions, a policy that kept people well and out of hospital.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific, named policy (repeal of free prescriptions) and its consequence. On-policy scrutiny of a government decision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, sadly, people, ambulances now cost 30 percent more too.
focus.explanation: Names a specific cost outcome (ambulance charges up 30%) in the context of health cost pressures — on-policy, though lightly rhetorical.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now one in six New Zealanders say they cannot afford to go to the doctor.
focus.explanation: A specific figure on access to care, directly on the healthcare-affordability policy at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have prioritised tax cuts for landlords, tax cuts for tobacco companies, and not putting money into our health system.
focus.explanation: Names specific fiscal policies (interest-deductibility/landlord tax changes, tobacco tax settings) and sets them against health funding — a policy claim, though carried on party framing about priorities.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The third example I’d give is the naming rights, also by New Zealand firm PikPok, to the video game Clusterduck—carefully and eponymously representing in so many ways the collective Opposition parties that we see today, to which we give them Clusterduck.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the Opposition parties as a collective — content-free mockery with no policy substance once the joke is removed. Directed at parties (not a person), so eligible, and it is exactly the tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve merged seven Crown research institutes (CRIs) into three public research organisations (PROs), creating some of the biggest research and development thematic institutions in the world.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance of the science reform he is defending — the specific structural change made. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Exports in one year are up from $500 million to around $750 million.
focus.explanation: A specific figure on gaming-sector export performance, tied to the CODE funding policy he goes on to discuss. On-topic to his portfolio, with light championing framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is Luxon’s fault that a visit in New Zealand now to the GP, a standard adult visit to the GP, can cost nearly $100.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a standard adult GP visit can now cost nearly $100. Contested and load-bearing to her argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published surveys of standard adult GP consultation fees (e.g. Health NZ / RNZ GP fee surveys, or the specific clinic she cites at $94); true if standard adult visits at some NZ clinics are near $100, false if the typical/maximum standard fee is materially lower. This claim is explicitly contested — she notes the Minister called it misinformation.

veracity.statement: They repealed free prescriptions, a policy that kept people well and out of hospital.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the government repealed the free-prescriptions policy. My recollection is the coalition reinstated the $5 co-payment in 2024, though free scripts were retained for some groups.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government policy record on prescription co-payments; true if the coalition reinstated prescription charges after Labour had made prescriptions free, false if universal free prescriptions remain in place.

veracity.statement: Well, sadly, people, ambulances now cost 30 percent more too.
veracity.explanation: Asserts ambulance costs rose 30 percent. A clean, specific, checkable figure; I am uncertain of the exact percentage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ambulance part-charge schedule (Hato Hone St John / Wellington Free Ambulance) before and after the stated period; true if the road-ambulance part-charge rose ~30%, false if the increase was materially different.

veracity.statement: Now one in six New Zealanders say they cannot afford to go to the doctor.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a survey statistic that one in six cannot afford to see a doctor. Recent surveys have shown roughly this order of magnitude for cost-related unmet GP need.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Health Survey / relevant poll on adults reporting they cannot afford or have delayed a GP visit due to cost; true if the figure is around one in six, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Exports in one year are up from $500 million to around $750 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific one-year jump in gaming exports from $500m to ~$750m. A large single-year jump; I am uncertain of the exact figures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Game Developers Association export-revenue figures for the years referenced; true if the sector's annual export revenue rose from ~$500m to ~$750m, false if the figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: It was the first time in space ever that high temperature superconducting magnets have been bolted on to the outside of the space station.
veracity.explanation: A superlative 'first ever' claim about high-temperature superconducting magnets externally mounted on the ISS. 'First ever' claims are hard to verify and I cannot confirm it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Robinson Research Institute / ISS payload records for high-temperature superconducting magnets mounted externally on the ISS; true if this was the first such external mounting, false if a prior instance exists.

focus.statement: The Government say fast tracking environmental destruction is going to create jobs.
focus.explanation: Engages the fast-track regime and its jobs justification — a live policy question — rather than a party's general character. The framing is loaded ('environmental destruction'), but the statement is about the measure, not tribal identity.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This small thinking Government is making way for a carbon bomb on the Denniston Plateau right now.
focus.explanation: Names a specific project (Denniston Plateau coal mining) and a policy outcome (emissions), which is on-policy scrutiny, but it is wrapped in party framing ('small thinking Government') and hyperbole ('carbon bomb'), so it is a real policy point in party dressing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New Zealand First—more like “Trans-Tasman Resources First”, more like “OceanaGold First”, more like overseas corporations first, New Zealand last.
focus.explanation: Content-free tribalism aimed at a party's supposed loyalties. It names no policy, measure or figure; strip the party jibe and nothing about the substance of any policy remains. This is the party-versus-policy gap Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s been two years since the election, when Christopher Luxon stood in front of voters in 2023 as an economic genius who declared that he would fix the cost of living and the economy, and he has failed to do so.
focus.explanation: Holds a named leader to a named commitment (fix the cost of living and the economy) and its outcome — legitimate accountability, which is on-policy. Sarcastic framing ('economic genius') pulls it slightly toward party point-scoring.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The same people in this coalition Government who crashed the economy leading to 36,000 fewer jobs the day that they took office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — 36,000 fewer jobs attributed to the coalition Government's arrival in office. Contested and load-bearing to her economic argument. The literal 'the day that they took office' is likely a live-speech compression for job losses over their term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / HLFS employment change over the period since the coalition took office in late 2023, and any published attribution of a ~36,000 job fall to Government action; true if a fall of roughly that magnitude is documented over the relevant window, false if employment rose or the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Over in the National Party we have our environment Minister destroying the name of her job, sitting outside of Cabinet for the first time in 50 years, providing no input—none—on fast-track projects that will destroy our taio and our moana.
veracity.explanation: Contains a checkable factual claim: that the current Minister for the Environment sits outside Cabinet, and that this is the first time in 50 years. The rest is opinion/attack, but the '50 years / outside Cabinet' assertion is verifiable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The current ministerial list and Cabinet membership for the environment portfolio, plus the historical record of whether the environment portfolio has previously been held outside Cabinet since ~1976; true if the current holder is outside Cabinet and no prior holder in 50 years was, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Earlier this year, 142 jobs were lost from Carter Holt Harvey’s Eves Valley sawmill.
veracity.explanation: A specific, non-obvious figure attributed to a named event: 142 jobs lost at the Carter Holt Harvey Eves Valley sawmill this year. A well-informed reader could not confirm it from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: News reports and Carter Holt Harvey announcements on the Eves Valley (Nelson) sawmill closure/redundancies in 2025; true if ~142 jobs are reported lost, false if the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Another 59 jobs are on the line at Sealord, after 79 were axed recently.
veracity.explanation: Two specific figures for Sealord job cuts (59 at risk, 79 already cut). Contested and precise enough to require checking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Sealord announcements and news coverage of 2025 redundancies; true if roughly 79 cut and 59 further at risk are reported, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: That’s why, in Budget 2025, the Government committed $250,000 to support rural New Zealand’s grassroots work.
veracity.explanation: A specific budget figure ($250,000 in Budget 2025 for rural grassroots work) attributed to her own Government. A precise, checkable and non-obvious claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 documents / Vote appropriations for a $250,000 commitment to rural New Zealand grassroots work; true if that allocation appears, false if absent or a different amount.

focus.statement: Everything is going up: transport, power, phone bills, the cost of study, and that’s pushing more and more personal debt on to people and household debt and consumer debt, and more and more people are withdrawing their KiwiSaver because of hardship.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages cost-of-living substance — named cost areas and a concrete effect (household debt, KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals). On-policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But instead of being clear with consumers about who will bear the cost of that, they have lumped it on to small businesses.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific policy (the surcharge ban) and its cost incidence — who bears the cost. Legitimate scrutiny of a named measure, high focus.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Explain that one to consumers on the doorstep, that under National if prices come down in a market event, that will be illegal.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the substance of the Government's pricing intervention and what it does. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They will be removed from the waiting list for any of that help under a Government who is excluding people from their ability to get that work that they say they prioritise.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific policy (jobseeker/MSD support and its eligibility rules) and the concrete effect on people seeking work. On-policy scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Thankfully, they never became a coalition in this Government, on the Government benches, but they have proven beyond reasonable doubt that they are an unholy alliance; that they are the “uni-party”; that they are one thing on that side of the House.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the opposition parties' character and cohesion — 'unholy alliance', 'uni-party'. No individual is insulted (so eligible), but no policy content at all: content-free tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They know that the unholy alliance on those Opposition benches will be arguing with each other to work out who’s going to lead them.
focus.explanation: About the opposition parties' internal divisions and leadership squabbles — no policy named or engaged. The Focus 0.0 case.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In health, there’s 16,000 more elective surgeries that have happened, 33 new cancer treatments, and 33 more medicines.
focus.explanation: Defends the Government's record with specific health-policy outputs — surgeries, treatments, medicines. Squarely on-policy substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Over the last 18 months, we’ve rebuilt the confidence of farmers, and we’re just hoping that the Greens do not get the opportunity to destroy it with a 33 percent tax on farmers.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (a 33 percent tax on farmers) but the weight is on the Greens 'destroying' confidence — party framing wrapped around the policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Explain that one to consumers on the doorstep, that under National if prices come down in a market event, that will be illegal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's pricing rule makes it illegal to lower prices — a factual characterisation of what the policy does.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The provisions of the Government's grocery/retail pricing legislation on price reductions; true if the rule actually prohibits dropping prices in a market event, false if it only restricts anti-competitive predatory pricing.

veracity.statement: Some 73,900 New Zealanders are hearing that message and have left—200 New Zealanders every day with no plan to get them back.
veracity.explanation: A specific figure for New Zealanders who have emigrated, with an implied daily rate (~200/day).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration data for the year referenced (gross departures of NZ citizens); true if ≈73,900 departed (≈200/day), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The cost of living was meant to be something that this Government could manage, but this economy is going backwards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the economy has contracted under the current Government — a checkable claim about economic performance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ real GDP series from late 2023 (Government took office) to the statement date; true if GDP contracted over that period, false if it grew.

veracity.statement: In health, there’s 16,000 more elective surgeries that have happened, 33 new cancer treatments, and 33 more medicines.
veracity.explanation: Specific figures for additional elective surgeries, newly funded cancer treatments and medicines since taking office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ / Ministry of Health figures since the 2023 election; true if ≈16,000 more electives, 33 cancer treatments and 33 medicines, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the economy, we’ve delivered tax relief for the first time in 14 years; we’ve introduced FamilyBoost.
veracity.explanation: Claims the tax relief was the first in 14 years — a specific, checkable comparison.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Date of the last personal income tax cut/threshold change before 2024 (IRD/Treasury records); true if the previous change was ~14 years prior (≈2010), false otherwise.

focus.statement: My key concern is how this central government “Coalition of Chaos” is undermining local government at every opportunity.
focus.explanation: A local-government concern is gestured at, but the weight is a party label ("Coalition of Chaos") and a sweeping "at every opportunity" with no specific measure named. Mostly party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Postal voting is no longer fit for purpose in a digital age.
focus.explanation: Engages the voting mechanism itself — the policy question of how local elections are administered. Squarely on-policy, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It will enable ministerial micromanagement and undermine the teaching profession and the academic profession in our universities.
focus.explanation: Engages the bill's substantive effects — ministerial powers and their impact on teaching and academic professions. On-policy scrutiny of the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill deprioritises Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and I think this is actually maybe our third or fourth example of legislation under the National Government where they do this.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about the bill (deprioritising Te Tiriti), but a good part of the weight is a party-pattern framing about the National Government doing this repeatedly.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This was something that was important to them, but I’m still yet to meet a university that says that this is one of their priorities.
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny — argues the freedom-of-expression provision is not sought by the universities it applies to. Engages the substance of the measure, not the other party as such.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In many areas, turnout was below 40 percent, and in some communities, it dropped into the 30s, which is a reflection of a voting system that is confusing, outdated, and disconnected from the lives of everyday New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual turnout figure for the 2025 local elections (below 40% in many areas, into the 30s in some). Load-bearing for her argument that the voting system is failing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official 2025 local body election turnout figures published by councils / Local Government NZ; true if turnout was below 40% across many areas and in the 30s in some, false if materially higher.

veracity.statement: This directly contradicts the Prime Minister in Monday’s post-Cabinet press conference saying he’s discussing the Electoral Commission running the local elections with Minister Watts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister said at Monday's post-Cabinet press conference that he is discussing the Electoral Commission running local elections with Minister Watts. Contested and load-bearing — the whole point is the alleged contradiction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transcript/recording of the Monday post-Cabinet press conference; true if the PM stated he is discussing the Electoral Commission running local elections with Minister Watts, false if no such statement was made.

veracity.statement: Under-resourcing voting systems is a form of voter suppression, though less blatant than this Government’s Electoral Amendment Bill, which would roll back voter enrolment for general elections by 13 days.
veracity.explanation: Contains the checkable claim that the Government's Electoral Amendment Bill would roll back voter enrolment for general elections by 13 days. Specific figure, contested, load-bearing (the surrounding rhetoric is opinion, not the veracity target).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the Government's Electoral Amendment Bill; true if it closes/advances general-election enrolment by 13 days (e.g. ends late enrolment 13 days earlier), false if it changes the enrolment deadline by a materially different amount.

veracity.statement: Despite the attacks on te reo, Te Tiriti, and Māori customary rights by the coalition partners, a strong majority across the country—as of today, 520,113 voters—voted to keep Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific national vote count — 520,113 voters as of that day — for keeping Māori wards. Precise, non-obvious figure a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Aggregated results of the 2025 Māori ward referenda/polls across councils; true if roughly 520,113 votes were cast to keep Māori wards as at 15 October 2025, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Only 13 percent supported this bill in its totality—13 percent out of hundreds of submissions that were received.
veracity.explanation: Specific figure: only 13% of the many submissions received supported the bill in its totality. Contested and load-bearing to his case that the bill lacks support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Departmental report / submissions summary for the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2) at the Education and Workforce Committee; true if about 13% of submissions supported the bill in full, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Most concerning: when I asked the Minister if she had come across any examples, any evidence that validated this particular change, that validated the time that we used in this wonderful Parliament of ours, the only example that Minister Stanford could offer me was Don Brash—Don Brash from Hobson’s Pledge and the ex-leader of the National Party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that when asked for evidence justifying the freedom-of-expression change, the Minister offered only Don Brash as an example. Checkable against the exchange record; contested.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Select committee transcript / official record of the Minister's answer to Halbert's question; true if Don Brash was the sole example the Minister gave, false if she offered other examples.

focus.statement: How are the Government expecting for schools to succeed in these so-called attendance management plans if they are not addressing child poverty?
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the bill's attendance management plan provisions and links them to the underlying policy question of child poverty. On-policy, names a specific mechanism in the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s really clear to me that the ACT Party, at no point in their negotiation agreement, thought of issues like the underlying causes of school attendance, like hardship, inequality, and the housing crisis, and instead are quite happy to use time in this Chamber to debate issues that actually will not lead to better educational achievements.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (that the bill's priorities miss the underlying causes of attendance) but wrapped in party framing about the ACT Party's negotiation choices. Mixed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And that’s why this bill is going to ensure that the school board’s paramount objective is to ensure that schools are able to attain their highest possible standard in educational achievement.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the substance of the bill — the change to school board objectives — describing the specific mechanism the legislation introduces. Entirely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The member, the Green Party member who spoke before me, instead of supporting that, he was actually providing excuses for students to not attend school.
focus.explanation: Characterises the opposing member's stance on attendance rather than engaging the policy directly; there is an attendance-policy point underneath but the weight is on framing the other side. Mixed.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You don’t need to believe me; you can just look at the Government’s own statistics of child poverty to see that more children are projected to not have their basic needs being met as a result of Government decisions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official child poverty projections show more children in material hardship as a consequence of government policy decisions. Contested and load-bearing for his whole argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / MSD official child poverty projections and the Government's own child poverty statistics; true if the official projections show an increase in children not having basic needs met attributable to government policy decisions, false if projections show no increase or a decrease.

veracity.statement: We are seeing more and more evidence of this, particularly with the removal of kupu Māori from children’s books.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that te reo Māori words (kupu) were removed from children's/reading books, presented as evidence of the Government narrowing learning. Contested and specific.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education decisions on te reo Māori words in the phonics/reading books distributed to schools; true if Māori words were removed from those children's books, false if they were not.

focus.statement: I think I’ve heard from the Opposition some criticism that this bill is a bit of a grab bag, but I disagree.
focus.explanation: Engages the bill itself — a criticism of its omnibus structure — rather than attacking the opposition as a party. On-policy debate about the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What this bill does is to clearly establish educational achievement as the paramount objective for school boards, rather than just being the first mentioned of a multitude of different objectives, all of broadly similar way.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the substance and mechanism of the bill — elevating educational achievement to the paramount statutory objective for boards. Squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I heard, effectively, from the Opposition was “Everything’s fine.” No, it’s not fine.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (the state of educational achievement) but delivered through party framing that characterises the Opposition's stance rather than naming a specific policy or figure in this passage.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: For all students, only 23 percent were at the level that they were supposed to be—23 percent; 62 percent were at least a year behind where they should be.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific year 8 maths achievement figures for early 2025 — contested (the argument for the bill rests on it) and non-obvious.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Education / NZ curriculum benchmarking (Curriculum Insights or equivalent) year 8 maths achievement data released in early 2025; true if ~23% at expected curriculum level and ~62% at least a year behind, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: For writing, pretty much the same for all students: 24 percent at level, 61 percent more than a year behind.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific year 8 writing achievement figures — contested and load-bearing for the case that the system is failing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The same Ministry of Education year 8 writing achievement benchmarking data for early 2025; true if ~24% at expected level and ~61% more than a year behind, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the last assessment—in 2022-2023, before this Government took office—reading has dropped in that time, from 2000 to 2023, by a full year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NZ PISA reading performance fell by the equivalent of a full school year of learning between 2000 and 2022. A specific, contested comparison central to the argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OECD PISA NZ reading mean scores 2000 vs 2022, converted to grade-level equivalents (roughly 20 PISA points ≈ one school year); true if the decline equates to about a full year, false if materially less or more.

veracity.statement: The term 2 attendance levels, where young people are at school for more than 90 percent of the time, in 2022, that was 40 percent—40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific regular-attendance figure (90%+ attendance) for term 2 2022. A checkable, non-obvious statistic underpinning the truancy argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education term 2 2022 regular attendance (attending more than 90% of the time) statistics; true if ~40%, false if materially different.

focus.statement: It’s a distracted and out-of-touch Government that is obsessed with imported culture wars.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government as distracted, out-of-touch and obsessed with culture wars. Attacks the other team's general character rather than engaging the bill's mechanism; no specific policy content once the framing is stripped out. Eligible (aimed at a party, not a person).
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is trying to fix a problem that’s not even a problem in the first place, and, in doing so, it’s a serious case of Government overreach into the freedom of expression of universities and a serious overreach on the ability of universities to be self-managing institutes.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the measure before the House: the claimed absence of a problem and the bill's effect on university autonomy and self-management. On-policy substance, whatever the strength of the inference.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s what the schools should be focusing on to ensure that every child learns, progresses, and succeeds, and this bill is about lifting student achievement, improving attendance, and making sure that every young New Zealander gets the best possible start in life.
focus.explanation: Directs the remarks at what the bill does for schools — achievement, attendance, outcomes. Genuinely policy-directed even though vague on detail (that vagueness is Specificity's concern, not Focus's).
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is a distraction from the very valid and urgent concerns of ordinary New Zealanders, who right now want a Government focused on jobs, the public health system, and housing.
focus.explanation: A real policy point — the bill's relationship to competing priorities — but delivered largely as a 'should be doing other things' pivot away from the measure itself. Partly on-policy, partly framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It must be difficult being on the Opposition benches today, as we put this piece of legislation through the House this afternoon.
focus.explanation: Content-free jibe at the Opposition benches with no policy substance once the framing is removed. Aimed at the other team as a group, not a person, so eligible and scores low.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Look at the results this Government is achieving by focusing on the simple things in education and getting them done.
focus.explanation: Gestures at education outcomes (a policy area) but the weight is on crediting the speaker's own Government's record rather than engaging the bill's substance.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the select committee stage, I asked questions of the Minister about how many universities in 2024 had actually restricted speakers from their campuses. The Minister’s answer was zero.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, at select committee, the Minister said zero universities restricted speakers from campuses in 2024. Contested and load-bearing — his 'no problem to fix' case rests on it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee transcript/record for the bill: what the Minister answered when asked how many universities restricted campus speakers in 2024. True if the Minister said none/zero, false if the Minister gave a non-zero figure or no such exchange occurred.

veracity.statement: As colleagues have already pointed out, the only example—the only example—that the Minister could come up with, when asked at select committee, was of the notorious incident of Don Brash, I think, being denied the opportunity to give a Hobson’s Pledge speech at Massey University.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Minister's only justifying example at select committee was the Don Brash/Massey University incident. Load-bearing for the 'manufactured crisis' claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee record for what example(s) the Minister gave when asked to justify the provisions, plus the 2018 record of Massey University's handling of a Don Brash/Hobson's Pledge speaking event. True if the Massey/Brash incident was the sole example the Minister offered, false if the Minister cited other examples or the Brash incident is misdescribed.

focus.statement: This bill guarantees that academics and students within universities will have free speech, but that academic freedoms will be limited, and that universities themselves will not, in fact, be able to have any free speech on issues that the ACT Party doesn't want them to be talking about—political issues, social issues, cultural issues.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill — what it does to academic freedom and institutional speech — rather than attacking a party in general. The 'ACT Party doesn't want' framing is present but the weight is on the mechanism of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They want the Government to be focused on the real issues, like rising cost of living, like the economy that is shrinking, and like the 73,000 New Zealanders who have left under their watch.
focus.explanation: Names concrete issues (cost of living, a contracting economy, emigration figures) but the point is about the Government's priorities rather than the bill before the House — a real policy point in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There's another one that just seems to allow the Minister to cross-subsidise international students with the fees of domestic students.
focus.explanation: Directly engages a specific provision of the bill — cross-subsidising international students from domestic fees — a substantive policy mechanism, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is another piece of legislation that proves and shows why National is more trusted in education compared to that lot these days, and so I commend this bill.
focus.explanation: Content-free party comparison — National 'more trusted' than 'that lot' — with no policy mechanism, figure or outcome named. This is the tribalism case Focus exists to catch; nobody is personally insulted so it stays eligible.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, making the three objectives of safety and rights, inclusion, and giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi subsidiary to one primary objective is contrary to the purpose of the Education and Training Act, which is to establish and regulate an education system that does four things.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance of the bill — the reordering of the Act's statutory objectives — and argues it conflicts with the Act's purpose. On-policy regardless of the argument's strength.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the very party that talks about wanting less Government is in fact, from the very respected Law Society, being told that they are adding needless complexity.
focus.explanation: Makes a genuine policy point (the bill adds needless complexity) but wraps it in party framing about ACT wanting 'less Government' — a real substantive claim carried in tribal packaging.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They want the Government to be focused on the real issues, like rising cost of living, like the economy that is shrinking, and like the 73,000 New Zealanders who have left under their watch.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 73,000 New Zealanders have left the country under the current Government — a specific, contested, load-bearing migration figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ net migration statistics for NZ citizens over the period since the current Government took office in late 2023; true if the net departure of NZ citizens is approximately 73,000, false if materially different from that figure.

focus.statement: It’s a grab bag of a bill. It addresses issues that do not need a new Act; they are already covered in existing regulation or law.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill — its claim is that the measure is redundant because the matters it covers already sit in existing law. That is a policy argument about the bill itself, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But instead, today, at a time when New Zealanders are facing a cost of living crisis, when we are seeing, day after day, people leaving New Zealand, people losing their jobs, this Government is choosing to waste their time with overreach into this area, where the experts are telling us it is not required.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point — the bill is unnecessary overreach that experts say is not required — but it is wrapped in general cost-of-living and emigration framing that carries much of the weight, so it sits between substance and mood-setting.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I have sat here and listened to about seven speeches from the other sides, and do you know what? I have not heard—I have not heard—about lifting the educational achievements of our children, and that is absolutely shameful.
focus.explanation: Names a topic (lifting educational achievement) but the weight of the statement is a complaint about what the other side chose to talk about — 'the other sides' and their 'shameful' speeches — rather than engagement with any provision of the bill. Party framing, not a policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is about lifting school and student achievement, improving attendance, and ensuring every young New Zealander gets the best possible start at life.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the bill's purpose — the outcomes it is meant to deliver (achievement, attendance). On-policy with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New Zealand’s children cannot learn if they are not in school, and this bill delivers a much-improved approach to attendance management.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific mechanism of the bill — its attendance-management provisions — and the reasoning for them. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we heard from Labour and the Greens is their contention that hearing different opinions is akin to some kind of violence.
focus.explanation: Touches the free-expression substance of the bill, but frames it as a characterisation of what Labour and the Greens supposedly contend, so the weight falls on the opposing parties' position rather than on the provision itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The purpose of this bill is to redesign the vocational education and training system and increase industry leadership in vocational education and training, particularly in the areas of standard setting and work-based training; and restore local decision-making to polytechnics and their communities which support regional development.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the bill's substantive purpose and mechanisms — industry leadership, standard setting, work-based training, local decision-making. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know why that is: it’s because the promise that the National Government sold last election—to reintroduce regional autonomy for polytechnics—this bill does not achieve that.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific commitment (reintroducing regional autonomy for polytechnics) and argues the bill fails to deliver it. Holding a named promise to account is on-policy, not tribalism. For Focus the subject is always the speaker's own conduct.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The cost is jobs—hundreds of jobs in the vocational sector: gone.
focus.explanation: Names a concrete outcome of the reform — job losses in the vocational sector — which is engagement with the policy's real-world effect rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The cost is jobs—hundreds of jobs in the vocational sector: gone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that hundreds of vocational-sector jobs have been or will be lost as a result of the reforms — a contested, load-bearing quantity claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reported net job losses across Te Pūkenga / the polytechnic and vocational sector attributable to the 2025 vocational-education reforms (e.g. TEC/Te Pūkenga restructuring figures, union or ministerial statements on roles disestablished); true if losses run into the hundreds, false if materially fewer.

focus.statement: The Minister knows that the reports and the advice that she has had is that she needs at least $200 million to stand up 16 polytechnics.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: names a specific figure ($200m), a specific object (16 polytechnics) and the gap between the funding provided and the funding advised. Scrutiny of a named commitment, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We can make all the promises in the world, but the reality of this legislation is that it has come at the cost of jobs, of courses, and of campuses.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill — its effect on jobs, courses and campuses. On-policy consequences of the measure, though stated without figures.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When we look at the numbers of NEETs increasing under this National Government—under Christopher Luxon—this bill does not take responsibility for that problem.
focus.explanation: Names a specific outcome (rising NEET numbers) and faults the bill for not addressing it — legitimate scrutiny. Some weight sits in the party framing ('under this National Government—under Christopher Luxon'), pulling it below the top of the scale.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The National Government simply cannot afford this legislation.
focus.explanation: Directed at the policy's financial viability, the central thread of the speech. Party naming is present but the point is about the measure's affordability.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We know that, under this Government, thousands and thousands less apprentices are graduating under their watch—thousands.
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny naming a workforce outcome (falling apprentice graduations) relevant to the vocational-training bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Twenty thousand construction workers have gone off to other parts of the world, and thousands of apprentices aren’t graduating or enrolling under their watch.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy consequence — workforce loss and falling apprentice numbers — with a specific figure, tying it to the skills the sector needs.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill does not have industry backing—it does not have industry backing—and it came through clearly in the submissions that were made and that the Education and Workforce Committee heard.
focus.explanation: On-policy: appeals to the substance of the select committee submissions on the bill, not to party character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It doesn’t make sense to disestablish workforce development councils and re-establish a whole new entity while giving them only half the funding that they used to have under the old model.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the structural mechanism of the bill — replacing WDCs with industry skills boards — and names a funding comparison ('half the funding'). Substantive policy critique.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I expect a high level of legislation coming into this House, but, particularly when it comes to our education sector, I believe that this is a space where we can work, in a bipartisan way, to address the systemic challenges that are in front of us.
focus.explanation: Addresses the policy process constructively — the standard expected of education legislation and scope for bipartisan work on systemic challenges. On-topic, no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister knows that the reports and the advice that she has had is that she needs at least $200 million to stand up 16 polytechnics.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Minister's own advice put the required figure at at least $200m against $20m provided. Contested and load-bearing to his financial-viability argument; I have no independent knowledge of the advised figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The official advice/reports provided to the Minister on the funding required to establish 16 stand-alone polytechnics; true if that advice states at least ~$200m is needed, false if the advised figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: When we look at the numbers of NEETs increasing under this National Government—under Christopher Luxon—this bill does not take responsibility for that problem.
veracity.explanation: Factual claim that NEET numbers have increased under the current government. Checkable against official statistics and load-bearing; NZ NEET rates did appear to rise through the 2024–25 downturn, so I lean true but am not certain of the trend over the exact window.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ NEET (not in employment, education or training) youth rate/count over the current government's term; true if NEET numbers rose across that period, false if flat or falling.

veracity.statement: Twenty thousand construction workers have gone off to other parts of the world, and thousands of apprentices aren’t graduating or enrolling under their watch.
veracity.explanation: Specific quantitative claim (20,000 construction workers emigrated). Contested and checkable; a construction downturn drove departures in 2024–25 but I cannot confirm the magnitude.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Migration/departure data for construction-sector workers over the relevant period (e.g. Stats NZ migration or industry workforce figures); true if roughly 20,000 construction workers left NZ, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: It doesn’t make sense to disestablish workforce development councils and re-establish a whole new entity while giving them only half the funding that they used to have under the old model.
veracity.explanation: Specific comparative claim that the replacement bodies get only half the former funding. Contested and load-bearing; I have no independent figure for either allocation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Funding allocated to the new industry skills boards compared with funding for the workforce development councils under the previous model; true if the ISBs receive roughly half, false if the ratio is materially different.

focus.statement: With nearly one-in-seven jobs lost, with campuses closed across the board, and with programmes disestablished, it’s hard to see that this is what success looks like for this National Government.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy outcome directly — named consequences (jobs lost, campuses closed, programmes disestablished) of the vocational education changes. Mild party framing ('for this National Government') but the weight is on substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If it was such a positive thing, why are polytechs required to be part of it but not required to be consented for it?
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the federation model mechanism — the compulsory-membership-without-consent design of the policy. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The only people that the Minister had to consult when appointing or removing the chairperson or deputy chairperson is the chairperson or the deputy chairperson themselves.
focus.explanation: A specific policy detail about consultation requirements for appointments — entirely on the mechanism of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New section 380 also makes provisions to disestablish the industry skills boards via Order in Councils, so there is some inconsistency in the legislation.
focus.explanation: Names a specific clause and identifies a drafting inconsistency — engagement with the substance of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I agree with my colleague Shanan Halbert that there should have been a lift and shift because, with the additional responsibilities that have been overlaid, essentially, they’re having to do twice the work with half of the funding that’s been required.
focus.explanation: Engages the industry skills boards' funding and workload under the policy — on the substance of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is really important and what we are doing through this bill is we are restoring regional decision-making.
focus.explanation: Describes what the bill does — restoring regional decision-making. On the policy, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is important because this is about local needs, this is about local jobs, and it’s about ensuring that local industries have a stronger voice.
focus.explanation: Gives the policy rationale — local needs, jobs and industry voice. Squarely on the substance of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s why that amendment was made in the select committee process to reflect that the council of a polytechnic should, as far as is reasonably practicable, reflect the communities in the region that the polytechnic serves.
focus.explanation: Explains a specific select-committee amendment and its wording — entirely on the policy detail.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have realised that there were issues with the vocational education and training system, but when they were in Government they didn’t realise that they didn’t ask those kind of questions.
focus.explanation: Primarily about the opposition parties' past record and inconsistency rather than the measure before the House; only glancingly names the VET system. Largely party framing, not policy substance.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: With nearly one-in-seven jobs lost, with campuses closed across the board, and with programmes disestablished, it’s hard to see that this is what success looks like for this National Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific, contested and load-bearing figure — that nearly one-in-seven jobs were lost in the polytech sector. Not a verdict.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Employment figures for the ITP/polytech sector across the Te Pūkenga restructuring period (e.g. TEC or union workforce data); true if roughly one-in-seven (~14%) of jobs were lost, false if the loss is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Again, I keep coming back to the words of the Treasury advice about how the ITP sector would, essentially, be the same, if not worse, than they would be coming out of Te Pūkenga as they did before Te Pūkenga was established.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim about what Treasury advice concluded on sector viability — checkable against the advice itself. Load-bearing to his opposition case.
veracity.subject: other
