focus.statement: This bill fulfils a specific coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National.
focus.explanation: On-policy: locates the bill within a named coalition commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think we go back to when the first claims were lodged under this Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, that every single centimetre of our coastline was subject to a claim.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy problem — the extent of coastline subject to customary marine title applications.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Prime Minister of the time, John Key, made it very clear that there would be very limited numbers of successful claims because of the need to prove uninterrupted title for the duration since 1840.
focus.explanation: On-policy: the expected scope of successful claims under the original test.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This piece of legislation is clarifying the intention of the original legislation, and, therefore, New Zealand First commends the bill to the House.
focus.explanation: On-policy: frames support around the bill's effect of clarifying the original Act's intention.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As a party, we are committed to one law for all and that every New Zealander is treated equally regardless of race, religion, or background.
focus.explanation: A party-values statement of principle rather than engagement with the bill's mechanism; the weight is on party identity, not the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The Minister acknowledged in the Committee of the whole House that he was concerned about the impact on the fishing industry of recognising customary rights.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Minister said in committee about the fishing industry and customary rights.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Committee of the whole House Hansard for this bill; true if the Minister expressed concern about the fishing industry's exposure from recognising customary rights, false if no such statement appears.

veracity.statement: Section 106(3) of the MACA Act states that, unless there is evidence to the contrary, non-extinguishment of customary interest will be assumed.
veracity.explanation: A specific, load-bearing claim about what section 106(3) of the 2011 Act provides — the presumption of non-extinguishment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of section 106(3) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011; true if it establishes a presumption of non-extinguishment absent contrary evidence, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: It is a thing that is recognised in other colonised lands that don't have treaties, such as Australia, and it was recognised from even the earliest days of Government in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that native/customary title is recognised in Australia (a jurisdiction without a treaty) and from the earliest days of NZ government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian native-title law (Mabo v Queensland (No 2) 1992 and the Native Title Act 1993); true if native title is a recognised doctrine there, false if not.

veracity.statement: That has, unfortunately, been undermined by a number of court decisions, including, obviously, the Edwards decision.
veracity.explanation: Claims court decisions, notably Edwards, undermined the exacting 2011 test for customary marine title.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ court decisions on the MACA customary marine title test, especially Re Edwards (Court of Appeal); true if they lowered/undermined the 2011 threshold, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: This bill fulfils a specific coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National.
veracity.explanation: Claims the bill discharges a specific National–NZ First coalition-agreement commitment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–NZ First coalition agreement (Nov 2023); true if it commits to amending MACA / the customary marine title test, false if no such commitment is present.

veracity.statement: I think we go back to when the first claims were lodged under this Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, that every single centimetre of our coastline was subject to a claim.
veracity.explanation: Claims essentially the entire coastline was subject to a customary marine title claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / High Court records of customary marine title applications under MACA; true if applications collectively covered essentially the whole coastline, false if substantial stretches were unclaimed.

veracity.statement: The Prime Minister of the time, John Key, made it very clear that there would be very limited numbers of successful claims because of the need to prove uninterrupted title for the duration since 1840.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to John Key a statement that successful claims would be very limited given the uninterrupted-title test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements / Hansard by PM John Key around passage of the 2011 MACA Act; true if he said successful claims would be very limited due to the uninterrupted-title requirement, false otherwise.

focus.statement: What they are doing with these foolish amendments is destroying the settlement that the National Party and the Māori Party reached in 2010.
focus.explanation: Strip the 'foolish' framing and a real policy point remains: the claim that the amendments undo a specific 2010 settlement. Names a concrete measure and outcome, so it engages the substance rather than being pure party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is the most racist policy—I'm talking about policy here; this is the most racist policy that this Government has supported probably in—what, the last two weeks?
focus.explanation: Despite saying 'I'm talking about policy here', the content is a characterisation of the Government and a jibe that they 'exceed themselves week by week'. No mechanism, cost, figure or outcome is named — it is party framing about a policy rather than engagement with it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I rise to speak on the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill, in support because New Zealanders already face a high cost, sitting in traffic.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House, engaging the problem it targets (the cost of congestion). No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is about freeing up traffic so we can have a more free-flowing system.
focus.explanation: Directly about the bill's purpose and mechanism (easing congestion); on-policy, no tribalism. Specificity is low but that is a separate attribute.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As the last speaker on this third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, I don’t want to drag it out, but I do want to just put on record that Ngāti Porou has got a carve-out from this Act and their takutai moana is not going to be affected by this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific, non-obvious fact: that Ngāti Porou is exempt from this Amendment Bill via a separate carve-out. Load-bearing and checkable against the statute.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whether Ngāti Porou's takutai moana is governed by a separate statute (the Ngā Rohe Moana o Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Porou Act 2019) that exempts its area from this Amendment Bill; true if such a carve-out exists and the bill preserves it, false if the bill applies to Ngāti Porou's area.

veracity.statement: We've never stopped access to the foreshore.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Māori exercise of customary rights since 2004/2011 has never blocked public access to the foreshore — a contested, load-bearing premise of his argument that the reforms are unnecessary.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whether any customary marine title award, or the operation of the 2011 Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, has removed or excluded public access to the foreshore; true if public access has been preserved throughout, false if any award has excluded public access.

focus.statement: Under this new regime, a whānau’s ability to control access to their rohe moana must be proven through continuous physical activity, as if tikanga can only exist when measured in footprints and fishing nets.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill's evidential test (continuous physical use vs tikanga-based connection). On-policy engagement with the mechanism, regardless of whether the argument is sound.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was a deal done as a dirty deal that legislated away Māori customary rights to gain power, and I want that on the record.
focus.explanation: Names a real policy effect (legislating away customary rights) but the weight is on party-motive framing ("dirty deal ... to gain power"). A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You can keep changing the rules. You can keep shifting the goal posts.
focus.explanation: Party-directed and about the government's conduct in altering the legal test; references the rule-change (a policy referent) but names no specific measure, figure or outcome. Not a personal attack, so eligible.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The amendments align the recognition of the customary marine titles more closely with tikanga and address concerns addressed by the courts.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what the amendments do (aligning recognition with tikanga, responding to the courts). On-policy engagement, though low in specific detail.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill seeks to restore the clarity to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, it seeks to protect property rights that foster legal clarity, and it seeks to reduce legal disputes and ambiguity.
focus.explanation: Addresses the bill's stated policy purposes (legal clarity, property rights, reducing disputes). On-policy, no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It applies the new test back to 24 July 2024, meaning that any case heard before the New Zealand courts can be reopened.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill applies the amended test retrospectively to a specific date (24 July 2024) and that decided cases can be reopened. Specific, contested and load-bearing to her retrospectivity argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement/application provisions of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill as reported; true if it applies the amended test to matters from 24 July 2024 and allows decided cases to be reopened, false if the date or the retrospective reach differs materially.

veracity.statement: Cabinet was explicitly warned by officials not to proceed in this way.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that officials advised Cabinet against proceeding with the retrospective approach. Contested and load-bearing to the "advice ignored" argument; she asserts it rather than relaying it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Regulatory Impact Statement or official advice / Cabinet papers on the Bill; true if officials advised against proceeding in this manner, false if no such advice was given.

veracity.statement: That advice was ignored and, as a result, up to seven cases may now need to be reheard, affecting more than 280 kilometres of coastline and consuming millions of dollars in costs.
veracity.explanation: A specific quantified claim: up to seven cases reheard, more than 280 km of coastline affected, millions in costs. Specific, non-obvious figures a well-informed reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official estimates (RIS or ministry advice) of cases affected by the retrospective provision; true if roughly up to seven cases and ~280+ km of coastline are implicated, false if materially fewer cases or less coastline.

veracity.statement: Hoi anō rā, I think the best way for me to address this bill is as a wīwī Nāti, as Ngāti Porou being the first and only iwi to have our own takutai moana bill.
veracity.explanation: Contains a specific, non-obvious factual claim: that Ngāti Porou is the first and only iwi to have its own takutai moana legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative record for iwi-specific takutai moana / marine title legislation; true if Ngāti Porou (e.g. Nga Rohe Moana o Nga Hapu o Ngati Porou Act 2019) is the only iwi with its own such Act, false if another iwi also has bespoke standalone legislation.

focus.statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
focus.explanation: Names specific policy decisions (halving the active-transport budget, raising farebox recovery) and a specific consequence (higher fares). This is legitimate scrutiny of a named government commitment, which is the job of an opposition MP and scores high on Focus regardless of the party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The fundamental problem with the transport policy is its obsession with building more roads and tunnels.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance of the transport investment policy (roads and tunnels) and makes a policy-directed critique. The word 'obsession' is mild framing, but the remainder is about the policy, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It clarifies that the revenue gained must be ploughed back in for the benefit of public transport in the scheme, in and around and within—as we’ve discussed in select committee—the area, and it clarifies the exemptions that are basically allowed.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill directly — the revenue hypothecation provision and the exemptions clause as amended in select committee. Entirely about the policy mechanism, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two factual claims about government funding decisions: that the walking and cycling budget was halved and that the public transport farebox recovery ratio was increased. Speaker is asserting these herself, not relaying them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget documents / NZTA and Ministry of Transport funding allocations for the walking and cycling activity class across the relevant years (true if the allocation was approximately halved) and the GPS/NZTA farebox recovery ratio target (true if it was raised). False if the active-transport budget was not roughly halved or the farebox recovery target was not increased.

veracity.statement: Because congestion is only one negative impact of our car dependency, the health costs from air pollution actually exceeds the cost of congestion itself, and yet this bill ignores that evidence entirely, presumably because it’s an inconvenient truth that air pollution from motor vehicles—and this is the 53rd Parliament, so no doubt the costs have increased, like everything else—causes approximately $10 billion in social costs every year, including 13,000 cases of childhood asthma prevalence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific quantified claims: that motor-vehicle air pollution causes approximately $10 billion in social costs annually and around 13,000 cases of childhood asthma. These are contested, load-bearing figures central to her low-emission-zone argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The HAPINZ (Health and Air Pollution in New Zealand) study figures for social costs of vehicle air pollution and childhood asthma cases; true if it reports roughly $10 billion in annual social costs and ~13,000 childhood asthma cases attributable to motor-vehicle emissions, false if the figures are materially different.

veracity.statement: The noise complaints in the city of Manhattan have fallen by 70 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — a 70 percent fall in noise complaints in Manhattan following the congestion-pricing scheme. A specific, non-obvious statistic a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NYC 311 noise-complaint data for the congestion-pricing (Manhattan CBD) zone before and after the January 2025 scheme launch; true if complaints fell by approximately 70 percent, false if the reduction was materially smaller or absent.

veracity.statement: The city raises $50,000—or $50 million I should say—each month from the scheme that it can then plough back into public transport, and buses travel faster in Manhattan as a result.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific monthly revenue figure (~$50 million) for the New York congestion-pricing scheme and that buses travel faster as a result. Self-corrects the figure mid-sentence; the intended claim is $50 million per month.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MTA reported monthly revenue from the Manhattan congestion-pricing scheme in 2025; true if it is approximately $50 million per month, false if materially different. Bus-speed data for the zone would settle the secondary claim.

focus.statement: This reform, and zoning reform to allow more intensification, particularly around transit corridors, is going to help us move our cities into a much more efficient and livable 21st century form.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure before the House — how time-of-use charging plus intensification changes urban form. Names the policy mechanism, no party framing. Squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By adding a small charge to the use of that particular roading network at particular times of the day, it will incentivise people to change their transport behaviour, to take another mode, to get on the train or the bus or the ferry or to time their journey for a less expensive hour when they don't have to pay that extra fee.
focus.explanation: Describes the actual mechanism of the charging scheme — the pricing signal and behavioural response. Entirely about the policy, no reference to the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So this bill encourages travel outside the peak hours, which can ease congestion and improve travel reliability.
focus.explanation: Directly engages what the bill does and its intended effect on congestion and reliability. On-policy, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: However, I made it clear in the select committee that I only support this bill with one clear condition: if any revenue is collected in the Mt Roskill electorate, I want it to return to Mt Roskill—for future transport infrastructure.
focus.explanation: States a specific, substantive condition on the bill — hypothecation of collected revenue to local transport infrastructure. Engages the measure itself, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We can say with certainty that it has the potential to reduce 10 percent or more of drivers at a particular time of day when the charging is in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific empirical figure about the effect of congestion charging on peak-time traffic, drawing on named overseas schemes. Contested and load-bearing to his case for the bill, so worth checking rather than scene-setting.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed or official evaluations of congestion / time-of-use charging schemes in London, Stockholm, Singapore, Milan and New York; true if documented traffic reductions of around 10 percent or more at charged times are typical, false if typical reductions are materially below 10 percent.

veracity.statement: It is not possible to keep adding more and more road space and think that that's going to reduce congestion, because it never does.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the induced-demand generalisation in absolute terms — that road expansion never durably reduces congestion in growing cities. This premise underpins his whole argument for the bill and is the sort of claim critics of congestion charging would dispute, so it is load-bearing and contested.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transport-economics literature on induced demand and road-capacity expansion in growing cities; true if capacity expansions in high-demand cities are shown not to durably reduce congestion, false if capacity expansion reliably reduces congestion.

focus.statement: Of course, the Auckland motorway and roading network is a network, and the spending needs to go across the network to ensure that the network functions effectively, which of course will, in turn, help people in Mount Roskill.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill directly — whether congestion-charge revenue should be spent locally or across the network. A policy-design argument, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We must ensure that they have a choice to either pay the congestion charge, or to move along less congested routes, or to take—and this would be, I guess, the best solution—public transport.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy mechanism: that congestion charging requires viable alternatives such as public transport for workers to choose. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are a number of reasons why congestion charging is a great idea: the environmental benefits, the revenue generation beyond what we already have, the sustainable infrastructure, improved cities, and, of course, economic efficiency, which is what we're all about on this side of the House: economic growth and efficiency.
focus.explanation: Lists genuine policy merits of congestion charging (environment, revenue, efficiency), so predominantly on-policy, though wrapped in some 'this side of the House' party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: London and Stokholm are both great examples of congestion charging working where traffic reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent in London; 20 to 25 percent in Stokholm.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the policy with concrete international evidence for whether congestion charging reduces traffic. On-policy accountability of the merits, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That's a viable solution along State Highway 16 now that a busway is at last being retrofitted into State Highway 16.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that a busway is being retrofitted into State Highway 16. Specific and non-obvious infrastructure claim a well-informed reader could not confirm from memory; load-bearing for her public-transport-alternative argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / NZTA Waka Kotahi project records on whether busway works are underway along State Highway 16 (the Northwestern corridor) as at October 2025; true if such construction is in progress, false if no such works exist.

veracity.statement: London and Stokholm are both great examples of congestion charging working where traffic reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent in London; 20 to 25 percent in Stokholm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific figures for traffic reduction under the London congestion charge and Stockholm congestion tax. Contested, load-bearing (the figures carry her claim that the scheme works), and precise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published evaluations of the London congestion charge and the Stockholm congestion tax on measured traffic reduction; true if London fell roughly 15-30% and Stockholm roughly 20-25%, false if materially different.

focus.statement: The reason for time of use charging is to reduce congestion at peak times.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the policy's stated purpose and mechanism (reducing peak congestion), with no party framing. On-policy substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s not about charging all the time; it’s about charging at the times when there is the highest traffic use.
focus.explanation: Clarifies how the charging mechanism works — timing tied to demand. Entirely about the measure, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Also, it potentially allows us to delay or to avoid expensive capital investment where that might otherwise be proposed just for the sake of relieving peak congestion.
focus.explanation: Engages a substantive policy rationale (avoiding capital cost by spreading peak demand). On-policy content, no tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The one we did argue about was public transport, because the whole rationale for time of use charging is to change the time or the mode, and public transport is about the mode.
focus.explanation: Reasons about a specific exemption (public transport) from the policy's own logic. Directly about the measure's design.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I also submitted, as Mayor of Wellington, along with Greater Wellington Regional Council on behalf of the Wellington region, to the 2021 inquiry on congestion charging, which Greg O’Connor chaired on behalf of the Auckland area—but, obviously, Wellington was very, very interested in this.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific, non-obvious fact: that the 2021 Parliamentary inquiry into congestion charging was chaired by Greg O'Connor. A verifiable attribution a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee record for the 2021 inquiry into congestion pricing (Auckland); true if Greg O'Connor was its chair, false if someone else chaired it.

focus.statement: We also think that new section 65C(2), inserted by clause 4, allows too much ministerial control, and that’s about protecting local autonomy.
focus.explanation: Engages a named clause of the bill before the House (section 65C(2), clause 4) and the specific concern it raises about ministerial control versus local autonomy. Squarely on the policy, no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m all for hypothecating the money—I think Auckland sounds like it needs it to address its own problems.
focus.explanation: Addresses a substantive policy design question — whether the congestion-charge revenue should be hypothecated to Auckland’s own transport problems. On-topic engagement with the measure, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We did have these half-price fares; the Government has removed them, so I’m keen to know what this Government is going to do to make sure the other side of the ledger of the congestion charge is about enabling people to get other forms of transport.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that half-price public transport fares existed and were removed by the current Government. Load-bearing to her argument that the congestion charge needs a public-transport counterpart, and the sort of record claim the other side might contest.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / Waka Kotahi records and Budget announcements on the half-price public transport fare subsidy: true if universal half-price fares were introduced and subsequently ended by the National-led coalition Government; false if they were never removed or never existed.

focus.statement: We respect the unions’ right to strike. We also encourage them to think about the impact they’re having on kids, parents, and patients.
focus.explanation: Engages the strike issue and its effects (a policy consideration) rather than attacking Labour, but stays at the level of rhetoric about impact rather than the mechanism the question raised.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we have said is that we expect teachers to be able to come around the bargaining table and negotiate with their employer, the Public Service Commissioner, and actually do the negotiation there.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the bargaining process and who negotiates with teachers — on-policy content, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When I looked at the numbers a few months ago—and don’t hold me to account—the 38 percent increase in the size of the gaming sector, I think it actually hit something like $780 million in the last year, which is fantastic.
focus.explanation: Directly on the gaming sector under discussion, citing sector figures rather than diverting to the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re getting a question on the third Labour policy of this week, but we didn’t get one for one and two. This is really the big deal that’s going to move the needle from Labour!
focus.explanation: Entirely about Labour's choice of questions and mocking their agenda — no policy content on the gaming rebate that was asked about. This is the content-free party framing Focus exists to catch; no individual is insulted so Civility passes it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government has come to the table and put a record investment in Budget 2025 of over $700 million.
focus.explanation: On-policy: engages the learning support investment substantively rather than turning to the opposition's record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why isn’t he aware that the gaming sector has grown 86 percent in the last 2½ years since the gaming rebate was introduced by the previous Labour Government and that his Government, despite repeated requests from the sector, has not been willing to expand eligibility so that the budget that was set aside for it actually gets spent?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny naming a specific policy (the game development rebate and its eligibility) and a specific outcome — accountability, not tribalism, so it scores high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she stand by her statement that “Costs are under control, and inflation is under control” when there have been four consecutive increases in inflation?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny grounded in a specific claimed outcome (four consecutive inflation increases) tested against the Minister's own statement — on-policy accountability.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When I looked at the numbers a few months ago—and don’t hold me to account—the 38 percent increase in the size of the gaming sector, I think it actually hit something like $780 million in the last year, which is fantastic.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the game development sector grew 38 percent and reached about $780 million in the last year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official figures on New Zealand's game development / interactive media sector revenue and growth for the most recent year (NZGDA annual survey / MBIE); true if the sector grew ~38% and reached ~$780m, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s also why we’re backing farmers because, actually, dairy’s up 14 percent, red meat’s up about 9 percent, and horticulture’s up 19 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific export/sector growth figures: dairy up 14 percent, red meat up about 9 percent, horticulture up 19 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries revenue figures for the stated period; true if dairy ~+14%, red meat ~+9%, horticulture ~+19%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It shows that the super fund's total size was $85 billion at 30 June 2025, with average return since its inception of 10.1 percent per annum.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the NZ Super Fund was $85 billion at 30 June 2025 with a since-inception return of 10.1 percent per annum, citing the annual report.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Super Fund 2024/25 annual report; true if total fund size ~$85b at 30 June 2025 and since-inception return ~10.1% p.a., false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Three years ago, it was 7.3 percent. It is now 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual inflation was 7.3 percent three years before October 2025 and is 3 percent now.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation rate for ~October 2022 and the most recent quarter to October 2025; true if ~7.3% then and ~3% now, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Government has come to the table and put a record investment in Budget 2025 of over $700 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2025 allocated over $700 million to learning support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 documents / Vote Education learning support allocation; true if new learning support funding exceeds $700m, false if materially less.

veracity.statement: Why isn’t he aware that the gaming sector has grown 86 percent in the last 2½ years since the gaming rebate was introduced by the previous Labour Government and that his Government, despite repeated requests from the sector, has not been willing to expand eligibility so that the budget that was set aside for it actually gets spent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts the gaming sector has grown 86 percent in the 2½ years since the rebate was introduced, directly contradicting the PM's 38 percent figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Game development sector revenue at the rebate's introduction (~2.5 years prior) versus now; true if grown ~86%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: How can she stand by her statement that “Costs are under control, and inflation is under control” when there have been four consecutive increases in inflation?
veracity.explanation: Asserts inflation has increased in four consecutive quarters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly CPI annual-rate series leading up to October 2025; true if the annual inflation rate rose in four consecutive quarters, false otherwise.

focus.statement: As I outlined to the House yesterday, the Government’s spending $1.2 billion to move the next tranche of the roads of national significance to the next phase of development following the board’s approval of the investment cases.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance directly — a named transport programme, a figure, and the decision stage. No party content; squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The East West Link is a very important project that I think some members have been familiar with for quite some time, and the Hamilton Southern Links project will unlock over 17,000 new houses and, it’s estimated, over 7,000 new jobs in this extremely fast-growing area of the upper North Island.
focus.explanation: Names specific projects and their projected outputs (houses, jobs). Wholly policy-directed; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: After the previous Government did not advance the case for Let’s Get Wellington Moving, we are committed to delivering meaningful improvements to State Highway 1 through Wellington, including a second Mount Victoria tunnel, a second Terrace tunnel, three-laning Vivian Street so you can no longer park on State Highway 1, Basin Reserve grade separation, and widening Ruahine Street and Wellington Road.
focus.explanation: Highly specific list of named works and locations. The glance at the previous Government is minor next to a detailed policy commitment; on-policy throughout.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, they’re not forced to do anything. I would like to just say that we have been listening to them, which is why we have delivered the biggest investment in learning support in a generation, more than they did in the last six years combined; which is why we have invested in paying for their teacher registration fees; which is why we’ve invested in an aspiring principal programme; which is why we’ve invested in a teacher bonding scheme, among many, many things we’ve done to back the sector.
focus.explanation: Answers with a list of concrete education-policy measures (learning support, registration fees, principal programme, bonding scheme). Only mild party framing ("more than they did"); the weight is policy substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, they do have a choice, and here is an example of a union that did have a choice: the Primary Principals’ Collective Bargaining Union, with over 500 members, chose not to strike; chose to be at the bargaining table with the Public Service Commission; chose to be open and transparent; chose to come to a settlement—a good, fair, and reasonable settlement.
focus.explanation: A real point about the bargaining process, but framed as a contrast between unions rather than the substance of the dispute; part policy, part positioning.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, it turns out I’ve got hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of friends, because that’s how many people are turning up to the Curriculum Roadshow to learn about the changes and the reform in education that is going to be raising achievement and closing the education gap in this country—which is more than those guys did in six years.
focus.explanation: There is a policy thread (curriculum reform, closing the education gap), but the statement is mostly a rebuttal about her own engagement capped with a party jibe ("more than those guys did in six years").
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why have over 40,000 educators been forced to take to the streets just to get their Minister to listen to their concerns?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny naming a specific outcome (the scale of the strike), though framed around the Minister not listening rather than a policy mechanism. On-policy accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he stand by his statement, in response to our questions yesterday, that nurses have safe staffing conditions, when Te Whatu Ora’s own data showed that 50 percent of day shifts were understaffed in 16 districts over 10 months last year in our hospitals?
focus.explanation: Named policy (nurse staffing), named source and specific figures. Classic scrutiny holding the Government to account for a stated position — scores high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will the Prime Minister commit to empowering Government negotiators to turn up to the bargaining table equipped with the resources necessary to meet the actual real-world need to fix our education and healthcare systems?
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance of the bargaining process and resourcing for health and education; policy-directed though not carrying a specific figure.

focus.statement: The fact that, in less than two years, we’ve added 2,100 extra nurses into Health New Zealand is a really good thing, and the fact that we’ve made consistent efforts and investments in the healthcare system—$17 billion in our first Budget; up another 7 percent in our second Budget—is all good stuff.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, in answer to the first part of the question, there is no hiring freeze.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the policy claim put to him (a health hiring freeze) and disputes it. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I’m just very proud of the progress that we’ve taken since the departure of a Labour-Greens Government—that, clearly, we have put more money in, in the history of New Zealand; we have put more workforce into the healthcare system; we have good clarity on targets; and we now expect delivery from Health New Zealand to support patients.
focus.explanation: Contains policy content (funding, workforce, targets) but leans on party framing ("since the departure of a Labour-Greens Government") and vague superlatives rather than engaging the neonatal-staffing question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Well, they’re not forced to do anything. I would like to just say that we have been listening to them, which is why we have delivered the biggest investment in learning support in a generation, more than they did in the last six years combined; which is why we have invested in paying for their teacher registration fees; which is why we’ve invested in an aspiring principal programme; which is why we’ve invested in a teacher bonding scheme, among many, many things we’ve done to back the sector.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a superlative comparison — the biggest learning-support investment in a generation and more than the previous Government's six years combined. Contested and load-bearing to her defence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare total learning-support funding committed by this Government (Budget 2024/2025 Vote Education) against the combined learning-support spending increases of 2017-2023; true if the current commitment exceeds the prior six years combined and is the largest in a generation, false if it does not.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, in response to our questions yesterday, that nurses have safe staffing conditions, when Te Whatu Ora’s own data showed that 50 percent of day shifts were understaffed in 16 districts over 10 months last year in our hospitals?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific, sourced statistic on hospital understaffing. Contested and load-bearing to the exchange.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Health NZ safe-staffing (CCDM/TrendCare) reporting for the period referenced; true if roughly 50% of day shifts were recorded as understaffed across 16 districts over the 10-month period, false if materially lower or unsupported by that data.

veracity.statement: The fact that, in less than two years, we’ve added 2,100 extra nurses into Health New Zealand is a really good thing, and the fact that we’ve made consistent efforts and investments in the healthcare system—$17 billion in our first Budget; up another 7 percent in our second Budget—is all good stuff.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific net workforce gain (2,100 extra nurses in under two years); contested and load-bearing to his rebuttal on staffing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand nursing workforce headcount/FTE change from late 2023 to the statement date; true if net additional nurses is approximately 2,100 within the roughly two-year window, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Well, in answer to the first part of the question, there is no hiring freeze.
veracity.explanation: A flat denial directly contradicting the questioner's premise; there were widely reported vacancy-control/recruitment restrictions the Government declined to call a freeze, so this is genuinely contested and load-bearing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ workforce/recruitment policy in force at the statement date; false if a hiring freeze or equivalent recruitment pause or vacancy-control was in effect, true if recruitment was open without such a control.

veracity.statement: I could point to the progress made on our ambitious target to see 20,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime by 2029, and the most recent data released for the 12 months to May shows there were 29,000 fewer victims than when we came into Government; 9,000 ahead of our target.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure: 29,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime in the 12 months to May than at the change of government, described as 9,000 ahead of a 20,000-by-2029 target. Contested, specific and load-bearing to the 'plan is working' claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Crime and Victims Survey (Ministry of Justice) victimisation figures for the 12 months to May cited; true if the reduction versus the 2023 baseline is ~29,000 victims of serious violent crime, false if materially different or if the comparison uses a different measure.

veracity.statement: Well, our trial of clamping and seizing the cars of people who have not paid their court fines and reparations began in July and is set to expand, after it achieved more than $225,000 in fines and the seizure of 115 vehicles.
veracity.explanation: Specific operational figures for the clamping trial: start in July, over $225,000 recovered, 115 vehicles seized. Non-obvious and checkable against Ministry of Justice / bailiff records.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice or Collections figures for the vehicle clamping/seizure trial; true if it recovered >$225,000 and seized 115 vehicles since July, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, alongside our target to reduce the number of victims of serious crime, we’ve also got a target led by Minister Chhour to reduce the number of children and young people with serious and persistent offending by 15 percent, which, the good news is, we have achieved as a Government already.
veracity.explanation: Claims the 15 percent reduction target for children and young people with serious and persistent offending has already been achieved. Contested and load-bearing to the youth-crime record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government target dashboard / Oranga Tamariki-Police data on serious and persistent youth offenders; true if the count has fallen ≥15% against the target baseline, false if it has not yet met 15%.

veracity.statement: In the last financial year, more than nine tonnes of illicit drugs were stopped from entering New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Specific quantity of illicit drugs interdicted in the last financial year. Checkable against Customs seizure data.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Customs annual report / drug seizure statistics for the last financial year; true if total interdicted illicit drugs exceed nine tonnes, false if materially less.

veracity.statement: In the last two years, an asset management plan has been put in place for the first time, which is quite a shocking revelation—that it’s only been done in the last two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that FENZ has an asset management plan in place for the first time, only within the last two years, implying none existed before. Contested and load-bearing to the 'legacy of decay' argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ / Internal Affairs records on when a fire appliance asset management plan was first adopted; true if the first such plan dates to the last two years, false if one existed earlier.

focus.statement: That’s why it is so important that we deal more effectively with youth crime, which was out of control a couple of years ago.
focus.explanation: Engages the youth-crime policy squarely; the 'out of control a couple of years ago' is a mild dig at the prior period but the weight is on the policy being addressed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she think it is in good faith to spend public money on messaging that attacks the bargaining position of doctors, nurses, and teachers?
focus.explanation: Opposition scrutiny of a specific policy decision — taxpayer-funded ads during the strike — naming the spending and its target. On-policy accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why should firefighters accept a pay offer that is a pay cut in real terms?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny question naming a specific policy outcome (a real-terms pay cut in the firefighter offer). Squarely on the substance of the bargaining policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is easy, in Opposition, to say that you think everybody should be paid more. However, it is also true that in these negotiations there are two sides that must be represented, and one of those are the New Zealanders who pay the cost.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — that pay settlements are funded by levy-payers and both sides must be represented — wrapped in party framing ('easy, in Opposition'). Policy remainder is substantial.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m sure that a Labour member will realise that red things aren’t always reliable. However, there is a commitment, as I have mentioned, to upgrade the fire appliance fleet, which is under way, in order to address those concerns.
focus.explanation: Opens with a party jibe (red = Labour, content-free), then returns to the policy — the committed fleet upgrade under way. Mixed: strip the jibe and a policy point remains.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Since coming into office, this Government has added around 2,000 more nurses to the public health system compared to 2023, alongside hundreds of additional doctors.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the health-workforce policy at issue, with a named figure and baseline (nurses, doctors, 2023). Engages the substance rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, the facts speak for themselves, and the facts are that there are more nurses working at Health New Zealand today than under the Labour-Greens coalition, which was more focused on restructuring our health system during a pandemic. We're focused on health delivery; they were focused on rearranging bureaucracy.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim (more nurses now than under the previous government), but the weight of the statement is party framing — 'we're focused on delivery; they were focused on bureaucracy' — a general characterisation of the other party rather than the staffing question asked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Who is correct: nurses across the country who are telling us that they do not have safe working conditions or the Prime Minister who said that nurses have safe working conditions?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: holds the Government to account on a specific, named claim (whether nurses have safe working conditions). Names the policy issue directly — this is the job of an opposition MP, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our mental health plan is focused on delivering results: faster access to support, more front-line workers, and a better crisis response.
focus.explanation: Engages the mental-health-services policy squarely — access, workforce, crisis response. Entirely on the substance of the measure under discussion.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will the Minister investigate the mental health crisis in Thames following a serious mental health incident that was brought to his attention by a local mental health rangatira in Hauraki earlier this Monday?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny directed at a named policy issue — a specific service failure in a named place (Thames/Hauraki). On-policy accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Where else are peer support workers being used to improve mental health services?
focus.explanation: A friendly question, but wholly directed at the policy — the deployment of peer support workers across mental health services. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Since coming into office, this Government has added around 2,000 more nurses to the public health system compared to 2023, alongside hundreds of additional doctors.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific net increase of roughly 2,000 nurses in the public system since 2023, plus hundreds more doctors. Contested (the exchange is a dispute over staffing adequacy) and load-bearing to his whole answer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand nurse headcount/FTE data for 2023 versus 2025; true if the net increase is around 2,000 nurses (with a corresponding rise in doctors), false if materially different or if the baseline is cherry-picked.

veracity.statement: That's backed by a record additional $16.68 billion investment in health over three Budgets, including initiatives focused on improving workplace safety and reducing wait-lists for patients.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific cumulative additional health spend of $16.68 billion over three Budgets. A precise, non-obvious figure a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget documents (Votes Health) across the three relevant Budgets; true if the cumulative additional health allocation is approximately $16.68 billion, false if the figure is materially different or double-counted.

veracity.statement: Quality safety measures are stable or improving over the past five years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that patient quality-and-safety metrics have held steady or improved over five years. Directly contested by the nurses' safe-staffing claims that prompted the question, and load-bearing to his rebuttal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health Quality & Safety Commission quality-and-safety indicators over the past five years; true if the balance of measures is flat or improving, false if key patient-safety indicators have deteriorated.

veracity.statement: Since coming into Government, the peer support lived experience workforce has grown by almost 100 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the peer-support lived-experience workforce has grown by almost 100 percent since the Government took office. A specific proportional figure, non-obvious and load-bearing to the 'plan is working' claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ / Ministry workforce data on peer-support (lived-experience) specialist numbers in 2023 versus now; true if the count has roughly doubled, false if the growth is materially smaller.

focus.statement: Two years into the term of this Government, it is now abundantly clear that all they have to offer New Zealanders is blame, excuses, and anger.
focus.explanation: Content-free characterisation of the Government's disposition ('blame, excuses, and anger'). No specific policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the tribalism case Focus exists to catch, not scrutiny of a named commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A future fund that uses our existing asset base to grow opportunities and grow jobs for New Zealand—a Government that backs innovation here in New Zealand is what the Labour Party stands for.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific policy proposal (a future fund built on the existing asset base to grow jobs). Squarely on-policy; low detail on mechanism is a Specificity matter, not Focus.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The game development rebate that's created jobs, that's seen the gaming development sector grow by nearly 80 percent during the 2½ years that that rebate has been in place—they want it expanded.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (the game development rebate), an outcome (~80% sector growth) and a timeframe (2½ years). Substantive policy engagement.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One job—they’ve got one job: come up with some policies to actually back up their words.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the Opposition's failure to produce policy; no policy, measure or figure of substance is engaged. Party-directed and content-free.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They don’t even understand how Temasek works: when you buy assets, you then sell assets for ones that have better returns.
focus.explanation: Strip the jibe ('they don't even understand') and a genuine policy point about the Temasek model / asset trading remains, bearing on the future fund. On-policy remainder, but weighted with party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve already got a programme of roads that are being rolled out as we speak, and those that were announced by Chris Bishop this week show the next pipeline of significant roads of national significance that are game-changers for our cities, for our regions, and for our communities.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific policy programme (roads of national significance) and a named recent announcement. Squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We heard earlier from the Minister of Justice about the progress we’re making on violent crime reduction, aimed at ensuring that there are 20,000 fewer victims of crime.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy target (20,000 fewer victims of violent crime) and the area of policy. On-policy accountability framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re not a horror show like the other side.
focus.explanation: Pure party comparison ('horror show like the other side') with no policy content. Tribalism, not scrutiny of a named measure.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our economy has been shrinking.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the New Zealand economy has contracted over the period of the current Government — a claim about GDP over the past two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series over 2023-10 to 2025-10; true if real GDP (or GDP per capita) shows net contraction across the period, false if net growth.

veracity.statement: Unemployment is increasing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the unemployment rate is on an upward trend.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate trend over recent quarters to 2025 Q3; true if the rate has risen, false if flat or falling.

veracity.statement: New Zealanders are voting with their feet; record numbers of New Zealanders are simply giving up and leaving the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts departures of New Zealanders (or net migration loss of citizens) are at a record level.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration data on NZ-citizen departures / net migration loss of citizens; true if at or near an all-time high for the period referenced, false if not.

veracity.statement: Instead of giving those young New Zealanders hope, we have a Government that describes New Zealand as “wet, whiny and miserable”; that calls New Zealanders “bottom-feeders”; and that says that our emerging businesses, those who are creating the jobs of the future, are “C-listers” and unworthy of Government support.
veracity.explanation: Relays three specific quotations he attributes to Government figures ('wet, whiny and miserable', 'bottom-feeders', 'C-listers'); the check is whether those characterisations were in fact made by ministers.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record (speeches, interviews, media) of the quoted phrases being used by Government ministers about New Zealand / New Zealanders / emerging businesses; true if the attributions are accurate, false if fabricated or materially misrepresented.

veracity.statement: The game development rebate that's created jobs, that's seen the gaming development sector grow by nearly 80 percent during the 2½ years that that rebate has been in place—they want it expanded.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the game development sector grew by nearly 80 percent over the 2½ years the rebate has been in place — a specific figure, independent of whether the policy point is well made.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Game Developers Association industry survey / sector revenue or headcount over the ~2.5 years the rebate has operated; true if growth is near 80%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: If we look at inflation: inflation has stayed within the band of 1 percent to 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts inflation has remained within the RBNZ 1-3% target band; load-bearing to the fiscal-discipline argument and contestable given inflation only recently returned to band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation figures for the quarters referenced; true if within 1-3% across the period claimed, false if outside the band for any of them.

veracity.statement: From a high of 7.3 percent—eight official cash rate drops.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable figures: that inflation peaked at 7.3 percent and that there have since been eight official cash rate cuts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI peak (the 7.3% claim) and the RBNZ record of OCR decisions since that peak; true if the peak was 7.3% and there have been eight OCR reductions, false if either count is materially wrong.

focus.statement: It’s so lacking in originality in terms of a policy platform, and of two years of policy seances, that’s the best they could come up with: a pale, cheap rip-off of our $100 billion sovereign wealth fund, announced some 14 months ago.
focus.explanation: A real policy is named (the $100 billion sovereign wealth fund) and the claim is that Labour's fund copies it, but the weight of the statement is party framing — 'lacking in originality', 'policy seances', 'cheap rip-off'. A policy point wrapped in tribal framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But I will give it something; at least Chris Hipkins knew that this policy was being announced.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal coordination (implying Labour usually announces policy without its leader's knowledge). No policy content remains. About the party's cohesion, not an insult to a person, so it stays eligible and scores 0.0 — the content-free-tribalism case Focus exists for.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Government has put its money where its mouth is: New Zealand First and National and a coalition agreement to put wool back into Government buildings.
focus.explanation: Squarely on a specific policy — a coalition-agreement commitment to use wool in government buildings. Names the measure and the mechanism (procurement as a demand signal). On-policy substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The fact that we have lost almost the size of Napier City in the last year should be concerning every single one of those Government backbenchers, because Kiwis vote with their feet.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny naming a specific outcome (net emigration equivalent to a city's population) and tying it to the government's record. Holding the government to account for a named outcome is on-policy, not tribalism. A little party framing ('those Government backbenchers') but the substance dominates.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The problem for me is that this Government has no plan for that, to stem that brain-drain.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny directed at a named policy gap — the government's lack of a plan to address emigration. Engages the substance of what the government is (not) doing rather than party character. On-policy accountability.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our main issue is it’s one of our policies, one that the Rt Hon Winston Peters announced some 14 months ago at our 2024 convention.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NZ First / Winston Peters announced this sovereign-wealth-fund policy at the 2024 party convention, roughly 14 months before this October 2025 speech. Contested (Edmonds disputes any comparable detail existed) and load-bearing to the 'they copied us' argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ First's 2024 party convention record and Winston Peters' speech from that convention (~August 2024); true if a sovereign wealth fund / Future Fund policy was announced there, false if no such policy was announced.

veracity.statement: The turn around is on: strong wool—I should have told the Prime Minister this; he could have quoted it earlier—up 32 percent this year; fine wool: up 34 percent; and mid-micron wool up 41 percent.
veracity.explanation: Three specific year-on-year price rises are asserted: strong wool up 32%, fine wool up 34%, mid-micron up 41%. Specific, non-obvious figures a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wool price indices for strong, fine and mid-micron wool over the year to October 2025 (e.g. AgriHQ / PGG Wrightson / Wool Exchange auction data); true if each rose by roughly the stated percentages, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The fact that we have lost almost the size of Napier City in the last year should be concerning every single one of those Government backbenchers, because Kiwis vote with their feet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts net migration loss over the past year of nearly Napier's population (~66,000). A specific, contested magnitude claim that is load-bearing to the brain-drain argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the year to mid/late 2025 — net migration loss (or net loss of NZ citizens); true if the relevant net loss is close to Napier's population (~60,000–66,000), false if materially smaller.

veracity.statement: Two hundred people every day—a plane load every day—are now going offshore because they can no longer find the opportunities for them, for their children, and for their families.
veracity.explanation: Asserts roughly 200 people per day (≈73,000/year) are departing New Zealand. A specific, contested figure central to the emigration argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ migration data on departures for the period referenced; true if departures (or net departures of citizens) run at about 200/day, false if materially different.

focus.statement: In the last two years, this Government has reduced inflation, got it down from record levels to one now that businesses have confidence to invest.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of economic policy — inflation and its effect on business investment — and points to a named outcome of the speaker's own government. On-policy, so high Focus regardless of whether the causal claim holds (that would be Rigor/Veracity).
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And we have seen a trade negotiation start with India when that Government, Labour, said it was not a priority for them: $12 billion of extra exports.
focus.explanation: Squarely about trade policy — a named negotiation (India) and a specific figure ($12 billion). The dig at Labour's priorities is framing around a genuine policy point, so Focus stays high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Anybody who doesn't know that really just has to understand that 80 percent of all our goods exports that go overseas come from the primary sector.
focus.explanation: Directly about the economy and the primary sector's role in exports, carrying a specific figure. On-policy substance, high Focus.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have reduced ram raids from records high all over the country, when New Zealanders were just expecting when they got out of bed there would be another ram raid in their community to now a level so low that we hardly hear about them.
focus.explanation: Law-and-order policy with a named outcome — ram raids reduced from a peak. Reporting the government's own record against a specific crime measure is on-policy, high Focus.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We have $629.4 billion fraud that goes on in this country, and this country does nothing about it.
focus.explanation: Engages a substantive policy point — the scale of tax evasion and the state's failure to act on it — with a specific figure, as a lead-in to Te Pāti Māori's redistribution solution. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Anybody who doesn't know that really just has to understand that 80 percent of all our goods exports that go overseas come from the primary sector.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 80 percent of NZ goods exports come from the primary sector — a specific, non-obvious share that can be checked against export data.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MFAT goods-export data broken down by sector; true if the primary sector (agriculture, forestry, horticulture, seafood) accounts for roughly 80% of goods exports, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: We have reduced ram raids from records high all over the country, when New Zealanders were just expecting when they got out of bed there would be another ram raid in their community to now a level so low that we hardly hear about them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts ram raids fell from a record high to a very low level — a checkable claim about recorded-crime trends over the term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Police recorded ram-raid / retail-crime statistics across the term; true if ram raids fell substantially from a peak to a markedly lower level, false if they did not fall or rose.

veracity.statement: We have $629.4 billion fraud that goes on in this country, and this country does nothing about it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that fraud (tax evasion) in New Zealand totals $629.4 billion — a specific, contested and load-bearing figure for the redistribution argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IRD / Tax Working Group estimates of tax evasion and the tax gap in NZ; true if total fraud/evasion is on the order of $629.4 billion, false if materially lower (note this figure exceeds NZ's annual GDP, suggesting a scale error).

focus.statement: We need to tax the wealthy. We need to tax those who are making all the biggest noises with the mass homeownership. We need to tax ghost houses. We need to tax and pursue tax evasion.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages tax policy — naming specific targets (the wealthy, multiple homeowners, ghost houses, tax evasion) rather than attacking the other party. On-policy, even though it carries little detail (that would be Specificity, not Focus).
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was recycled, it was uninspired, it was lazy, and, worst of all, it merely reflected what is actually happening already.

focus.statement: This wasn't the first time that Labour has made promises about GP fees. In 2017, they pledged to reduce fees and review funding, but once in Government, that promise vanished.

veracity.statement: This wasn't the first time that Labour has made promises about GP fees. In 2017, they pledged to reduce fees and review funding, but once in Government, that promise vanished.

veracity.statement: The report called for a significant uplift of up to 231 percent for very low-cost access practices.

veracity.statement: We've implemented the largest increase to baseline funding since capitation began.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health/Te Whatu Ora records of annual GP capitation baseline funding increases since capitation was introduced. True if the recent increase is the largest in that series, false if a prior increase was larger.

focus.statement: The Greens, instead, would choose to properly invest in public health systems, ensuring that our GP visits are free; that our nursing visits are free; that our dental care is free; that we provide vans in our rural areas and communities; diagnostic abilities; and also properly fund community and healthcare providers.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The coroner's finding on the 2023 death of a woman at Waikato Hospital's emergency department; true if the coroner found the death preventable and the ED five nurses short at the time, false if the finding differs materially.
