veracity.statement: So consequently, suddenly, we became the only country in the world that instead of transitioning to renewables, we’re going away from gas to coal—to coal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand was the ONLY country in the world moving from gas back to coal rather than transitioning to renewables. The 'only country in the world' universal is the checkable, contested and load-bearing part.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: International energy statistics (e.g. IEA/Ember) on coal-vs-gas generation trends over the relevant years; true if no other country increased coal generation at the expense of gas in that period, false if any other country did (which many did).

focus.statement: And wouldn’t it be better if we were to use coal that we had in our own country rather than importing it?
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the policy question the bill turns on — whether to mine domestic coal versus importing it — naming a concrete mechanism and trade-off. On-policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It won’t reduce our impact on emissions in this country; it’ll make it worse because the coal’s got to be imported.
focus.explanation: Directly addresses the bill's substantive effect via a named mechanism (imported coal raising net emissions). On-policy. Whether the inference actually holds is a Rigor question, not a Focus one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s obviously a trigger word. Coal is clearly a trigger word. Gee, they’re really excited on the other side of the house, aren’t they?
focus.explanation: Content-free commentary on the other side's reaction with no policy content once removed. Not aimed at an individual (so it stays eligible here rather than going to Civility), but names no measure, figure or outcome — the tribalism case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because it’s just the idealistic nonsense you get from people on the other side who don’t understand the implications of making these sorts of decisions.
focus.explanation: Mostly about what 'the other side' are like rather than about the measure; a thin gesture at energy decisions survives stripping the party framing, but the weight is on characterising the opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The sad part about this, as I just heard the previous Government member talk about people laughing—and they are laughing: they are laughing at the lack of vision that this Government has and the absolute embarrassment that it has for the future generations who want to hear what is the solution.
focus.explanation: About the Government's supposed lack of vision and embarrassment — party-level framing. No specific policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so the content is tribal rather than on the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we have here, and it’s not disputable, is that coalmining directly fuels the climate crisis and the issues that we have as a nation.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure — the environmental effect of coal mining that the bill targets. Squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I think, you know, again, the only people that really benefit from this are the shareholders.
focus.explanation: A policy claim about who benefits from the coal industry, but expressed as general framing rather than a named outcome or figure. On-policy but only partly substantive.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill prohibits new coal mines and any expansion of existing coal mines after the 1 January in 2025.
focus.explanation: States the operative content of the bill — what it prohibits and from when. Directly on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the point I do want to acknowledge here is that while it does create a strict ban on expansion and means no new permits for existing mines, it means that the continuation is allowed, and existing coal mines can continue to operate after 1 January 2025 with their current permitted activities.
focus.explanation: A detailed, accurate engagement with the mechanism of the bill — that it grandfathers existing operations rather than closing them. Squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a scare tactic, really, where they constantly use the line that we need more mines in order to keep the lights on when it comes to energy, and anyone who knows anything about the subject matter knows that that would only get us part of the way.
focus.explanation: A real policy point about the energy-supply argument, but wrapped in party framing ("scare tactic", "they constantly"). Half on the substance, half on the other side's conduct.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There hasn’t been much action, like many things under this Government in the past two years.
focus.explanation: A general jab at the Government's record over two years with no specific policy or outcome named. Party framing rather than engagement with the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But the point I do want to acknowledge here is that while it does create a strict ban on expansion and means no new permits for existing mines, it means that the continuation is allowed, and existing coal mines can continue to operate after 1 January 2025 with their current permitted activities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the bill permits existing mines to keep operating under current permits after the ban date, contra what Government members claim. A contested, load-bearing claim about the bill's actual content.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill as introduced; true if the bill bars only new mines and expansions while permitting existing mines to continue under their current permits after the ban date, false if it also forces existing mines to cease operating.

focus.statement: The reason that power prices have been so high is because there are so many unbuilt but consented renewables available to us—wind farms that could have been built.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the energy-supply substance behind the bill — consented-but-unbuilt renewables and their effect on prices. On-policy regardless of whether the causal inference holds (that would be Rigor).
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, people talk in terms of the “just transition”, but let’s cash out what that actually means: it means protections for workers; it means training for workers; it means ensuring that there are good, well-paying jobs that people who currently work in coal mines can transition to, very much preferably in the places where they already live.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy mechanism directly — what a just transition consists of for coal-mine workers (protections, training, local jobs). Pure substance, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Julie Anne Genter’s bill would make energy scarcer, prices higher, and New Zealand weaker.
focus.explanation: Names the measure and asserts its effects on supply and prices. About the bill, not the person; the predicted outcomes engage the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Importing more coal from overseas while banning efficient domestic supply is economic and environmental nonsense.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy trade-off at the heart of the bill — imported versus domestic supply and its economic/environmental consequences. On-substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill also kneecaps regional economies that have powered New Zealand for generations.
focus.explanation: Addresses the bill's effect on regional economies. Colourful verb aside, it engages a policy consequence rather than attacking a party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a child doing homework in a cold house because Parliament decided to grandstand and that’s what we had from Labour and the Greens for six years.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about energy poverty, but the weight sits in party framing — pinning it on Labour and the Greens 'for six years'.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We should be talking about energy security in this country.
focus.explanation: Directs the debate to the policy question of energy security. Vague on detail (that is Specificity's concern) but squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve already seen, from the Opposition’s gas and oil ban, how economic growth in this country was stifled under that announcement.
focus.explanation: Names a specific prior policy (the gas and oil exploration ban) and asserts an outcome — this is scrutiny of a record, on-policy. Focus is always the speaker's; the inference's validity is Rigor's concern.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: People are laughing at that type of ideology that is coming from the Opposition parties.
focus.explanation: Content-free tribalism about the Opposition parties' 'ideology' — no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. Exactly the policy-versus-party gap Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The first is that, if we are to meet net zero emissions by 2050, we simply must have no new coal mines or extensions of existing ones.
veracity.explanation: Relays the IEA's stated position that meeting net zero by 2050 requires no new coal mines or extensions. A specific, contested attribution to a named body.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IEA 'Net Zero by 2050' roadmap (2021): true if it states no new coal mines or extensions of existing ones are compatible with the net-zero pathway; false if it makes no such statement.

veracity.statement: That’s kind of interesting because they’ve always had this focus on ensuring a secure supply of fossil fuels, but not only have they said that, the International Energy Agency has said that the decline in fossil fuel demand is so significant that no new investments in coal projects are required beyond those which were already committed as of 2021.
veracity.explanation: Relays a second, distinct IEA claim: that no new coal investments are required beyond those committed as of 2021. A specific attribution with a dated baseline.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: IEA net-zero scenario / World Energy Outlook publications: true if the IEA stated no new coal project investment is needed beyond commitments existing in 2021, false if not.

veracity.statement: That’s why we export millions of tons of it to India, South Korea, and Japan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts NZ exports coking coal on the order of millions of tonnes to three named countries. Specific quantity and destinations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ overseas merchandise trade / MBIE coal export statistics by destination: true if NZ coking-coal exports are of the order of millions of tonnes going to India, South Korea and Japan, false if volumes or destinations differ materially.

veracity.statement: We’ve given coal- and gas-fired power stations the same one-year priority as renewables under the amended Resource Management Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific government action: thermal power stations given the same one-year consenting priority as renewables under the amended RMA.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacted RMA amendment / fast-track consenting provisions: true if coal- and gas-fired stations were granted the same one-year priority pathway as renewables, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: What I can’t understand is that we’re still bringing Indonesian coal into this country from—I just googled—over 750,000 kilometres away, nearly 800,000 kilometres away.
veracity.explanation: Asserts NZ is still importing Indonesian coal. The load-bearing, contested claim is the fact of Indonesian coal imports; the '750,000 kilometres' figure is an evident mis-speak, not the claim being resolved.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ coal import records (Stats NZ overseas trade) for 2025: true if NZ imported coal from Indonesia, false if no such imports occurred.

veracity.statement: We also don’t talk enough about the fact that 0.17 percent is our emissions—0.17 percent is the emissions that we are producing here in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts New Zealand produces 0.17 percent of global emissions. A specific, checkable figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ share of global greenhouse-gas emissions per official inventories (NZ GHG Inventory / Global Carbon Project): true if ≈0.17%, false if materially different.

focus.statement: If we’re going to have to burn coal, let’s at least burn New Zealand coal.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual policy question — where the coal that is burnt should be sourced — rather than the other party's character. On-policy, though light on detail.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No one wants to burn down the planet, but people on that side of the House seem to want to burn down our economy in the pursuit of it.
focus.explanation: There is a real climate-versus-economy trade-off gestured at, but the weight of the sentence is party framing about what 'that side of the House' supposedly wants, not a named policy or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The reason that poor countries have higher emissions is because they can’t afford it.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance — the link between wealth and emissions — as an argument about the policy of restricting coal, not tribal point-scoring. Whether the reasoning holds is a Rigor question, not Focus.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Banning coal would be like just banning petrol in New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Directly addresses the coal-ban proposal by analogy. On-policy; the strength of the analogy would be a Rigor matter, not deducted here.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It kind of sounds nice, it doesn’t do what it says, and it creates more problems, and that’s why we’re not supporting the bill.
focus.explanation: States a reason for opposing the bill and claims it will not work, but the content is generic ('doesn't do what it says', 'creates more problems') and framed as typical of 'that side of the House' — a policy point mostly wrapped in party framing, no specific mechanism or figure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The coal is the most expensive kilowatt hours to generate electricity, and the overall price is all priced at the marginal price.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the electricity market directly — marginal pricing and the cost of coal generation — the substance of the debate over whether coal restrictions drive power prices.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Fast track is going to be used to destroy a living museum, a national treasure, the Denniston Plateau, because of this Government, in order for Bathurst to expand coal mining operations that will not be used, will not have anything to do with electricity generation, which will cost the country more than they will pay in royalties, more than we will earn in having those jobs.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (fast track), a specific site (Denniston Plateau), a specific company (Bathurst) and specific claimed outcomes (royalties, jobs). Policy scrutiny with concrete referents, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All of those Government parties are blind ideology, refusing to accept the evidence around public good, that electricity is public good.
focus.explanation: Contains a policy idea (electricity as a public good) but the sentence is chiefly a characterisation of the government parties as 'blind ideology' — mostly party framing with a thin policy thread.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m sorry, the Government is a bunch of dreamers, but they’re looking to the past.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the Government as a party — 'dreamers', 'looking to the past' — with no policy, measure or figure. No individual is insulted, so Civility passes it; this is the content-free tribalism Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The International Energy Agency concluded in 2021—so that was four years ago—that no new coal mines, mine extensions, or unabated coal plants should be developed in order for us to achieve net zero by 2050.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific, attributable conclusion from a named body — contested by the government side and load-bearing to her argument that new coal is unnecessary.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IEA's 2021 'Net Zero by 2050' roadmap: true if it states no new coal mines, mine extensions, or unabated coal plants are needed on the net-zero-by-2050 pathway; false if it contains no such conclusion.

veracity.statement: The coal is the most expensive kilowatt hours to generate electricity, and the overall price is all priced at the marginal price.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the NZ wholesale electricity market: that coal is the most expensive per-kWh generation and that the market clears at the marginal price. Contested and load-bearing to her whole argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electricity Authority documentation on NZ wholesale market design (true if it operates on marginal/spot clearing pricing) and generation cost data (true if coal/thermal peaking is among the most expensive per-kWh sources setting the marginal price); false if the market is not marginal-priced or coal is not the costliest marginal generation.

focus.statement: If you take a look at the bill, the bill will permit non-consented small stand-alone dwellings, commonly referred to as granny flats, to be built without a building consent, subject to certain conditions.
focus.explanation: Engages the actual mechanism of the measure before the House — what the bill permits and under what conditions. Squarely on-policy, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill will help to increase the supply of affordable housing options for both young and old New Zealanders, as well as for people with disabilities and those in the rural sector, particularly rural workers.
focus.explanation: About the policy's intended effect and who it affects. Promotional in tone but directed at the substance of the bill, not at another party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is a sensible change that is designed to stimulate more building work at a time when the construction sector desperately needs it, and to improve people's access to simple buildings that will be built in connection with people's single homes on parcels of land which can accommodate them.
focus.explanation: Addresses the purpose and effect of the measure — stimulating construction work and improving access to simple buildings. On-policy, not tribal.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It creates a new system for councils to be able to notify people of any risks associated with that, and that remains something that the Labour Party will continue to watch and determine whether that works because, as I have noted along the way in this process, there are systems in this which have been designed quickly; we do not know the full impact of them.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific mechanism of the bill — the new council risk-notification system — and flags a substantive scrutiny concern about its untested design. Directed at the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wanted to highlight for the House, at this point—the third reading—just how important this is for New Zealand because, at a time when we are seeing more Government policy that makes it harder for people to afford their rents and harder for them to afford their housing cost, there should be some element of Government action on this.
focus.explanation: A real supply-side policy point (that government should act on housing affordability), but the weight is generic party framing about 'more Government policy that makes it harder', with no specific policy named.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Before getting into the detail of the bill itself, it’s worth noting that this bill is widely supported by the public and across the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill enjoys broad public and cross-party support — a factual claim about submissions and House positions, not an opinion. Load-bearing to his framing and non-obvious as to degree.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transport and Infrastructure Committee submission tally on this bill (share supporting vs opposing) and the House voting record for its readings; true if submissions were predominantly supportive and it passed with support from multiple parties, false if submissions were mixed/opposed or it passed on coalition votes alone.

focus.statement: The big difference in housing policy arose in the 1990s when a National Government implemented a housing policy that involved slashing all controls around people's access, and increasing rents.
focus.explanation: Squarely on housing policy: it names a specific policy shift (removing controls, raising rents) and locates it historically. This is on-policy scrutiny, not content-free party-bashing, even though it references a National government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Where they are in the country makes a big difference, and how they are received by their communities makes a big difference because people need to buy into this and it will change the way some neighbourhoods look and feel.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of how the bill's dwellings will land in practice — location, community acceptance, neighbourhood effect. Directed at the measure, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Instead of a consent process, councils will now provide the project information memorandum, the PIMs, and it reduces their liability in some ways, and it quite dramatically changes their role.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the bill directly — the shift from consenting to PIMs, the liability change, the altered council role. Pure policy substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Most critically, this bill does absolutely nothing for social housing or addressing homelessness.
focus.explanation: A policy-directed critique of what the measure does and does not do (its scope excludes social housing and homelessness). On-policy scrutiny, no personal or tribal content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These dwellings are going to reduce neither car dependency nor emissions.
focus.explanation: Addresses the policy's substantive consequences for transport and emissions. Directed at the measure's effects, not at the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, they want applause for enabling a few thousand granny flats over a decade.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (the modest scale of the measure) but the weight is carried by party framing about the government seeking credit, so it sits mid-scale rather than at the on-policy top.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Rates rose over those two decades that were post-war years to increase housing ownership from about half to about two thirds.
veracity.explanation: A specific, checkable historical claim that NZ home ownership rose from ~50% to ~two-thirds across the post-war decades. Contested and load-bearing to her argument that State-backed programmes drove ownership up.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / Census owner-occupancy figures for the post-war decades (roughly 1940s–1960s); true if home ownership rose from around one half to around two thirds over that period, false if the level or the change is materially different.

veracity.statement: Some people saw their rents of State houses go up 300 percent in six months.
veracity.explanation: A specific quantified claim about state-house rent rises under the 1990s market-rents reform. Checkable against reform records; the magnitude and timeframe are precise enough to settle.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Housing New Zealand / market-rents reform records from the early 1990s; true if some state-house rents rose by around 300% within a six-month window, false if the largest documented increases were materially smaller.

veracity.statement: The previous Government built over 13,000 public homes, the most since the 1970s.
veracity.explanation: A specific, contested figure with a historical comparison ('most since the 1970s'). Checkable against public-housing delivery records; load-bearing to her contrast with the current government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / HUD records of net public homes delivered 2017–2023 and historical build figures; true if that government delivered 13,000+ public homes and this exceeds any period since the 1970s, false if either figure or the 'most since the 1970s' comparison does not hold.

veracity.statement: This Government has cancelled 3,479 homes, cut $1.5 billion from Kainga Ora, and is selling off existing stock.
veracity.explanation: Two precise figures (3,479 homes, $1.5 billion) about current-government housing decisions. Specific, contested and central to her argument; checkable against Kāinga Ora and Budget records.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora and Budget 2024 records; true if approximately 3,479 planned public homes were cancelled and about $1.5 billion was cut from Kāinga Ora, false if either figure differs materially.

focus.statement: We do not need any more demand-side intervention like KiwiBuild and other flops that did nothing but drive up the cost of housing in New Zealand and make the other side of the House ungovernable.
focus.explanation: Engages the real policy distinction (supply-side vs demand-side, KiwiBuild) but part of the weight is party framing ('make the other side of the House ungovernable') — a genuine policy point wrapped in tribal framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Under this bill, councils are not consent authorities and are not on the liability hook, as they are when they have to process normal building consents.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill — what councils will and won't be responsible for. No party content; directly engages the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, unfortunately, just about everything this Government has done has made things worse for Kiwis.
focus.explanation: A sweeping claim about the Government's general record with no named policy, measure, figure or outcome — content-free party framing, which is exactly the low-Focus case.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill’s regulatory impact statement tells us that there's going to be something like 7,800 new buildings in the next decade.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the substance — cites the projected supply figure from the bill's own regulatory impact statement to argue about scale. Names a specific measure and number.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: People building small granny flats is not going to help get people into homes.
focus.explanation: Engages the core mechanism of the bill — whether small stand-alone dwellings will actually address housing need. On-policy critique of efficacy, no personal or party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We do not have housing in Port Chalmers in Ōtepoti Dunedin because of the failure to build the homes that were ready to be built.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny naming a specific outcome and location — homes that were ready but not built. Holding the Government to account on a concrete case is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It's a practical solution to our housing challenges, and I wish to thank the Minister, Hon Chris Penk—a great, hard-working Minister—for shepherding this bill through the House.
focus.explanation: Strip the praise of the Minister and a policy-directed remainder remains ('a practical solution to our housing challenges'), but it is vague and carries no specific mechanism, cost or outcome, so only moderately on-substance.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have seen many examples, during this process, for less than $250,000, which is well under the average building cost for New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that small complying dwellings were shown to committee for under $250,000 and that this is well below the NZ average build cost — a specific, load-bearing figure supporting the affordability case.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Evidence presented to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee of complying small dwellings costing under $250,000, and the average residential building cost for New Zealand (e.g. Stats NZ building consent values / QV build-cost data); true if sub-$250k example builds are documented and that is below the NZ average, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: This bill’s regulatory impact statement tells us that there's going to be something like 7,800 new buildings in the next decade.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific decade-long dwelling projection (~7,800) to the bill's regulatory impact statement; checkable against that document and load-bearing to his 'patch-up' argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's Regulatory Impact Statement projected number of new dwellings enabled over the next decade; true if it states approximately 7,800, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora was building 5,000 homes a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific annual build rate for Kāinga Ora, used as the comparison baseline against the bill's projected supply; a contested, non-obvious figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual new-build delivery figures; true if it built approximately 5,000 homes in a year, false if materially different.

focus.statement: It’s always interesting to see my colleague Dan Bidois comment on other actions and showing up to the House on time, when, in fact, I think his own party has issues in getting votes right and practices in this House.
focus.explanation: Strip the jibe and nothing about the bill or any policy remains — it is entirely about the other party's conduct and practices in the House. This is the content-free tribalism Focus exists to catch. A policy question (the granny-flats bill) is before the House, so Focus is eligible.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But here is a Government that is putting up granny flats as that alternative, with less regulation in order to enable people to live in a warm, dry home.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the substance of the measure — the mechanism (reduced regulation on small dwellings) and its purpose (an alternative housing option) — rather than the other party in general.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As Labour’s tertiary spokesperson, I’m very clear that in the last two years, we’ve graduated 9,000 fewer apprentices in this country.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of the government's record with a named outcome (a specific decline in apprentice graduations), tied to the workforce needed for the housing/construction policy at issue. Holding the government to a specific figure is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For many ethnic communities in New Zealand, including the Pacific and Asian families, multiple-generation living is not just practical; it is culture.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure — who the policy affects and why the dwelling type suits multi-generational households — rather than attacking the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We see this as a sensible change, and what we are pleased about is that the new builds will still have to comply with the building code.
focus.explanation: Directly engages a mechanism of the bill (building-code compliance for the exempt dwellings), a substantive policy point rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As Labour’s tertiary spokesperson, I’m very clear that in the last two years, we’ve graduated 9,000 fewer apprentices in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantified change: 9,000 fewer apprentices graduated over the last two years. A figure, contested, and load-bearing for the workforce argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission / MSD apprenticeship completion (graduation) counts for the two years referenced vs the prior comparable period; true if the drop is ~9,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Labour Government, despite doing the largest public housing build since the 1970s, particularly, has been criticised for transitional housing options and using motels as an alternative.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2017–2023 Labour Government delivered the largest public (state) housing build since the 1970s — a specific, non-obvious historical comparison about his own government's record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora / HUD net additions to public housing stock by year since the 1970s; true if the 2017–2023 build exceeds every intervening period, false if an intervening government built more.

veracity.statement: That’s the highest that Salvation Army Glenfield have ever reported.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific, non-obvious attributed claim: that the Glenfield Salvation Army's current homelessness register (150 people) is the highest they have ever recorded.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Salvation Army Glenfield's own historical records of its homelessness register figures; true if the current figure exceeds all prior years, false if a prior year was higher.

veracity.statement: The other thing I'll mention is we've already seen up to 29 percent of real estate sales going to first-home buyers in New Zealand. That's the highest on record.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure (up to 29% of real estate sales to first-home buyers) and a record claim, used to argue the Government is delivering. Contested, load-bearing and specific.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: CoreLogic NZ First Home Buyer report on first-home buyers' share of property purchases in 2025; true if the share reached ~29% and this is the highest recorded share, false if materially lower or not a record.

focus.statement: We want to increase the supply of housing because, currently, it's far too hard to build a home in New Zealand. Even the simplest dwellings are tied up in red tape.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the policy problem the bill addresses — housing supply and consenting/regulatory burden — with no party-directed content.

focus.statement: The risks that come with that, with the lack of infrastructure required, are health and safety risks, and just—well, quite frankly, we risk Soweto-type situations popping up around communities.

focus.statement: But if the Filipino Embassy had contacted me and asked me to share posts related to Filipino Restaurant Week, under the really vaguely defined provisions of the legislation, my posting that and encouraging people to celebrate Filipino Restaurant Week could potentially constitute a crime, if you interpret that under this legislation.

focus.statement: There are three things I want to touch on in terms of amendments that came through the Justice Committee: replacing “enemy alien” with “citizen of a State at war with New Zealand”, just to make that really clear what that reference related to; secondly, making it a question of law whether a person owes allegiance to New Zealand, so a judge will make that decision instead of a jury—that was a suggestion of the New Zealand Law Society—and, finally, a safeguard for protesters to ensure that engaging in protest, advocacy, or industrial action would not, by itself, be criminalised.

veracity.statement: Out of those 705 submissions, 620 submitters opposed the bill, 34 supported it, and the remaining 51 were either unclear or did not take a position on this bill.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's summary of submissions on the Crimes (Countering Foreign Interference) Amendment Bill; true if the recorded tallies are 620 opposed, 34 in support and 51 neutral/unclear out of 705, false if the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: It took everyone by surprise, especially the trade Minister Todd McClay, because the very next day we got pinged with 50 percent tariffs.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements by Kash Patel at or around the opening of the FBI Wellington office; true if he stated the office is about countering China, false if he made no such statement.

veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ wholesale electricity spot price data (e.g. Electricity Authority / EMI) for the relevant period; true if spot prices exceeded $800/MWh, false if they did not reach that level.

focus.statement: This bill would just think to clip their wings and prevent them from expanding. We’re a Government that’s keen on restoring the economy, growing the economy, and building the economy. Why would we support something that shrinks something based on ideology and not on fact?

focus.statement: Foreign interference from any country is simply unacceptable and it often disrupts the rights of New Zealanders, including their right to freedom of expression.

focus.statement: We cannot defend democracy by weakening the very principles that underpin it. focus.statement: Labour will therefore continue to seek assurances that these laws will not be misused to target individuals exercising their democratic rights, to silence critics under the guise of security, and make sure New Zealand is protecting its democracy and protecting its freedom of expression as much as it means countering covert influence.

veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's National Security Strategy publication record: true if a National Security Strategy was published in 2023 and it identifies foreign interference as a key/growing threat; false if no such strategy was released that year or it does not name foreign interference.

veracity.statement: I’m appreciative of the of the 49 oral submitters and 705 submitters, in general, that expressed their concerns.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / court statistics on case disposal times and caseloads across NZ courts and tribunals; true if the Disputes Tribunal is among the fastest and busiest, false if it sits mid-pack or lower.

veracity.statement: Around 11,000 people each year use the tribunal to sort out their issues.
veracity.explanation: A specific annual usage figure for the Disputes Tribunal — not something a well-informed reader could confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Disputes Tribunal annual statistics on cases filed or applicants per year; true if approximately 11,000, false if materially different.

veracity.falsification_criterion: District Court filing-fee schedule (is the relevant fee about $260?) and the fee-waiver / remission regulations for the District Court versus the Disputes Tribunal; true if the $260 comparison holds and only the District Court has a hardship waiver, false if the fees or waiver availability differ from stated.

focus.statement: I want to talk about the elephant in the room in this debate, and that is the quite well publicised activities of operatives from the Chinese Government who have been engaging in, I think, foreign interference, in the way that it is defined in this bill—their activities would qualify as foreign interference.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, I regard myself as a principled critic of this Government’s headlong rush into the arms of the United Military Alliance, effectively with the United States, to counter China’s growing strength in the Asia-Pacific region.

focus.statement: Let’s just be really clear about what the legislation is intending to do here: it’s about strengthening the criminal law, and providing a means to better hold people accountable for undertaking foreign interference.
focus.explanation: Directly addresses the mechanism and intent of the bill before the House. Entirely on-policy, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re looking to support this bill and continue to remind the House, though, that, on a day when communities across the country are striking, we must continue to respect and also protect the ability for our people here in this country to peacefully protest, for advocacy, and for industrial action.

veracity.statement: It’s also, in my view, unacceptable that that the Chinese Government, through its United Front Works Department, deploys resources of the State to influence the behaviour and the publicly expressed opinions of the diaspora communities in New Zealand by controlling and influencing Chinese language media outlets who serve the diaspora communities in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific, contested factual attribution: that the UFWD uses state resources to control/influence Chinese-language media outlets serving NZ diaspora communities. Load-bearing to the case for the bill. Not scored here; the resolver searches.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Public reporting and academic research (e.g. Anne-Marie Brady's 'Magic Weapons' work and NZSIS threat assessments) on whether the CCP United Front Work Department funds or directs Chinese-language media serving NZ diaspora communities; true if such control is documented, false if no credible evidence of it exists.

focus.statement: We still believe that that filing fee is too high and it will be prohibitive to those who want to pursue justice through the courts.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re increasing the jurisdiction of the Disputes Tribunal—up to $60,000; so that’s the amount that they can look at—and that’s going to improve the ability for people with disputes to be able to get in front of them.

focus.statement: There are mechanisms under which the fees can be addressed through existing processes within the justice system.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy point in dispute — whether the filing fee's hardship impact is already handled by existing mechanisms, which was the substance of the committee-stage debate.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Again, you know, this is the most significant increase in the financial jurisdiction threshold for the disputes tribunal that we have seen in a while.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the $30,000→$60,000 jump is the largest recent increase in the disputes tribunal's financial jurisdiction — a specific, non-obvious historical comparison.

veracity.statement: We’ve already seen an improvement in court timeliness, and I know Minister McKee is going to continue to work on that throughout this term because it is very important.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court timeliness statistics (e.g. disposal times / case age) comparing the current term to the prior baseline; true if timeliness measurably improved, false if unchanged or worse.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Disputes Tribunal Act/rules and fee regulations on whether filing fees can be waived or reimbursed for hardship; true if such mechanisms exist for the disputes tribunal, false if fee relief is unavailable there.

focus.statement: Permits will be “use it or lose it”, which I think is important with the provisions, meaning that, if a project fails to start or progress, the area can be made available to other developers.

veracity.statement: What we do know is that, under the last Government, the issue was around consents; there was interest, but obviously people were waiting—it was reported publicly—eight years for consents.

veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory work behind this bill began under the previous Government and was continued by the current Government — a factual claim of policy lineage the other side might dispute.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE/Government records on whether work to establish an offshore renewable energy regulatory regime began under the 2017–2023 Government; true if such work was under way, false if the current Government initiated it de novo.

focus.statement: So it’s a very reliable source of power with offshore wind farms, and it’s a source of power that we need to tap in to if we are going to meet out climate commitments.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It just seems to me that the offshore wind industry is one of those areas where people can work and where there are jobs to be had.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the transition — jobs in the offshore wind industry as fossil-fuel work winds down. On-policy, no party attack.

focus.statement: However, we do have some things to say about this bill given that the Government is promoting fast track as a solution to everything, and we’ve seen what happens with fast track with Trans-Tasman Resources being written into the legislation and BlueFloat floating away.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (fast track) and a concrete instance (Trans-Tasman Resources written into the legislation, BlueFloat withdrawing), so there is real policy content, but it is wrapped in party framing ('promoting fast track as a solution to everything').
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is time that we focused on the renewables transition we want rather than simply seeking to extract more minerals and destroy our reputation internationally.

focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: One of the interesting things about offshore wind farming is that there is a fairly constant flow of wind and of air so that the turbine is turning maybe about 40 percent of the time, which is actually pretty good for land-based wind turbines.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Reported capacity factors for New Zealand onshore wind farms (e.g. MBIE/Transpower generation statistics or wind-farm operator reports); true if typical NZ onshore capacity factor is around 40%, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Those two uses are going to be particularly difficult to put together, but here we have reports from October 2024—so about this time a year ago—of wind power firm BlueFloat Energy cancelling its plan for wind farms in New Zealand, and the major reason was that a seabed mining firm wanted to mine offshore from the south coast of Taranaki.

focus.statement: For the foreseeable future, not just as a temporary measure, New Zealand will need flexible thermal generation powered by gas and, yes, of course, that reliable trusty black nugget, coal.

focus.statement: Now, we should also learn from Australia, particularly our cousins in Victoria, where declared areas for offshore renewables and transparent milestones give developers clarity and give communities confidence about what’s coming next.

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You promised it in June last year. Where the hell is it?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny naming a specific commitment (the national policy statement) and its non-delivery. Holding the government to a named promise is on-policy accountability, not tribalism; the mild 'where the hell' does not change that. Focus is scored on the speaker's own conduct.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: While he proposes you can build wind turbines with sticks and bits of wood, I tell you what: the wind turbines coming out of North America, Europe, and China right now are made out of critical minerals; they’re made out of epoxy resins made from oil and gas and coal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual composition claim: modern wind turbines are built from critical minerals and from epoxy resins derived from oil, gas and coal. Load-bearing to his 'you can't have one without the other' argument and non-obvious, so worth checking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Engineering/manufacturing sources on the material composition of utility-scale wind turbines; true if turbine generators/blades use critical minerals (e.g. rare-earth magnets) and petroleum-derived epoxy resins, false if they are predominantly made without such minerals or fossil-derived resins.

veracity.statement: You promised it in June last year. Where the hell is it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific factual claim about when the government promised the national policy statement ('June last year'). Contested and load-bearing to the accusation of a broken promise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/ministerial announcements on the promised delivery date of the National Policy Statement for renewable electricity generation; true if it was promised by around June 2024, false if no such June 2024 commitment was made.

focus.statement: We are used to the trivial nature of the Government.
focus.explanation: Characterises the Government's nature with no policy content — content-free party framing on a bill genuinely before the House. Nobody is personally insulted, so Civility passes it; this is the policy-versus-party gap Focus exists for.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are still risks if there are multiple uses in that area, and these risks don’t magically disappear when we limit some things, because if we’ve got large boats that are seeking to operate in the area, we have risks to big bits of kit—to our wind turbines.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the measure directly: the physical risk of competing marine uses to offshore wind infrastructure. Squarely on the policy mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is really problematic because we've been told that this Government wants to double or triple renewable electricity generation, yet it can't deliver on time the legislation we need to meet that target.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific government goal (double/triple renewable generation) and a specific failure (undelivered enabling legislation). Holding the government to a named commitment is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If only this Government did not rush legislation and get it wrong so often.
focus.explanation: A thin process point (rushing legislation) but the weight is a general characterisation of the Government's conduct rather than engagement with a named measure. Mostly party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We had a promise from this Government that by June 2023, 2024, we would have a national policy statement for renewable electricity generation. That still has not been delivered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a dated government commitment to an NPS for renewable electricity generation and that it remains undelivered. Contested and load-bearing to his critique of the renewables transition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/MfE record on whether a National Policy Statement for Renewable Electricity Generation was committed for delivery by 2024, and whether an NPS-REG had been gazetted as of 22 October 2025. True if such a commitment existed and no NPS-REG was in force by that date; false if an NPS-REG had been finalised, or if no such delivery commitment was made.

veracity.statement: There was the Board of Inquiry into the Proposed National Policy Statement for Renewable Electricity Generation in 2010. It was gazetted and implemented in 2011.
veracity.explanation: A specific, non-obvious historical dating: a 2010 Board of Inquiry and a 2011 gazettal of the NPS-REG. Precise enough that a well-informed reader could not confirm it from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Gazette / MfE records for the National Policy Statement for Renewable Electricity Generation 2011: whether a Board of Inquiry process ran in 2010 and the NPS was gazetted and came into force in 2011. True if both dates match, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This is really, really important because at the moment, the $10 billion per annum of fossil fuels we import costs us, costs everybody, costs every household heavily, in a cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: A specific figure ($10 billion/annum of fossil fuel imports) that is load-bearing to his cost-of-living argument. Checkable against trade statistics.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade data on the annual value of New Zealand's fossil fuel (crude oil, refined petroleum, coal, gas) imports. True if roughly $10 billion per annum in the relevant year, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The fast-track bill: I do want to speak about that, as we hear often in the House about the fast-track bill and, at the moment, I think there’s 22 renewable projects in the fast-track bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — 22 renewable projects listed in the fast-track regime. Contested and non-obvious; a well-informed reader could not confirm it from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published project list for the Fast-track Approvals regime; count how many are renewable energy generation projects. True if approximately 22, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: There are already dozens of consents.
veracity.explanation: A factual assertion offered to contest Arbuckle's claim that certainty is lacking — that many renewable projects are already consented. Load-bearing to the exchange and genuinely disputed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Count of existing resource consents granted for renewable electricity generation projects at the date stated. True if on the order of dozens, false if only a handful.

veracity.statement: The first term of the Labour Government was a New Zealand First coalition Government, with supply and confidence from the Green Party.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the composition of the 2017 government — a Labour–NZ First coalition with Green supply and confidence — to rebut the 'Labour-Green Government' characterisation. Contested framing, checkable fact.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The formal 2017 government-formation record (Labour–NZ First coalition agreement and the Green confidence-and-supply agreement). True if that is the arrangement, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Australia has set a very aggressive and impressive emissions reduction target of 62 percent to 70 percent.
veracity.explanation: A specific figure attributed to Australia's emissions reduction target, used as a comparator against New Zealand's. Non-obvious and checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australia's officially announced 2035 emissions reduction target (its NDC). True if the range is 62–70% below the baseline year, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: If you contrast that with New Zealand’s, of 51 percent to 55 percent by 2035, I do think there are things we can learn from them in that regard.
veracity.explanation: A specific figure for New Zealand's 2035 emissions reduction target, contrasted with Australia's. Checkable against the official NDC.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's officially announced 2035 emissions reduction target (NDC). True if 51–55% by 2035, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: One of the things that they took away when they first came into office was the decarbonising industry fund, which was a really important component.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the government cut a specific, named fund (the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry fund) on taking office. Contested and checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget/appropriation records on the Government Investment in Decarbonising Industry (GIDI) fund after the government took office. True if the fund was discontinued or defunded, false if it continued.

focus.statement: It is disappointing, as we’ve gone through fast track, that the Opposition parties have not realised the potential to actually get some runs on the board, especially in the renewable space.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (renewable projects via fast track) but the weight is party framing — the Opposition parties' failure to see the potential. Policy content wrapped in a jab at the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think you could look at it something like spatial planning; in the Resource Management Act, we look at spatial planning on the land, and maybe here we need spatial planning in the sea, so it’s that same kind of concept.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the policy substance — how competing marine uses (wind, seabed mining) might be managed via a spatial-planning mechanism. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As great as it will be to get the infrastructure in, there will be a time and a place to actually have these decommissioned, and to have a plan in place for that.
focus.explanation: An ordinary, on-topic contribution engaging a concrete part of the regime — the need for a decommissioning plan for the infrastructure. Addresses the substance, not the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the things that they took away when they first came into office was the decarbonising industry fund, which was a really important component.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny naming a specific policy and outcome — that the government discontinued the decarbonising industry fund. Holding the government to account for a named programme is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The member Simon Court also said that ACT exercised disproportionate influence in this Government and was trusted with important jobs, and we certainly agree with them in that regard; they’ve definitely exercised disproportionate influence.
focus.explanation: Content-free party point about ACT's influence within the government — what the other party is 'really like' — with nothing addressed to the bill before the House. Not a personal attack, so eligible, but off-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: New Zealand implemented similar mechanisms for oil and gas in 2021 through amendments to the Crown Minerals Act 1991.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific past legislative fact: that decommissioning/financial-security mechanisms were introduced for oil and gas via 2021 amendments to the Crown Minerals Act 1991. Specific, dated and non-obvious — a reader could not confirm it from memory, and it is load-bearing for his claim that the bill's decommissioning regime follows established precedent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crown Minerals (Decommissioning and Other Matters) Amendment Act / 2021 amendments to the Crown Minerals Act 1991: true if 2021 amendments introduced decommissioning obligations and financial-security requirements for oil and gas permit holders, false if no such mechanism was added in 2021 or the date/instrument is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: International developers are exploring offshore wind projects in New Zealand, and this bill will give them greater certainty to invest, as well as allow them, and the Government, to select the developments that best meet our national interests.
veracity.explanation: The checkable factual clause is that international developers are actively exploring offshore wind projects in New Zealand. This is load-bearing — it is the stated justification for why the regulatory certainty in the bill is needed. (The remaining clauses about what the bill 'will' do are intention, not the item being resolved.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public records of declared offshore wind interest in NZ waters (e.g. proponents such as BlueFloat/Energy Estate, Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, or others announcing South Taranaki/offshore projects): true if one or more international developers had announced or lodged offshore wind exploration in NZ as of Oct 2025, false if no such developer interest existed.

focus.statement: Permits will have a use-it-or-lose-it provision, meaning that if a project fails to start or progress, the area can be made available to other developers.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism of the bill directly — a use-it-or-lose-it condition on permits and what it does to unused areas. Squarely on the policy, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: A key recommendation from the select committee concerned the issue of competition for space between offshore renewable energy and seabed mining.
focus.explanation: Addresses a substantive policy question raised in select committee — allocation of marine space between offshore wind and seabed mining. On-policy, no tribal content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to reflect on that, because we don't want this legislation to enable someone to be able to buy a patch of ocean floor, hold on to it—you know, invest not in infrastructure, not in building any wind turbines, but sitting on it—to be able to sell in the future and to make a profit, and nothing to actually be done.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific mechanism in the bill — the risk that permits could be bought and held speculatively rather than developed. Squarely on the policy, names the concrete concern.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So looking at what this legislation does: the obligations regarding decommissioning and financial security to ensure the permit holders and owners of those reflected places—that the decommissioning is done and they are liable for it, which we need to make sure.
focus.explanation: Directly addresses the bill's decommissioning and financial-security provisions and where liability sits. On-policy substance, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So we did make a number of changes to the bill around the feasibility permits, changing the permitting regime, making sure that the decommissioning obligations were clarified, including being clear about what infrastructure is excluded as part of the feasibility and commission regime, and also dealing with the competing offshore renewable energy applications and how that was to be addressed.
focus.explanation: Details the specific select-committee changes to the bill — feasibility permits, the permitting regime, decommissioning obligations, excluded infrastructure, competing applications. Entirely policy substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wanted to let some of the members opposite, whose characterisation of our position on this side of the House is not entirely accurate, know that we were early starters on this issue and it's taken a long while for this current Government to get to this date.
focus.explanation: Contains a real policy-timeline point — that action on offshore renewables has been slow — but the weight is party positioning about who started the work rather than the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My advice to any overseas investor that wants to come here is that you beat a path to all stakeholders in Taranaki and make sure that those relationships are strong and that they are active in allowing that investment to move forward; failure to do so would be a mistake, and, actually, it should not be a tick-box exercise through this legislation.
focus.explanation: Addresses how the legislation should handle stakeholder and iwi engagement for investors — substantive policy content about how the regime should work, not party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It was just under $450 million of taxpayers' money that was spent in terms of the decommissioning.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — just under $450 million of Crown money spent on decommissioning the Tūī field. A contested, load-bearing quantity underpinning his argument for a robust decommissioning regime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury / MBIE published cost of the Crown-funded Tūī oil field decommissioning; true if total taxpayer spend was approximately $450 million (near but under), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It was already in train when we were in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that work on the offshore renewable energy regime was already under way under the previous Labour government. Contested (he flags members opposite characterise Labour's position inaccurately) and load-bearing to his claim of early action.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE/government records on when work on an offshore renewable energy regulatory regime began; true if a discussion document, consultation or policy work was under way under the previous Labour-led Government, false if it began only under the current Government.

focus.statement: So, look, the National Party are committed to this as part of our Electrify New Zealand, which of course is all about the goal of doubling renewable energy generation by 2050—we are now delivering.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House and situates it in a named policy (Electrify New Zealand) with a stated goal (doubling renewable generation by 2050). Squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of course, despite what the Opposition may tell you on the black and white tiles, we are committed—National’s committed, this Government is committed—to meeting New Zealand’s long-term energy needs, hence why you’re hearing a lot about the energy sector coming from this Government.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point (commitment to long-term energy needs) but wrapped in party framing that opens by rebutting 'the Opposition'. The weight is split between the policy and the party contrast.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is around clarifying how maritime space conflicts will be managed in terms of mining and aquaculture; it’s about strengthening environmental compliance obligations under exclusive economic zone and Resource Management Act frameworks; and as my colleague the Rt Hon Adrian has said, enhancing Treaty of Waitangi recognition and Māori engagement.
focus.explanation: Engages the detail of the regime directly — maritime space conflicts, EEZ and RMA compliance obligations, Treaty recognition. Entirely on the substance of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We will be keeping a close eye on that, given that sometimes we see one side of the ledger enhanced and enabled under Christopher Luxon’s Government without the surrounding protections and safeguards to ensure that the transitions can happen.
focus.explanation: Makes a real policy point about protections and safeguards for the transition, but frames it around 'Christopher Luxon's Government' rather than the mechanism alone. Policy content present, but half the weight is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s critically important that, at the earliest possible moment, proposals such as these start with conversations with iwi.
focus.explanation: Addresses a substantive feature of how such projects should proceed — early iwi engagement. On-policy, no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s recently been established that you can easily have gigawatts of wind generation and the potential of the Trans-Tasman Resources proposal existing together.
focus.explanation: Engages a concrete substantive question — whether the offshore wind development and the Trans-Tasman Resources seabed proposal can coexist in the South Taranaki Bight. On the policy, not the parties.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s also good news for the guardians of the New Zealand Super Fund, which, of course, have in their guardianship over $85 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure: the New Zealand Superannuation Fund holds over $85 billion under guardianship.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Super Fund's reported net asset value as at October 2025 (NZ Super Fund / Guardians of NZ Superannuation official reporting); true if the fund exceeds $85 billion, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: I’m really pleased that the House had the opportunity to hear from my colleague the Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe to correct the record, really, that this is a piece of work that Labour started because of our commitment to unlocking the potential for renewables, and it has been picked up by this Government, which we are really happy about.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that this offshore renewable energy legislative work originated under the previous Labour government and was subsequently continued by the current government. A contested origin/credit claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The policy development history of the offshore renewable energy regulatory regime (MBIE discussion documents / ministerial announcements 2021-2023); true if the work was initiated under the previous Labour government, false if initiated by the current government.

veracity.statement: So what that means is that it’s equal to some of our largest hydro stations and more than eight Harapaki Wind Farms combined.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific comparison: the ~1 GW offshore project would equal more than eight Harapaki Wind Farms combined (and rival the largest hydro stations).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The rated capacity of the Harapaki Wind Farm (~176 MW) multiplied by eight versus 1 GW; true if 1 GW exceeds eight Harapaki capacities (~1.4 GW), false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Now, if we think about the current stored generating capacity of all the wind turbines in New Zealand at the moment just being north of one gigawatt, this one farm can be actually immense—huge, in fact.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the total current generating capacity of all wind turbines in New Zealand is just north of one gigawatt.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Total installed wind generation capacity in New Zealand as at 2025 (Electricity Authority / MBIE / NZ Wind Energy Association figures); true if just above 1 GW, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Government in the last two years has seen FENZ introduce an asset management plan, which had not been put in place, for some reason, between 2017 and 2023 after FENZ was formed from the voluntary and professional wings of New Zealand’s firefighting.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that FENZ had no asset management plan in the 2017-2023 period and that one was introduced only under the current government. Contested and load-bearing to his defence of the fleet record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: FENZ's published asset/fleet management plans and their dates, or OIA/annual-report record; true if no asset management plan existed 2017-2023 and one was introduced in the last two years, false if a plan existed earlier.

veracity.statement: That has come down 14 percent in the last two years.
veracity.explanation: Claims harm to children in State care/residences fell 14 percent over the last two years. A specific, contested figure central to the answer.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki reported figures on harm to children in residences/State care over the stated two-year period; true if a ~14% reduction is recorded, false if the data show otherwise.

veracity.statement: It’s the first time that there has been a reduction of harm to children in State care, as we understand it, in the country’s history.
veracity.explanation: A historical-superlative claim that this is the first-ever recorded reduction of harm to children in State care. Contested and non-obvious.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Historical Oranga Tamariki / predecessor-agency records of harm to children in State care; true if no prior year-on-year reduction is on record, false if an earlier reduction exists.

veracity.statement: In relation to teachers, in the last three years, there has been a 14.5 percent increase in pay for teachers.
veracity.explanation: A specific figure — a 14.5 percent teacher pay increase over three years — that is contested and load-bearing to his rebuttal on pay.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Teacher collective-agreement pay scales / Ministry of Education records over the stated three years; true if cumulative base pay rose ~14.5%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It is simply a mischaracterisation for the Labour Party to say that tobacco companies have been given $300 million.
veracity.explanation: Denies that tobacco companies were given $300 million, disputing an Opposition claim. Contested and load-bearing to the exchange.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/Customs costings of the heated-tobacco excise change; true if no $300m payment or equivalent benefit to tobacco companies is recorded, false if the policy confers a ~$300m benefit as the Opposition claims.

veracity.statement: Seasonally adjusted export values were up 0.9 percent in September, following increases of 7 percent in August and 2.2 percent in July.
veracity.explanation: Specific month-by-month seasonally adjusted export-value figures attributed to a Stats NZ release; non-obvious and precisely checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Overseas Merchandise Trade release for the stated months; true if seasonally adjusted export values rose 0.9% (Sep), 7% (Aug), 2.2% (Jul), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Taking an annual view, in the year to September export values were up 13.5 percent over the previous year.
veracity.explanation: A specific annual export-growth figure (13.5 percent year to September) that a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Overseas Merchandise Trade annual comparison for the year to September; true if export values rose ~13.5% year-on-year, false if materially different.

focus.statement: This is very good news, and it has come because of a precise and deliberate set of actions by the Minister to improve the quality of staffing, to require staff to wear uniforms, to crack down on contraband—for example, by requiring staff to have clear bags so that they couldn’t smuggle contraband in—and by proactively managing behaviour in the sites.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy substance directly — the specific operational mechanisms (staffing, uniforms, contraband controls) said to have produced the outcome. Squarely on-policy.
