focus.statement: There’s a real contradiction for the Labour Party here: they want the State to do more, they want more Government agencies to do more stuff—to invest in video games, to start sovereign wealth funds—and yet they don’t want to pay the people directing these proposed entities, or even the current ones, even nearly as much as directors get in the private sector.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point about board/director remuneration, but the weight is carried by party framing (Labour's alleged contradiction) rather than the governance-pay substance itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is why they’re over there, and we adults are over here.
focus.explanation: Pure tribalism directed at the other party's character with no policy content remaining once the framing is removed; nobody individual is insulted, so this is the Focus case.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, the Government has been saying, through the Public Service Commission, that we are prepared to meet and work through the weekend to get a deal to avoid these strikes.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the question — the government's negotiating posture on pay/strikes — naming a specific channel and offer. On-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Dairy, meat, fruit, and wood together make up over half of New Zealand’s goods exports, and these figures are something to celebrate even though Willow-Jean Prime seems to disagree.
focus.explanation: Squarely about export composition and value. Stripping the mild jibe at Prime leaves a substantive policy claim, so it scores high on Focus.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, that’s exactly why this week and next week we’ve been holding the curriculum roadshow, with hundreds of principals and leaders in venues across the country.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the policy raised — curriculum change and teacher support — by pointing to the roadshow. On-policy, no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But what I would say to the unions is the fact that they told principals and teachers to boycott the very thing that was going to provide them the supports that they needed to implement the curriculum is a real shame.
focus.explanation: Names a specific action (boycott of the curriculum roadshow) tied to the policy at issue, but the weight is on criticising the unions' conduct rather than the policy mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, it's tempting to make comments around policy wobbles this week, but what I will say is the most important people who will benefit from the Bikes in Schools programme are our young kids who will learn how to ride a bike safely.
focus.explanation: Explicitly declines the party jibe he flags and returns to the substance of who the programme benefits. Stripping the aside leaves an on-policy answer.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yes, I absolutely stand by that target. We know it’s challenging, but our goal is to grow the economy and help more Kiwis into work as we had seen welfare dependency balloon, when we came into office.
focus.explanation: Defends the named jobseeker-reduction target and the policy goal behind it; engages the substance rather than attacking the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is she condemning basic requests for decent pay and working conditions when we lose 50 percent of high school teachers in the first five years?
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny of teacher pay and retention, anchored to a specific attrition figure. This is the accountability role of an opposition MP, so it scores high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she stand by her statement, “We have so many brilliant teachers, and when we back them we get results”, and, if so, does she think backing teachers means pitting them and unions against whānau and students?
focus.explanation: Engages the policy of how teachers are supported, though wrapped in framing about pitting groups against each other. A real policy point remains after the framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it backing teachers to have 55 percent—well over the OECD average of 33 percent—reporting that their stress is due to keeping up with curriculum or programme changes, especially when schools are already unable to properly staff existing subjects?
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny of the workload effects of curriculum change, anchored to specific figures and a staffing point. High Focus.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it the case that she is now closer to adding 50,000 job seekers than she is to removing 50,000 job seekers, and, if so, will she resign if the target is not met?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy target (the 50,000 jobseeker reduction) and whether it is being met. Naming the specific commitment is accountability, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many of the 249 people who have lost their jobs recently in Tokoroa are now on jobseeker?
focus.explanation: On-policy question tied to a specific redundancy event, testing the government's jobseeker/employment response. Named figure and outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Dairy, meat, fruit, and wood together make up over half of New Zealand’s goods exports, and these figures are something to celebrate even though Willow-Jean Prime seems to disagree.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that four primary-product categories combined account for more than half of NZ's total goods export value.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade, goods export values by commodity for the year to September 2025; true if dairy, meat, fruit and wood together exceed 50% of total goods export value, false if materially under.

veracity.statement: Meat exports were up 18 percent, fruit up 33 percent, and wood up 8 percent.
veracity.explanation: Three specific year-on-year export-growth figures for the year to September.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade, year to September 2025 vs the same period a year earlier; true if export-value changes are ~+18% meat, ~+33% fruit, ~+8% wood (± rounding), false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Stats NZ notes that a stand-out performer is kiwifruit, now a $4.5 billion a year industry, up from $2.6 billion just two years ago.
veracity.explanation: Claims kiwifruit export value is $4.5b/year, up from $2.6b two years ago — roughly a doubling.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ kiwifruit export value; true if currently ~$4.5b/year and ~$2.6b two years prior, false if either figure is materially off.

veracity.statement: This deficit reached its highest levels in 2022 and 2023, peaking at a whopping $17 billion.
veracity.explanation: Claims the annual goods trade deficit peaked at about $17 billion in 2022–2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ annual goods trade balance for 2022–2023; true if the peak annual goods trade deficit was ≈$17 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This week’s data shows an annual trade deficit of only $2 billion.
veracity.explanation: Claims the latest data shows the annual trade deficit has narrowed to about $2 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker

focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Reform of the electricity market to provide confidence with stable prices and investment in renewable energy and storage are key.
focus.explanation: On-policy: identifies electricity-market reform, price stability, and investment in renewables and storage as the substance. No party-bashing; addresses the mechanism, so Focus is high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It demonstrates a lack of strategy or planning for our future and no one gains from the oil and gas ban fantasy that this Government repeats ad nauseam.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (the oil and gas ban is not the cause of the shortfall) wrapped in party framing ('fantasy that this Government repeats ad nauseam'). Strip the framing and a policy claim remains, but the weight leans on characterising the Government, so it sits mid-scale.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So we know that right at the moment around about 90,000 households are without power.
veracity.explanation: A specific, non-obvious quantity about a current event. Asserts that about 90,000 households were without power during the storm on the day of the debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Power distribution / Civil Defence outage figures for the 23 October 2025 storm; true if roughly 90,000 households were without power that day, false if materially fewer or more.

veracity.statement: If you go to the actual data issued by Stats and look at the actual index and do the calculation, the actual inflation wasn’t 3 percent; it was actually 3.046875, but, of course, the rounding God smiled upon that.
veracity.explanation: A precise, checkable arithmetic claim that the true annual CPI inflation to 30 September 2025 was 3.046875% and only rounded down to 3%. Specific, non-obvious and load-bearing to her point about power prices pushing inflation toward the Reserve Bank band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index for the September 2025 quarter: recompute the annual rate from the published index values; true if the unrounded annual CPI change is ~3.046875%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In particular, in the Stats New Zealand release, the prices and deflation spokesperson said that, in actual fact, the 11.3 percent annual increase in electricity prices over the last year is the largest since the March 1989 quarter.
veracity.explanation: She relays a specific figure and comparison attributed to the Stats NZ spokesperson — an 11.3% annual electricity price rise, the largest since March 1989. Checkable against the release; scored as a relayed claim.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI release electricity sub-index and its commentary; true if the annual electricity price increase was 11.3% and described as the largest since the March 1989 quarter, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: The evidence is really clear that gas production peaked in 2001 and has been declining since 2014, four years before the oil and gas ban.
veracity.explanation: Specific dated claims used to rebut the 'ban caused the crisis' narrative — that gas production peaked in 2001 and has declined since 2014, before the 2018 ban. Contested and load-bearing to his argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE oil and gas production statistics; true if NZ gas production peaked around 2001 and has declined since 2014 (with the exploration ban in 2018), false if the peak/decline dates are materially different.

veracity.statement: Over 100,000 people cannot afford to pay their bills.
veracity.explanation: A specific quantity on energy hardship — that over 100,000 people cannot afford their bills. Non-obvious and central to his case for restoring EECA's budget.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Energy hardship / energy affordability statistics (e.g. EECA or MBIE estimates of households unable to pay energy bills); true if the figure is on the order of 100,000 or more, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: The Frontier report showed how to bring the total cost of electricity to consumers down by over $2 billion per year simply by taking control of Huntly and using it strategically by pricing it separately as a system backstop.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific quantified finding attributed to the Frontier report — a >$2 billion per year saving from repricing Huntly as a system backstop. Checkable against the report.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The named Frontier (Economics) report on the electricity market; true if it concludes total consumer electricity costs could fall by over $2 billion per year via strategic separate pricing of Huntly as a backstop, false if it says otherwise.

focus.statement: We’ve made massive progress by repealing Labour’s ban on offshore oil and gas exploration. That cost this country billions in dollars of economic vandalism, and it pushed us to burn more imported coal.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named policy (the offshore oil and gas exploration ban) with named consequences (cost, more imported coal). On-policy, though carried on 'economic vandalism' party framing rather than pure mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s why ACT in Government is leading the charge to replace the Resource Management Act (RMA) with a system based on property rights that respects environmental limits.
focus.explanation: Directly about a named policy (RMA replacement) and the proposed alternative framework. On-policy, mild party framing ('ACT in Government').
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Energy is our greatest infrastructural vulnerability, and we’ve had widespread calls for—and, actually, we’ve heard in this debate as well—for a long-term energy strategy, and I completely agree with that.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the debate — the need for a long-term energy strategy. No attack on the other party; addresses the policy question directly.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What Labour did—of those three objectives—is they went for the virtue-signalling sustainability at huge cost to affordability and security.
focus.explanation: A real policy point (a claimed trade-off between sustainability and affordability/security) but the weight sits on party framing — 'Labour', 'virtue-signalling'. A policy claim wrapped in tribal framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We lost 1,000 megawatts—1,000 megawatts—of gas-fired power stations; that is the effect of that.
focus.explanation: On-policy scrutiny with a specific figure attributed to a specific policy — lost gas-fired generation capacity. Engages the substance, not the other team's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Pre-oil and gas ban, the price of electricity was around $75 per megawatt, and in 2024, $250 per megawatt.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy with concrete before/after price figures. On-policy substance rather than party characterisation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And this is from a party that used to be a blue-collar party—it used to be a blue-collar party—that sabotaged Northland, closed down Marsden Point, sabotaged Taranaki—with the oil and gas ban—and it’s still going: central North Island.
focus.explanation: Names specific outcomes (Marsden Point, Taranaki) but the weight is on what Labour's party is 'really like' — a blue-collar party that betrayed its base. More party characterisation than policy engagement.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So where’s the national policy statement? In June last year—in June last year. Another broken promise, with nothing there.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific commitment (a national policy statement due last June) and a specific outcome (not delivered). Holding the government to a named promise is on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’ve made massive progress by repealing Labour’s ban on offshore oil and gas exploration. That cost this country billions in dollars of economic vandalism, and it pushed us to burn more imported coal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the ban led NZ to burn more imported coal. Coal use at Huntly did rise in the low-hydro/low-gas years after 2018, though the causal attribution to the ban specifically is arguable; the checkable core is whether imported coal burning rose.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ coal import/consumption data after the 2018 exploration ban versus before (MBIE energy statistics; Genesis Energy Huntly coal use); true if imported coal use materially rose in the years following, false if it did not.

veracity.statement: We lost 1,000 megawatts—1,000 megawatts—of gas-fired power stations; that is the effect of that.
veracity.explanation: Claims 1,000 MW of gas-fired power stations were lost. Some gas plant did retire over this period, but 1,000 MW is a large specific figure whose accuracy and attribution to the ban I am unsure of.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Records of gas-fired generation capacity retired in NZ since 2018 (MBIE/Transpower and generator decommissioning announcements); true if roughly 1,000 MW of gas-fired capacity was withdrawn, false if materially less.

veracity.statement: Pre-oil and gas ban, the price of electricity was around $75 per megawatt, and in 2024, $250 per megawatt.
veracity.explanation: Pre-ban wholesale prices near $75/MWh is plausible; a 2024 figure of $250/MWh matches winter spot spikes but likely overstates the annual average, so the pairing as stated may be inflated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ wholesale electricity prices ($/MWh) pre-2018 versus 2024 from Electricity Authority EMI data; true if the pre-ban level was around $75/MWh and 2024 around $250/MWh, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: So where’s the national policy statement? In June last year—in June last year. Another broken promise, with nothing there.
veracity.explanation: Claims a national policy statement promised for June last year was not delivered. Plausible that such a statement slipped its timeline, but which instrument and the exact commitment date need checking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whether the Government committed to release a national policy statement (energy/electricity related) by June 2024 and whether it had been released by the time of this debate; true if promised by that date and not delivered, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: We took 20 percent of all energy use off.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that industrial closures/curtailment in winter 2024 removed 20 percent of all energy use — a specific, contested, load-bearing quantity underpinning his argument about gas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Transpower/Electricity Authority and MBIE data on winter 2024 industrial demand reduction (Winstone Pulp, Kinleith, Methanex); true if curtailment approached ~20% of national energy/electricity use, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: They are going to have to convert at the cost of something like $10,000 to $13,000—the current estimate per household.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific per-household gas-to-electric conversion cost of $10,000–$13,000 to EECA. A named figure with a named source, checkable and non-obvious.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: EECA published estimates of the per-household cost to convert from gas; true if within ~$10,000–$13,000, false if materially outside that range.

veracity.statement: Yes, renewables, but also, we need the firming part of that, whether it’s geothermal—just remember that solar energy works, effectively, at about 16 percent of capacity all the time; wind, about 46-, 47 percent; geothermal is about 98 percent, for example.
veracity.explanation: Gives specific capacity-factor figures for solar (~16%), wind (~46-47%) and geothermal (~98%) in New Zealand — precise, non-obvious numbers a reader could not confirm from memory.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE/Electricity Authority capacity-factor data for NZ solar, wind and geothermal generation; true if each figure is within a few points, false if any is materially off.

veracity.statement: Natural gas currently provides about 20 percent of our electricity generation, particularly during peak demand and dry years.
veracity.explanation: A specific share (about 20 percent) for gas in NZ electricity generation — load-bearing to his case for gas as a firming fuel, and contestable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE electricity generation statistics on gas's share of generation; true if around 20% (especially in dry years), false if materially lower on average.

veracity.statement: In fact, over 19,000 businesses rely on gas every single day.
veracity.explanation: A specific count of over 19,000 businesses relying on gas — a precise, non-obvious figure used to argue the sector's economic importance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Gas Industry Co / MBIE data on the number of NZ businesses connected to or dependent on gas; true if ~19,000+, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: The other solution that they’ve come up with is that we’re just going to keep looking for some more natural gas, even though we haven’t found any for—what?—20 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts no significant new gas has been found in New Zealand for about 20 years — a checkable, contested claim about the discovery record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Record of NZ commercial gas field discoveries (NZP&M/MBIE); true if no significant discovery in ~20 years, false if a material discovery occurred within that window.

veracity.statement: After that announcement, which was nothing apart from a letter, a big tank, and a promise to keep looking, what happened was that the profits and the shared value of all of those gentailers went up several million dollars.
veracity.explanation: Claims gentailers' share value rose by several million dollars following the Government's announcement — a checkable market-movement claim, load-bearing to her argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZX share price / market capitalisation movements for the listed gentailers around the date of the announcement; true if their value rose materially, false if flat or down.

focus.statement: The one thing I do agree with the Opposition on is that we do need some firming to sit behind and underpin the whole system, and the State has a role in doing that.
focus.explanation: Squarely engages the energy-policy substance — the need for firming capacity and the State's role — rather than attacking the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Until we have more renewable generation and large-scale storage, natural gas is our insurance policy, a stabilising force in an increasingly complex energy system.
focus.explanation: Engages the policy mechanism directly — gas as transitional firming until renewables and storage scale up — with no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That fundamental reform that was promised by the Minister, quite simply, did not materialise.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific commitment (the Minister's promised 'fundamental reform') and holds the Government to account for its non-delivery — on-policy, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The question I want to ask is: if the profits that are baked into those gentailers are reliant upon fossil fuels, how does the Government plan to incentivise investment in renewables?
focus.explanation: A substantive policy question about market design and incentives for renewable investment — engages the mechanism directly with no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It reminds us on a daily basis how out of touch this Government is.
focus.explanation: Content-free tribalism: no policy, measure or outcome named — purely about what the other team is 'really like'. This is the gap Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Firm energy, sustainable and secure, that secures our supply; and clean energy, because geothermal plants produce 7 percent of the emissions of a typical coal plant.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that geothermal electricity plants emit only 7 percent of the emissions of a typical coal plant. This is a specific, load-bearing figure underpinning her 'clean energy' claim, and the sort of comparison that can be checked against emissions-intensity data.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Life-cycle greenhouse-gas emissions intensity of geothermal electricity versus coal generation (e.g. IPCC/IEA figures in gCO2e per kWh); true if geothermal emissions are approximately 7% of a typical coal plant's, false if materially higher or lower.

veracity.statement: We are very pleased to say that this week, “Minister MegaWatts” himself announced that wood energy could replace around 40 percent of fossil fuels process heat by 2015 and displace 300,000 tonnes of coal at Huntly.
veracity.explanation: Relays specific projections attributed to the Government's Wood Energy Strategy announcement — that wood energy could replace ~40% of fossil-fuel process heat and displace 300,000 tonnes of coal at Huntly (the '2015' date is an evident spoken slip). The figures are specific, non-obvious and checkable against the strategy document.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's Wood Energy Strategy announced the week of 2025-10-23; true if it states wood energy could replace about 40% of fossil-fuel process heat and displace ~300,000 tonnes of coal at Huntly, false if those figures are not what the strategy states.
